title: Block 2: Code Review
text:
Part 1: Why code review matters
⏱ ~15 minutes
This morning, in the reproducibility chapter, you ran the many-analysts activity: the same C. elegans reproduction dataset, the same broad question, meaningfully different results from different participants. That illustrated the problem of underspecified methods: analytical decisions that are not documented produce variable, non-transparent science. You then cleaned the raw data and built a documented project.
Code review addresses a related but distinct failure: the code does not actually do what the analyst thinks it does. It is possible to write a fully specified, well-documented analysis plan, implement it in R, and still have the code contain errors that silently produce wrong results. No amount of pre-registration prevents this; only someone actually reading the code can catch it.
The paper for this chapter:
Spend five minutes reading the abstract and Figure 1 now.

title: Block 2: Code Review
text:
Ivimey-Cook, E.R., Pick, J.L., Bairos-Novak, K.R., Culina, A., Gould, E., Grainger, M.J., Marshall, B.M., Moreau, D., Paquet, M., Royauté, R., Sánchez-Tójar, A., Silva, I., & Windecker, S.M. (2023). Implementing code review in the scientific workflow: Insights from ecology and evolutionary biology. Journal of Evolutionary Biology, 36(10), 1347–1356. https://doi.org/10.1111/jeb.14230


Types of coding error
Errors take three forms, all of which are common:
Conceptual: the wrong model for the data type, such as Gaussian errors on offspring counts (which are non-negative integers and often overdispersed); a fixed effect where a random effect is needed; comparing models that are not comparable.
Programmatic: the right model implemented incorrectly, such as selecting columns by position rather than name; an operator-precedence slip that quietly changes which rows are analysed; a column name that breaks on a round-trip through disk.
Syntactic: misspelled function names, wrong argument orders. These at least cause a visible error rather than a silent wrong result.






Tip



Opening poll (post in Slack)
“Have you ever found an error in your own analysis code that had already influenced something — a figure in a draft, a number in a report, a decision?”
A: Yes, in my own code B: Yes, in someone else’s code I tried to reproduce C: Both D: Not yet, but I think it is possible
Keep the results visible. We will return to them.


Quick check


What type of error is this? A Gaussian model fitted to offspring counts.

Conceptual
Programmatic
Syntactic

Conceptual: the wrong model for the data. Offspring counts are non-negative whole numbers and often overdispersed, so a count model fits them better.



What type of error is this? names(dat1)[c(2, 5)] <- ... renames the wrong columns after someone reorders the data file.

Conceptual
Programmatic
Syntactic

Programmatic: the idea (rename these columns) is right, but choosing them by position breaks silently when the column order changes. Rename by name, for example with rename().



True or false? Syntactic errors are usually the least dangerous of the three, because R stops with a visible error.

TRUE
FALSE

True. A misspelled function or a wrong argument usually stops R with an error you can see. Conceptual and programmatic errors often run without complaint and give wrong numbers.

title: Block 2: Code Review
text:
Part 2: The 4Rs framework
⏱ ~20 minutes
Ivimey-Cook et al. (2023) organise what a code reviewer should evaluate around four questions, the 4Rs (Figure 1 of the paper):



The 4Rs of code review (Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023, Figure 1)

#
R
Question
Tagline



1
Reported
Is the code as reported?
Methods and code must match (note in this case we are simply using the code to help us link to the methods)


2
Run
Does the code run?
Code must be executable


3
Reliable
Is the code reliable?
Code runs and completes as intended


4
Reproducible
Are the results reproducible?
Results must be able to be reproduced





Each R in the context of ANALYSIS.R

Reported. A reviewer should be able to hold the methods section in one hand and the code in the other and verify they describe the same analysis. ANALYSIS.R has no header and almost no comments: a reviewer cannot tell what the intended analysis is, why one worm is dropped, or which of the three models that get fitted is meant to be the result. Its variable names (block, total_offspring) also drift from the data dictionary you wrote this morning (B, TO).
Run. Can the code be executed on a different machine, in a clean R session? ANALYSIS.R reads its data from an absolute OneDrive path, and lines 23–24 call libray(), a typo for library(), so the script does not even run to the end. Failing at this stage is common: when Trisovic et al. (2022) re-ran more than 9,000 archived R files, 74% failed on the first attempt.
Reliable. The hardest R. Code can run without error and still produce a wrong result every time. In ANALYSIS.R: an operator-precedence slip changes which worms are analysed; the 9999 “not recorded” sentinel you met this morning is never handled; and a count outcome is fitted with a Gaussian model. None of these throw an error.
Reproducible. Given the same data and code, does re-running produce the reported outputs? ANALYSIS.R fits three models, designates none of them as the answer, saves no model output to disk, and writes a figure called final2.jpg, whose “2” hints at undocumented earlier versions.


Activity: map ANALYSIS.R to the 4Rs (5 minutes)


Open ANALYSIS.R. Without running it, post one specific example for each R in Slack:


Reported: Something a reader could not understand without asking the author

Run: Something that would stop it running on your machine right now

Reliable: Something that could produce a silently wrong result

Reproducible: Something that would prevent recovering the reported numbers



Quick check


Which R does libray(tidyverse) fail first?

Reported
Run
Reliable
Reproducible

Run. libray() is not a function, so R stops at that line and nothing after it runs.



Which R does it fail first? The 9999 sentinel is never handled.

Reported
Run
Reliable
Reproducible

Reliable. The script runs, but every 9999 enters the models as a real count, so the estimates are wrong every time.



Which R does it fail first? Three models are fitted, and none is named as the result.

Reported
Run
Reliable
Reproducible

Reproducible. Without knowing which model is the result, and with nothing saved to disk, nobody can recover the reported numbers.



Which R does it fail first? The script calls the batch column block, but the data dictionary calls it B.

Reported
Run
Reliable
Reproducible

Reported. The code and the documented data no longer describe the same thing, so a reader has to work out the mapping for themselves.

title: Block 2: Code Review
section: Part 3: Performing a structured code review
text:
Part 3: Performing a structured code review
⏱ ~50 minutes
The script to review
ANALYSIS.R from https://osf.io/jgeq9/ is an analysis script for the C. elegans strain × diet experiment, the same experiment you cleaned this morning. It was written for this course, but every problem in it is one we regularly find in real archives. It is reproduced here for reference:

library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
library(stringr)
library(rvest)
library(readr)
library(knitr)
library("data.table")
library(gplots)
library(ggridges)
library(shiny)
library(lme4)
library(rpart)
library(caret)
library(randomForest)
library(glmnet)
library("xgboost")
library("plotly")
libray(tidyverse)
libray(hablar)

dat1 = read.csv("~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofGlasgow/AllFiles/Other Projects/Workshops/REPROCODE_ANALYSIS/celegans_repro_raw.csv")

names(dat1)[c(2, 5)] <- c("block", "total offspring")
dat1$worm_id <- as.numeric(dat1$worm_id)

dat2 <- dat1 %>% filter(worm_id != 5)

full.dat <- dat2[complete.cases(dat2$`total offspring`), ]

write.csv(full.dat, file = "~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofGlasgow/AllFiles/Other Projects/Workshops/REPROCODE_ANALYSIS/celegans_datafinal.csv", row.names = F)

full_dat = read.csv("~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofGlasgow/AllFiles/Other Projects/Workshops/REPROCODE_ANALYSIS/celegans_datafinal.csv")

summary(full_dat)

plot(as.factor(full_dat$strain), full_dat$total_offspring)

full_dat <- full_dat %>%
  convert(fct(worm_id, block, strain, diet)) %>%
  filter(strain == "daf" | strain == "empty_vector" & total_offspring > 0) %>%
  mutate(total_offspring = as.numeric(total_offspring))

m1a <- lmer(total_offspring ~
              + strain
            + diet
            + (1|block),
            data = full_dat)
summary(m1a)

m1b <- lmer(total_offspring ~
              strain * diet
            + (1|block),
            data = full_dat)
summary(m1b)

m1c <- lm(total_offspring ~
            + strain * diet,
          data = full_dat)
summary(m1c)

anova(m1a, m1b, m1c)

Na <- full_dat[complete.cases(full_dat$strain), ]

ggplot(data = Na, aes(x = as.factor(strain), y = total_offspring, colour = as.factor(diet))) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(linetype = "dotted", method = "lm", colour = "black", fill = "light grey") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_boot", geom = "errorbar", shape = 0, width = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_boot", geom = "point", shape = 0, width = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Strain", y = "Total Offspring", colour = "Diet")

ggsave(filename = "final2.jpg", path = "~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofGlasgow/AllFiles/Other Projects/Workshops/REPROCODE_ANALYSIS/", dpi = 300, device = "jpg")







Note



A bridge from this morning. ANALYSIS.R analyses the same experiment as the reproducibility chapter, but its author used different names: block for B, and total_offspring for TO. That drift between code and data dictionary is itself a small Reported problem, but to keep the review readable we use the script’s own names below.


Step 1: First read (3 minutes)
Read the script end to end without annotating. Ask yourself:

What does this script try to do?
What is the intended analysis?
What immediately strikes you as wrong?
Could the style be improved? Would an automatic code formatter such as styler or Air help?

Then move to the checklist.
The 4Rs review checklist
Work through the script systematically. Record ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail / ⚠️ Unclear for each item, and write one sentence describing the issue.



4Rs review checklist for ANALYSIS.R

R
Review item
Verdict
Note (one sentence)



Reported


Reported
Could a reader tell what the intended analysis is, without asking the author?




Reported
Is the worm_id != 5 exclusion described and justified?




Reported
Is it stated which of m1a / m1b / m1c is the reported model?




Reported
Do the variable names match the project's data dictionary?




Reported
Are packages documented with version numbers anywhere?




Run


Run
Does the script use absolute file paths?




Run
Would the script parse and run on a clean machine in a fresh session?




Run
Are all loaded packages actually used, and all function calls spelled correctly?




Run
Is there a README explaining how to set up and run the project?




Reliable


Reliable
Is the analysis sample selected with correct use of filter arguments?




Reliable
Are data columns selected by name rather than by position?




Reliable
Is the 9999 'not recorded' sentinel handled before modelling?




Reliable
Is total_offspring (a count) modelled with an appropriate distribution?




Reliable
Does anova() compare models that are actually comparable?




Reliable
Are model diagnostics (residuals, singularity) checked anywhere?




Reproducible


Reproducible
Is it unambiguous which model's results are the reported result?




Reproducible
Are model outputs saved to disk, or only printed to the console?




Reproducible
Is the saved figure named meaningfully and reproducibly?




Reproducible
Is sessionInfo() called, or renv used?







Step 2: Complete the checklist (15 minutes)


Activity: complete the checklist (15 minutes)


Work through ANALYSIS.R against every item. Record your verdict and a one-sentence note.
Then post in Slack:

Your verdict for the three items you think are most consequential
One issue you found that is not on the checklist





Solution

The problems revealed



Issues in ANALYSIS.R

#
R
Lines
Issue
Severity



P1
Run
23–24
libray(tidyverse) and libray(hablar) are typos for library(). R throws 'could not find function libray' and execution stops here, if it gets this far (see P3). (library(lme4) is also loaded twice — lines 1 and 16.)
Critical


P2
Run
26, 35, 37, 78
Absolute OneDrive paths in read.csv(), write.csv(), the re-read, and ggsave(). The script only runs on the original author's machine.
Critical


P3
Run / Reported
1–24
About 22 library() calls, the great majority unused (xgboost, glmnet, caret, randomForest, rpart, rvest, shiny, plotly, gplots, ggridges, ...). Slows loading, hides the real dependencies, and any one missing package aborts the script: on a machine without gplots, it stops at line 13. One real dependency is hidden altogether: stat_summary(fun.data = 'mean_cl_boot') needs Hmisc, which is never loaded. No versions recorded.
High


P4
Reliable
45
Operator-precedence bug. filter(strain == 'daf' | strain == 'empty_vector' & total_offspring > 0) is meant to drop impossible negative counts, but & binds tighter than |, so R reads it as daf OR (empty_vector AND count above 0). The check only applies to empty_vector worms, and the one negative count (TO = -46) belongs to a daf worm, so it goes into the models.
Critical


P5
Reliable
28, 35–37, 41, 43–46
Line 28 names column 5 'total offspring', with a space. After write.csv() then read.csv() (lines 35–37) it becomes total.offspring, so full_dat$total_offspring on line 41 silently returns NULL (the plot shows strain counts, not offspring), and the pipeline at lines 43–46 stops with 'object total_offspring not found'.
Critical


P6
Reliable
28
names(dat1)[c(2, 5)] renames columns by position. If the column order ever changes, the wrong columns are renamed — with no error.
High


P7
Reliable / Reported
31, 45
Rows disappear without a word. filter(worm_id != 5) drops worm 5 with no reason given, and also drops the two worms with a missing worm_id. The exact-match strain filter (line 45) quietly loses the 24 'DAF' and 3 'empty_vector ' rows, while 'eodf' stays in as a third diet level and the duplicated rows are never removed.
High


P8
Reliable
33
complete.cases() on 'total offspring' removes only NA. It does NOT handle the 9999 'not recorded' sentinel from the raw data (reproducibility chapter): all three 9999s enter the models as real offspring counts, and the empty_vector/EODF mean jumps from about 185 to about 590.
Critical


P9
Reliable
66
anova(m1a, m1b, m1c) puts two lmer models and an lm in one call. R refits the mixed models with ML (with only a brief message), reorders all three by number of parameters and tests each against the next. That chain compares m1a with m1c, which are not nested (they differ in both fixed and random effects), so that row's test is meaningless; no hypothesis says which comparison matters.
Critical


P10
Reliable
48–64
total_offspring is a count, but all three models are Gaussian (lmer / lm). A count GLMM (Poisson or negative binomial) is not considered; no residual or distributional checks.
High


P11
Reliable
70–76
geom_smooth(method = 'lm') over a categorical x (as.factor(strain)) with colour groups draws nothing at all: each strain × diet group has only one x value, so there is no line to fit. Both stat_summary() calls pass a parameter their geom does not use (shape to the errorbar, width to the point); ggplot2 ignores them with a warning.
Medium


P12
Reproducible
48–66, 78
Three models are fitted but none is designated as the result and no model output is saved to disk. The figure is saved as final2.jpg (the '2' implies undocumented earlier versions). No sessionInfo(), no renv, no versions; full.dat / full_dat / Na are confusingly similar names, and after a run the folder holds two different 'final' data files, celegans_repro_final.csv and the script's own celegans_datafinal.csv.
Medium





The three that matter most:


P1 stops the script at line 23 (libray), but fixing it doesn’t make the script right.

P4 is the dangerous one: the author did try to remove impossible counts, the code looks fine, and the precedence slip quietly lets the −46 through.

P8 is this morning’s 9999: complete.cases() only drops NA, so every “not recorded” worm enters the models with 9,999 offspring.

Once the crashes (P1, P2, P5, and any missing packages from P3) are fixed, the script runs, and P4, P7, P8, P10 and P12 make its numbers wrong without a single error.


Step 3: Write the review (12 minutes)


Activity: write the review (12 minutes)


Write a structured code review of ANALYSIS.R as if emailing it to the author. Be kind but direct. Organise by R, reference line numbers, and suggest a concrete fix for each issue. Use this template:
CODE REVIEW: ANALYSIS.R
Reviewer: [your name]  |  Date: [today]  |  Approx. time: [X] minutes

SUMMARY
[2 sentences: overall impression, most important finding]

REPORTED
- Line [X]: ...

RUN
- Line [X]: ...

RELIABLE
- Line [X]: ...

REPRODUCIBLE
- Line [X]: ...

RECOMMENDATION
[ ] Ready to submit  [ ] Minor revision  [ ] Major revision required
When done, paste your SUMMARY and your RECOMMENDATION in Slack.








Note



Debrief (5 minutes):

Did everyone identify P8 (the 9999 sentinel)? This is the same lesson as this morning, and the error with the largest effect on the result, yet the code runs without complaint. What does that say about automatic testing vs human review?
Did anyone give “ready to submit”? P4 and P8 together mean that, beyond being poorly documented, the analysis gives a numerically wrong central estimate. Would this have passed peer review as written?
P12: which of the three models is the answer? Is there any way a journal reviewer reading only the paper would catch this without seeing the code?



Quick check


filter(strain == "daf" | strain == "empty_vector" & total_offspring > 0) meets a daf worm with total_offspring of −46. Is the worm kept or dropped?

Kept
Dropped

Kept. & binds more tightly than |, so R reads the filter as daf | (empty_vector & total_offspring > 0). The check only applies to empty_vector worms, so every daf worm is kept, including the one with −46 offspring.



Which filter does what the author intended (both strains, and only positive counts)?

strain %in% c('daf', 'empty_vector') & total_offspring > 0strain == 'daf' | (strain == 'empty_vector' & total_offspring > 0)strain == 'daf' | strain == 'empty_vector' | total_offspring > 0strain == c('daf', 'empty_vector') & total_offspring > 0


%in% keeps both strains, and & total_offspring > 0 then applies to all of them. The second option is how R actually reads the original. The last one compares row by row against a recycled c('daf', 'empty_vector'), so it runs without an error (at most a recycling warning) and quietly drops about half the worms.



x <- c(250, NA, 9999). What does sum(complete.cases(x)) return?


2. complete.cases() only drops NA. 9999 is an ordinary number, so it counts as complete, which is exactly why P8 slips through.



Line 28 renames column 5 to total offspring (with a space). After write.csv() and read.csv(), what is the column called?


total.offspring. read.csv() cleans the header with make.names(), which turns the space into a dot. The script then asks for total_offspring, which does not exist.



True or false? In the original figure, geom_smooth(method = "lm") draws one line per diet across the two strains.

TRUE
FALSE

False. With a categorical x, each strain × diet group has only one x value, so there is no line to fit and geom_smooth() draws nothing.

title: Block 2: Code Review
text:
Part 4: Fixing the script
⏱ ~30 minutes
Most of the twelve problems disappear when the script is rewritten as a plain, linear, well-commented analysis: relative paths, a documented sample, the sentinel handled, one model fitted and saved on purpose. No clever functions needed: a flat script a reviewer can read top to bottom is the easiest to check.
A corrected version
Here is ANALYSIS.R rewritten. It also slots into the project structure you built this morning: the cleaning happens in 01_data_cleaning.R, so this script reads the cleaned file and only analyses. Each numbered section names the problems (P1–P12) it resolves, and it uses the documented data-dictionary names (TO, B).

# analysis/02_analysis.R  -- corrected analysis script
# Author:  [your name]
# Date:    [today]
# Purpose: C. elegans total-offspring analysis -- daf-2 RNAi x diet
#
# Input:   data/processed/celegans_clean.csv   (produced by 01_data_cleaning.R)
# Output:  results/model_summary.csv
#          figures/offspring_by_strain.png
#          results/sessionInfo.txt
#
# Pre-specified model (as in the write-up, celegans_analysis.Rmd, on osf.io/jgeq9/):
#   TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B)        TO = total offspring (a count)

# -- Packages: load only what is used --------------------------------- fixes P1, P3
library(tidyverse)    # readr, dplyr, ggplot2
library(lme4)         # glmer.nb
library(broom.mixed)  # tidy() for mixed models
library(here)         # project-relative paths -- fixes P2

# -- 1. Load the cleaned data ----------------------------------------- fixes P2, P8
# Cleaning -- including dropping the 9999 "not recorded" sentinel -- is done
# in 01_data_cleaning.R. This script only analyses; it never re-cleans.
dat <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "celegans_clean.csv"),
                show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    strain = factor(strain, levels = c("empty_vector", "daf")),
    diet   = factor(diet),
    B      = factor(B)
  )

# -- 2. Select the analysis sample ------------------------------------ fixes P4, P7
# No worm is dropped here without a reason (P7): every exclusion is made,
# and logged, in 01_data_cleaning.R. Flagged values are kept there, marked
# flag_implausible, and left out here, in one visible line.
# Keep the two strains of interest AND require diet to be recorded.
# %in% plus a separate condition is the fix for P4: the original wrote
#   strain == "daf" | strain == "empty_vector" & total_offspring > 0
# which R reads as  daf | (empty_vector & count > 0)  -- not the intent.
# (Impossible counts such as -46 are now removed, and logged, in cleaning.)
dat <- dat |>
  filter(strain %in% c("empty_vector", "daf") & !is.na(diet)) |>
  # pre-specified: flagged values stay out until verified;
  # rerun without this line as a sensitivity check
  filter(!flag_implausible)

# -- 3. Fit ONE pre-specified model ----------------------------------- fixes P9, P10
# TO is a count, so a Gaussian lmer is the wrong family. Fit one
# negative-binomial GLMM (handles the overdispersion typical of brood
# counts) and report it -- no comparing across model classes.
m <- glmer.nb(TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B), data = dat)

# -- 4. Diagnostics --------------------------------------------------- fixes P10
plot(m)                                   # residuals vs fitted
if (isSingular(m)) warning("Model is singular -- check the batch (B) random effect.")

# -- 5. Save the reported model --------------------------------------- fixes P12
write_csv(tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE),
          here("results", "model_summary.csv"))

# -- 6. Figure: categorical x, so show data + group means ------------- fixes P11
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = strain, y = TO, colour = diet)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.3) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Strain (RNAi)", y = "Total offspring", colour = "Diet") +
  theme_classic()

ggsave(here("figures", "offspring_by_strain.png"), p,
       width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)

# -- 7. Record the computational environment -------------------------- fixes P12
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()),
           here("results", "sessionInfo.txt"))







Note



Notice what this rewrite does not do: it does not wrap every step in a bespoke function. For a script this size, a flat sequence of clearly commented blocks is easier to review than a set of custom functions, because the reviewer sees exactly what happens, in order, with nothing hidden behind a call. Reach for a function only when you genuinely repeat a block three or more times.




Activity: map the fix to the problems (10 minutes)


Working from the corrected script above and the P1–P12 table:

For each numbered section (1–7), name which problems it fixes. Two of the twelve are not fixed by this script — which two, and why? (Hint: both happen in the renaming step at the top of the original).
Section 1 of the corrected script reads celegans_clean.csv instead of re-cleaning the raw file. How does separating cleaning (01_data_cleaning.R) from analysis (02_analysis.R) make both scripts easier to review?
The corrected script fits one model and saves it. What did we lose by dropping m1a/m1b/m1c, and is that a loss worth accepting?

Post your answers in Slack.


Tidy the project, not just the script
ANALYSIS.R reads its data from one folder and writes its outputs back to the same folder. Look at what is actually in that folder on the OSF page: the data files, ANALYSIS.R, an old_code.R, celegans_analysis.Rmd and its rendered .html, and five loose image files, all in one flat directory.
That is exactly the messy structure you saw in Part 4 of the reproducibility chapter, and the folder structure you built there fixes it. Three things a reviewer should flag:


old_code.R should not be there. It is a superseded earlier version. Dead code left in the project root invites a collaborator to run the wrong script. Move it to an archive/ folder, or, once the project is under version control, delete it: Git keeps the old version.

The five image files are loose. Generated outputs belong in figures/, produced by the code, not committed by hand next to the scripts.

There is no README. You built one this morning in the reproducibility chapter, and that same README.md belongs in the project root here. It is what lets a reviewer answer the Reported questions at all.

Re-using the structure you created in the reproducibility chapter (data/raw, data/processed, analysis/, figures/, results/) makes the project navigable and makes the Run check (“can I tell which script to run, and in what order?”) answerable at a glance.
Reviewing the whole archive: the SORTEE stages
The 4Rs are a lens for reviewing a script. The SORTEE Guidelines (Pick et al. 2026) provide the complementary lens for reviewing a whole archive (the data, the code and the metadata together) as six ordered Stages of Review:



The six SORTEE Stages of Review (Pick et al. 2026)

Stage
Stage of review
Goal it serves



1
Data are archived and adhere to the FAIR principles
Data re-use


2
Archived data correspond to the data reported in the manuscript
Data re-use


3
Code is archived and adheres to the FAIR principles
Transparency


4
Archived code corresponds to the workflow reported in the manuscript
Transparency


5
Archived code runs with the archived data
Reproducibility


6
Results can be computationally reproduced by running the code
Reproducibility





The stages build on each other: Stages 1–2 deliver data re-use, Stages 1–4 deliver transparency, and all six together deliver full computational reproducibility.
DCQC, the SORTEE Data and Code Quality Control Shiny app (https://github.com/SORTEE/DCQC), does not check anything automatically. It is a structured walk-through: it takes a reviewer (a journal data editor, or you, reviewing your own archive before submission) through these six stages in order, recording the outcome of each. Think of it as the counterpart, for the whole data-and-code package, of the 4Rs checklist you used on the script.






Note



What no tool can do for you. DCQC structures the review; it does not pass judgement. Stage 5 (“does the code run?”) and Stage 6 (“do the results reproduce?”) still require you to run the code. And the 4Rs Reliable question (does the code do what the analyst intended?) is the one neither DCQC nor an AI assistant can answer for you. That is the human reading you did in Part 3.




Exercise: which stage does it pass? (5 minutes)


Imagine the REPROCODE_ANALYSIS folder from this morning was shared with a paper exactly as it was: zipped and put on the author’s website, with no README and no licence.
Work through the six SORTEE stages in order. Post in Slack the last stage it passes, and the smallest set of changes that would get it through Stage 3.




Solution

It fails at Stage 1. The data are online, but a personal website gives no persistent DOI, there is no licence, and without a README there is no metadata to say what the files contain. To reach Stage 3 it needs the TADA! steps from this morning: deposit the data and code in a repository such as Zenodo (with a DOI for each), add separate licences for code and data, and add a README. Stage 2 and Stage 4 also need someone to check the archive against the paper, and Stage 5 needs ANALYSIS.R to actually run, which it does not.

Quick check


Why does the corrected script use glmer.nb() rather than glmer(family = poisson)?

Poisson models cannot include random effectsBrood counts are usually overdispersed (more variable than a Poisson allows), and a negative binomial models that extra variationglmer.nb() always gives smaller p-valuesNegative-binomial models do not need the data to be counts


Counts like these usually vary more than a Poisson model allows. The negative binomial has an extra parameter for that variation; a Poisson fit would give over-confident standard errors.



An archive’s code runs on the archived data, but its numbers do not match the paper. Up to which SORTEE stage has it passed?


Stage 5: the archived code runs with the archived data. It fails Stage 6, computationally reproducing the results.



True or false? DCQC runs your code automatically and tells you whether the results reproduce.

TRUE
FALSE

False. DCQC is a structured walk-through that records the reviewer’s verdict at each stage. Someone still has to run the code and compare the numbers.

title: Block 2: Code Review
text:
Part 5: Building the review habit
⏱ ~15 minutes
Setting up a code review group
Most code review never happens because no one organises it. Ivimey-Cook et al. (2023), drawing on their experience building SORTEE’s peer code review club, set out five practical considerations for getting a group off the ground. They aren’t novel, but they’re the ones that decide whether a group survives past meeting three or quietly dies.


Start collaborating early. Review works best when it’s continuous, not a one-off pre-submission check. Build in regular sessions from project kickoff and use GitHub issues or pull requests to anchor discussion to specific lines rather than vague impressions.

Set a clear goal for each session. “Learn together” and “find the bug in my analysis before I submit” need different time, different reviewers and different rules. Decide which one you’re doing before people show up.

Normalise errors and make it judgement-free. There is no such thing as bad code (Barnes 2010) and there are usually multiple defensible ways to solve the same problem (Silberzahn et al. 2018; Gould et al. 2025). The fastest way to kill a group is to let it become a place where the most confident voice rewrites everyone else’s style.

Mind the group size. Small (even 1-on-1) is better for focused review of specific code; larger groups work for general principles and discussion. Pick on purpose.

Think about credit up front. A reviewer who catches a meaningful bug deserves more than a thank-you: MeRIT acknowledgement (Nakagawa et al. 2023) or co-authorship where the fix changes the conclusions. Agree the default before the first review, not after.







Tip



Plan your group (~5 min — post in Slack)
Without overthinking it, commit to specifics on the following five questions. Two-line answers are fine; the point is to write them down, because “we should review each other’s code” without specifics is a sentence that ages badly.


Who: name 2–4 people you’d actually invite in the next month.

What: readability/learning, or pre-submission error-checking? (Pick one for the first meeting.)

When and where: cadence and platform (in-person, Zoom, async via GitHub).

First case: whose code goes first, and what’s the explicit scope of that review (which of the four Rs)?

Credit: what’s your default acknowledgement, and what triggers escalating to MeRIT or co-authorship?

When you’ve written your five, post the one you’re least sure about and we’ll workshop it briefly as a group.


Online lab culture
For groups working entirely online, the pull request model on GitHub provides the most practical structure for code review. The author opens a PR, writes a description explaining what the code does and why, and requests review. The reviewer comments on specific lines. Nothing merges until approved. We cover this in the GitHub session tomorrow.
Quick check


In your review group, one senior member rewrites everyone’s code into their own style. Which consideration is being ignored?

Start collaborating earlyMind the group sizeNormalise errors and make it judgement-freeThink about credit up front


Normalise errors and make it judgement-free. There are usually several defensible ways to write the same code, and a group where the most confident voice rewrites everyone’s style soon stops meeting.



True or false? It is best to decide how to credit a reviewer after the review, once you know how much they found.

TRUE
FALSE

False. Agree the default (acknowledgement, MeRIT, or co-authorship when a fix changes the conclusions) before the first review, so nobody has to negotiate after a bug is found.









Tip



Closing reflection (post in Slack)
Return to the opening poll. Has anyone’s answer changed?
Then: “Based on ANALYSIS.R — which of the 12 problems is most likely to appear in code from your own field? Why?”
And: “The one change I will make to my workflow before my next submission is…”

title: Block 2: Code Review
text:
Glossary




Term
Definition



4Rs
Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible — evaluation criteria for code review (Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023)


Reported
Code matches the methods; packages and versions documented


Run
Code executes from a clean session on any machine


Reliable
Code does what the author intended; no silent errors


Reproducible
Running the code produces the outputs stated in the paper


Operator precedence
The order R applies operators; & binds tighter than |, so a | b & c means a | (b & c) — a frequent source of silent filter() bugs


Sentinel value
A number used to encode a special meaning (e.g. 9999 = 'not recorded'); must be handled before any model is fitted


Count GLMM
A generalised linear mixed model for count outcomes (Poisson or negative binomial); appropriate for offspring counts, unlike a Gaussian lmer


isSingular()
lme4 function checking whether a model has converged to a singular fit (random-effect variance ~ 0)


SORTEE Stages of Review
The SORTEE Guidelines' six-stage framework for reviewing an archive, from data archiving (Stage 1) to computational reproducibility (Stage 6)


DCQC
SORTEE Data and Code Quality Control Shiny app; a structured walk-through of the six SORTEE Stages of Review — it organises a review, it does not automate one


Pull request
GitHub mechanism for proposing changes; a natural structure for code review in online collaborative groups

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
How we see data
Our visual system did not evolve to read graphs. Some visual features are detected before conscious attention engages: a red dot among grey dots, a single triangle in a sea of circles, an unusually large shape in a field of small ones. This is called pre-attentive processing (Healey and Enns, 2012). If you encode important information as a feature the eye picks up automatically, readers see it without having to search. Encoding the same information as a subtle change in line style or a slightly different shade requires the reader to look for it.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Game: spot it
We’ll go through the tabs one at a time. Each plot hides one odd point among 80: type found in the chat as soon as you spot it, and don’t click ahead to the next tab.


Colour
Shape
Colour and shape, mixed up


































Watch the chat: the colour target gets a flood of “found”s almost instantly, the shape target a moment later. In the third tab the odd point is the only grey triangle, and no single feature gives it away, so everyone has to check points one by one. This is the cost of making readers combine features (a conjunction search).

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Game: guess the value
Each round shows five values. A is always the same. Your job: what percentage of A is B? Post your guess in the chat before you check it in the box. One round at a time, no peeking at the next tab.


Round 1
Round 2
Round 3
Round 4











B is what % of A?  (within 5 points counts)










B is what % of A?  (from here on, within 10 points counts)










B is what % of A? 










B is what % of A?  (use the key: white is 0, black is 100)





What just happened?

The answers were 62%, 38%, 45% and 71%. Look back at the chat: Round 1 guesses are usually tight, and they spread out with each round after that. In Round 3 most guesses are too high, because we underestimate differences in area: the small circle looks closer in size to the big one than it really is. In Round 4, even with a key, the shades are hard to place.
You have just played a version of Cleveland and McGill’s (1984) experiment (they tested bars and pie slices; Rounds 3 and 4 go further). People read the same ratio most accurately as position on a common scale, then length, angle, area, and last shading and colour saturation. Mackinlay (1986) extended the ranking to categorical data: position is still best, but colour hue rises to second. Shape is weaker but useful as a redundant cue.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
The encoding hierarchy








The practical rule is: assign your most important variable to the highest-ranked encoding available to you. For two continuous variables, both go to position (a scatter plot). For a continuous variable grouped by a category, position handles the continuous variable and colour hue handles the category, with shape added redundantly for accessibility.


Colour
Shape
Both




penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm,
             colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)",
       y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm,
            shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)",
       y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       shape = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm,
             colour = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)",
       y = "Flipper length (mm)",
       colour = "Species",
       shape = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










Two continuous variables to position (rank 1), one categorical to colour hue (rank 2 for categorical data), with shape added as a redundant cue. The figure works on a colour monitor, in greyscale print, and for a reader with colour vision deficiency. Treat this as the minimum for every figure.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Colour as a tool
Colour hue is the second-most powerful encoding for categorical data, and it is pre-attentive, so readers pick it up without searching. It is also the encoding most often misused. Three palette types exist, each for a different data structure:







Palette type
Data structure
Example use



Qualitative
Discrete groups with no inherent order
Species, treatment arm


Sequential
Continuous, running in one direction from a minimum
Gene expression, density


Diverging
Continuous, with a meaningful midpoint
Log fold-change, temperature anomaly











Using the wrong type for the data structure is one of the most common errors. A sequential palette applied to categorical data implies an ordering that does not exist. A categorical palette applied to a continuous variable conceals the ordering that does exist.
The package colorspace (Zeileis et al., 2020) provides palette generators for all three types with documented design rationale, and is the project default for palette construction. The Dark2 palette ships directly:

# Categorical (Dark2): for discrete groups with no order
colorspace::swatchplot(
  colorspace::qualitative_hcl(8, palette = "Dark2")
)







The same package provides scale_*_discrete_qualitative(), scale_*_continuous_sequential(), and scale_*_continuous_diverging() functions that integrate directly with ggplot2. Prefer these over manual hex vectors.
Quick check: which palette type?

Treatment arm (control, drug A, drug B): 
Qualitative
Sequential
Diverging

Change in body mass after a season, where 0 = no change: 
Qualitative
Sequential
Diverging

Number of eggs per nest: 
Qualitative
Sequential
Diverging

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Accessibility
Roughly 8% of men have some form of colour vision deficiency (Sharpe et al., 1999); red-green is by far the most common. Using red and green to distinguish two groups will fail for a non-trivial fraction of any audience. The Okabe-Ito palette was designed to remain distinguishable under deuteranopia and protanopia (Okabe and Ito, 2008), and the viridis palette family is perceptually uniform under colour vision deficiency and in greyscale.
Beyond palette choice, the main rule is redundant encoding: never let colour be the only cue distinguishing groups. Use shape redundantly for points, linetype redundantly for lines, and direct labelling wherever it is legible (we will cover direct labelling in Block 4).
The colorBlindness package gives you the verification step. colorBlindness::cvdPlot() produces, by default, a four-panel simulation: the original (“normal vision”), deuteranopia, protanopia, and a desaturated (greyscale) version. This lets you see whether the figure still works when colour fails. Extra “enhanced” panels can be requested through its layout argument; note that it does not simulate tritanopia.

fig <- penguins_complete |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_minimal()

colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig)







Tip



After the workshop, run cvdPlot() on three or four figures from your own thesis chapter or recent paper. Be honest about which ones fail.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Data-ink ratio
Tufte (1983) introduced data-ink ratio: the proportion of a figure’s visual elements that actually encode data, as opposed to decoration, borders, gridlines, shadows, and three-dimensional effects that exist for their own sake. High data-ink ratio means most of the visual complexity of the figure carries information.
The default ggplot2 theme_grey() already fails this test: a grey panel background and white gridlines exist purely as decoration. Move to theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), or a project-specific theme function as your default.






Warning



Avoid theme_grey() (the ggplot2 default) in any figure intended for human consumption. Set theme_minimal(base_size = 12) or theme_classic(base_size = 12) as your project baseline.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Graph crimes
A figure that violates these principles distorts what the data actually say. Five recurring crimes are worth recognising on sight:










Truncated bar chart axes. A bar encodes magnitude as length from a baseline. If the axis does not start at zero, the visual ratio between bars is no longer the data ratio.

Manipulating the y-axis. Compressed or expanded vertical ranges can make tiny effects look enormous or hide real effects.

Cherry-picking time ranges. Choosing a window of time that supports a story while ignoring the surrounding data.

Wrong chart for the data. Pie charts for many categories; line charts for unordered categorical data; dual y-axes pretending two arbitrary scales are commensurable.

Convention violations. Inverted colour scales (light = high); inverted y-axes; latitude on the x-axis. Readers bring expectations, and figures that violate them mislead.

A bonus crime: spurious correlation. Two variables with a strong correlation may have no causal relationship at all. Showing a strong correlation without acknowledging the confounders is a misrepresentation of evidence.
Warm-up: graph crimes


Exercise: name the crime (3 minutes)


For each figure below, write one line in the form problem → fix (e.g. “truncated axis → start at zero”), and say whether the problem is one of distortion (the visual misrepresents the data) or omission (the figure leaves out something the reader needs). Post your lines in Slack, then compare them with the verdicts below.




Example 1
Example 2
























Bonus. Look closely at the error bars.










The verdicts



Example 1: guilty of distortion. The y-axis starts at 80, so Japan’s 84 looks twice the height of Spain’s 82 when the real difference is under 3%. The 15-colour legend adds nothing the axis labels could not. Sentence: start the axis at zero, or show points on a sensible range, and drop the legend.

Example 2: guilty of distortion. The axis starts at 120, so a $123M opening looks almost nothing next to $177M. Sentence: bars from zero, or a dot plot with labelled values.

Bonus: guilty of everything. The “error bars” are the capital letter T typed above each bar. They show no variability at all, on top of a dynamite plot that hides the raw data. Sentence: plot the raw points with a real interval.


Exercise: fix a graph-crime scene


Fix the crime scene (12 minutes)


The code below was found at a crime scene. It uses chickwts, a dataset built into R: the weight of chicks after six weeks on one of six feed supplements. Copy it into RStudio and run it. There are at least eight graph crimes in it.


Investigate (4 min). List every crime you can find, then post your list in Slack.

Rehabilitate (8 min). Rewrite the code into an honest, accessible figure in your own RStudio.

Check. Post a screenshot of your fixed figure in Slack, then go through the case file below: which crimes did you spot, which did you fix, and which did you miss? We’ll put a few fixed figures on screen and talk through the choices.


chickwts |>
  group_by(feed) |>
  summarise(mean_weight = mean(weight), se = sd(weight) / sqrt(n())) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = feed, y = mean_weight, fill = feed)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_weight - se, ymax = mean_weight + se), width = 0.2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(150, 350)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rainbow(6)) +
  labs(x = "feed", y = "mean_weight") +
  theme_grey()





Case file: the crimes and a rehabilitated figure



Dynamite plot. Bars of means hide the 71 individual chicks.

Truncated axis. The bars start at 150 g, so horsebean looks a fraction of casein’s weight; the real ratio is about half.

Undefined error bars. They are ± 1 SE, but nothing says so.

Rainbow palette. Not colour-blind safe (red vs green), and the lightness jumps around.

Redundant legend. Colour repeats the x-axis, so the legend is pure eye-travel.

Unordered categories. Alphabetical order hides the ranking.

Variable names as labels. “mean_weight” with no units.

theme_grey(). The grey panel fails the data-ink test.


chickwts |>
  mutate(feed = fct_reorder(feed, weight, .fun = median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weight, y = feed)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, colour = "grey45") +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 23,
               size = 3.5, fill = "#D95F02") +
  labs(x = "Chick weight at six weeks (g)", y = "Feed supplement",
       caption = "Points: individual chicks. Diamonds: medians.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Every chick is visible, the feeds are ranked, there is one colour with a job (the median), the axis has units, and no legend is needed. Because these are points rather than bars, the axis does not need to start at zero.

title: Block 2: Choosing the right figure
text:
The chart-type table
Data: penguins_complete from Block 1’s setup chunk, which is palmerpenguins::penguins without its incomplete rows (Which penguins?).
Before anything else, the structure of your data determines the chart type. Variable count and variable type narrow the choice. The table below is a guide rather than a rule: your scientific question may demand something else, but you should be able to justify it.
A few rules are worth memorising: no pie charts (use a labelled proportion); no 3D effects of any kind; no dual y-axes (use two panels instead); no dynamite plots (bar charts of means with error bars) where raw data are available, so show a raincloud or strip plot instead (Weissgerber et al., 2015).
Chart chooser. Use the table to pick a default.

Wing length of 40 butterflies from each of three sites:

Daily soil temperature over a year at two field stations:

Line chart, one line per group. A continuous variable over time: one line per station shows the seasonal pattern and lets readers compare the stations directly.

Heatmap of counts. Counts in a grid of two categorical variables: a heatmap shows the whole table at once. Dual axes and 3D bars distort the comparison.

title: Block 2: Choosing the right figure
text:
Descriptive vs explanatory framing
Every figure communicates at two levels: it presents the data, and it makes an argument. The framing of the title and the legend determines which level the reader engages with first.
A descriptive title states what the figure shows in neutral language: “Body mass of three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago”. The reader is shown the data and invited to interpret.
An explanatory title states what the figure means: “Gentoo penguins are substantially heavier than Adelie and Chinstrap”. The reader is told the conclusion and invited to verify it from the data.
Neither is wrong. The choice is determined by the audience. Journal figures and lab reports use descriptive framing because the reader is expected to bring their own judgement and the figure legend below carries the necessary methodological detail. Talks, posters, and public engagement use explanatory framing because the reader has limited time, attention, or technical background to derive the conclusion themselves.

title: Block 2: Choosing the right figure
text:
Audience design
The same finding becomes a different figure for different audiences. The table below summarises the design choices that should change with context:









Element
Journal / lab report
Poster
Talk
Public engagement



Title above figure
No
Yes (explanatory)
Yes (explanatory)
Yes (explanatory)


Figure legend below
Yes (four elements)
Optional, abbreviated
No
No

Where it does not break convention
Yes
Yes
Yes

No

Yes

Sparingly
Yes

Base font size
12pt (floor)
