title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Block 1: framing
This block introduces the two words you will use all day, the three tools and how they differ, what a large language model is, and why its context window matters. It ends with a short discussion and a quiz.
⏱ ~20 minutes: presentation, a short discussion and a quiz, while any set-up problems are sorted out.
Assistants and agents
Two words recur all day. An assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. is any AI tool that helps you write or understand code. An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. is an assistant that acts: it reads your project and, if you let it, edits files and runs commands. Claude Code and Posit Assistant are agents; a chat window that only answers is not. To see how one works inside, you build a small one yourself in Block 6.
Three tools, and the models behind them
The course uses three tools. They differ in where you type, what they can read and what they may do.



Claude Code: the main tool all day


Type in the Terminal tab


it reads


Your project folder and the output of its own commands, but not your R console


and may


Edit files and run commands, asking first in Manual mode




Posit Assistant: the alternative in most blocks


Type in its chat pane in RStudio or Positron


it reads


Project files and your live R session, including the names and types of your objects


and may


Edit files and run R code in your session, as its mode allows




GitHub Copilot in the editor: self-study


Type code in a script


it reads


Your open files


and offers


Grey suggestions you accept with Tab or ignore




The Copilot cloud agent: self-study


Write a task on github.com


it reads


Your repository, on GitHub’s servers


and returns


A pull request for you to review



Each row reads from left to right: where you type, what the tool reads, and what it may do. The more a tool reads and does, the more there is to check.


A tool is not a model. The tool decides where you type, what it can read and what it may do. It then sends your request, with the context it has gathered, to a large language modelA model trained on a large body of text, code included, that predicts the next fragment of text from what came before. Claude, GPT and Gemini are families of large language models; tools such as Claude Code, Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot send your requests to one., which writes the answer.


You type a request


into


The tool (Claude Code, Posit Assistant or Copilot), which adds the context it has read


and sends it all over the internet to


The model (for example Claude, GPT or Gemini), which writes the reply


The reply comes back through the tool, which shows it to you or asks you to approve an action. Claude is a family of models: Claude Code is one tool that uses them, and Posit Assistant and Copilot can use Claude models too.










Tool
Where you use it
Models it can use
In this course



Claude Code
The Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron
Anthropic’s Claude models
The main tool, in every block from Block 2


Posit Assistant
A chat pane inside RStudio or Positron
Posit AI, or a provider key you add, such as an Anthropic API key
The alternative in most blocks: see each block’s Using another tool callout


GitHub Copilot
Inline suggestions in the editor; the cloud agent on github.com
A choice of models, including Claude, GPT and Gemini
The two self-study pages only



You do not need strong opinions about which model is best. You only need to know that the choice exists and changes the output.
What is a large language model?
A large language model (LLM) predicts the next fragment of text from what came before. It has learnt from a large share of the public internet, code included. Every tool today is built on one. Models differ in code quality and in how often they invent functions that do not exist. If a model gives you consistently poor suggestions and your plan lets you switch, try another: switching is a cheap experiment.
Model and effort level. Two settings change what you get. The model is which LLM answers: larger models, such as Opus, are more capable and cost more per token; smaller ones, such as Sonnet and Haiku, are faster and cheaper. The effort levelHow much a model reasons before it answers. In Claude Code it runs from low to max; a higher level can help with hard problems, but it is slower and uses more tokens. sets how much the model thinks before it answers: higher effort can help with hard problems, but it is slower and uses more tokens. The defaults are fine for today; the quick reference shows how to change both. Whatever you use, record the model in your AI-use log.
Why the context window matters
An LLM has no memory between calls: each one starts with only what you supply, up to the limit of its context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.. That one fact explains the day. Instruction files and skills give the model context it would not otherwise have. They are only requests, so Block 5 adds controls that hold either way, and tests check the result.
Remember: the AI sees only what you give it, and everything it sees has left your machine.
Discussion
Take three minutes, then post a short answer to each question in the Zoom chat:

What is one task you would like to hand to an agent by the end of the day, and how would you check it? Is there anything you would not delegate at all?
How do you use AI tools now: browser chat, IDE chat, a terminal agent?

Claude Code ignores AGENTS.md, so the instruction never reaches the modelAn instruction file only adds context the model may or may not follow; rules and tests hold either wayPermission rules make the model more accurate, so it follows the instruction more closelyTests stop the agent reading the raw data, so it never sees the files it might edit

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipChanging the model in other tools





In Posit Assistant, use its model picker. In Copilot Chat, use the model menu (inline completions have a separate setting). In R, ellmer::chat_anthropic() takes the model as model =, and the effort level as params = params(reasoning_effort = "low"); Block 6 sets the model this way.









TipTwo modes of execution





The tools you use today are synchronous and local: they act on files on your machine, respond in seconds, and can be interrupted. An asynchronous, remote agent, such as the Copilot cloud agent, works on its own branch on someone else’s servers. It returns a pull request minutes later; the self-study page on the Copilot cloud agent walks through it. The first kind invites you to watch and interrupt. The second invites you to write a precise specification and review what comes back. Block 3 turns this into a ladder of autonomy.









TipThe thread, in more detail





Day 1 introduced renv; Day 4 checks that an agent has kept to it. On Day 2 you saw what a reviewable project needs (TADA! and the README, and the SORTEE checklist). Day 4 shows how AI can help produce that record without inventing any of it. Many journals, funders and institutions now ask authors to declare AI use, and a log written at the time is easier and more accurate than one reconstructed later.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


characterisation test
A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.


codebook
A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.


context window
The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.


effort level
How much a model reasons before it answers. In Claude Code it runs from low to max; a higher level can help with hard problems, but it is slower and uses more tokens.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.


instruction file
A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.


large language model
A model trained on a large body of text, code included, that predicts the next fragment of text from what came before. Claude, GPT and Gemini are families of large language models; tools such as Claude Code, Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot send your requests to one.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


skill
A reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.


token
The unit a model reads and writes, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Providers charge per token, and because the whole conversation is re-sent with each request, a long conversation costs more per question.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Before you install: three questions
Claude Code is an AI agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. that runs in the Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron. It reads, edits and runs the files in your project, asking your permission as it goes. You need very little terminal: one command to start it, and the R console and Git pane for everything else.
⏱ 45–60 minutes, before the workshop day (most of it waiting for packages to install). You need a Claude account for Claude Code and, for Block 6, an Anthropic API key with a little prepaid credit (Step 7). If a command here fails, check the Claude Code setup page first.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Are you permitted to use it on this work? Claude Code sends what it reads, and the output of commands it runs, to Anthropic. Check your institution’s policy and, near research data, your ethics approval and data agreements (Block 3).

Which account? A Claude Pro or Max subscription, a Claude Team or Enterprise seat, a Claude Console account (billed per request), or access your institution has set up through a cloud provider.

Is your computer supported? macOS 13 or later, Windows 10 (1809) or later, or a recent Linux.

title: Setting up Claude Code
section: Step 1: Open the Terminal tab in your IDE
text:
Step 1: Open the Terminal tab in your IDE


RStudio: the Terminal tab next to the Console.

Positron: Terminal → New Terminal.

With a project open, the Terminal tab starts in the project’s root folder. Claude Code needs to run there. You never need to cd.
Which shell is it? A prompt starting PS is PowerShell (Windows); one ending $ or % is Git Bash (Windows), or bash or zsh (macOS, Linux).

title: Setting up Claude Code
section: Step 2: Check git and R are reachable
text:
Step 2: Check git and R are reachable
In the terminal:
git --version
Rscript --version
Both should print a version number.


git not found: install git (on Windows, Git for Windows).

Rscript not found (common on Windows): run R.home("bin") in the R console, then add that folder to your PATH (Windows: Start menu → “Edit environment variables for your account” → Path). Then quit and reopen RStudio or Positron: its terminals keep the PATH they started with.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Step 3: Install Claude Code
macOS or Linux, in the terminal:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Windows, in PowerShell (a prompt starting PS; if your Terminal tab is Git Bash, open the PowerShell app for this one step):
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
Then quit and reopen RStudio or Positron, and check the version in the Terminal tab:
claude --version
You are done when it prints 2.1.281 or later. This minimum is about your instruction file: by this version, Claude Code reads your AGENTS.md directly and lists it in /memory. An older version ignores AGENTS.md without saying so, because the workshop template deliberately has no CLAUDE.md. The installer above keeps Claude Code up to date by itself. An install made with Homebrew or WinGet does not, so update it the same way (brew upgrade claude-code or winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode).

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Step 4: Prepare your workshop repository
Do this before you sign in, so that Claude Code starts in the right folder.


Fork, clone and open the template in one step, in the R console: usethis::create_from_github("<template-owner>/<template-repo>", fork = TRUE). Your instructor gives you the exact name.

Restore the packages: run renv::restore() in the R console, once. It installs the versions in the template’s lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment. and can take several minutes.

Start clean. If the Git pane (RStudio) or Source Control view (Positron) shows any changed file, commit it, so the day starts with no changes.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Step 5: Sign in
With your workshop repository open, type claude in its Terminal tab. On first launch a browser window opens: sign in with your account (/logout and /login switch accounts later). If a Terminal tab was open before you switched projects, close it and open a new one.






WarningUsing an API key





If you use a Console API key, set it as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, for example in .Renviron, and never commit that file. The template stops Claude Code reading a .Renviron in the project folder, but not the one in your home folder. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is already set for another tool, Claude Code may use it instead of your subscription and bill per request. /status shows which credential is in use.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Step 6: The essentials
Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in Manual mode (default), a permission modeThe setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).. In this mode it asks before every edit and before most commands (read-only ones, such as head, run without asking). Claude Code’s own default is auto, where a second model approves actions for you; the project setting overrides it. Read each request before you answer. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Shift+Tab changes the mode, /plan asks for a plan first, and the Claude Code quick reference lists the rest.
Where am I typing?






Where
What runs there



The Claude Code prompt, inside the Terminal tab
Your requests to Claude Code. A line starting ! runs a shell command, and its output is added to the conversation, so it reaches the model too.


The terminal’s own prompt (PS, $ or %), after /exit

Shell commands: claude, git, Rscript



The R console
R code. Claude Code cannot see it, or anything you load there.


The Git pane (RStudio) or Source Control view (Positron)
Git status, diffs, reverting and committing, on the same repository



While Claude Code is running, the Terminal tab belongs to it, so check its work somewhere else.
Checking work while Claude Code is running


To check…
In the R console or Git pane



What changed
The Git pane: Diff shows the changes line by line; Revert (Positron: Discard Changes) undoes one you did not want.


That a script runs in a fresh R session

Session → Restart R (Positron: the restart button in the Console), then source(here::here("scripts", "name.R")). Or, without restarting, callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "name.R")), which runs it in a separate fresh session (how it works)


That the tests pass in a fresh R session

Session → Restart R, then testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))



That the packages match the lockfile
renv::status()



These work the same on Windows, macOS and Linux. Each Rscript call Claude Code makes is a fresh R process too, so objects never carry over to it from your console.






NoteAt the command line





The same checks from a terminal (after /exit, or in a second Terminal tab): git status, git diff, git restore <file>, Rscript scripts/name.R, Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')" and Rscript -e "renv::status()".

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Step 8: Check everything works


Pre-workshop check (15 minutes)


Goal: confirm that Claude Code, R, your repository and your API key all work, so that the day starts with the first block rather than with set-up problems.
Start state: your workshop repository is open, and the Git pane shows no uncommitted changes.
1. Manual mode. Type claude in the Terminal tab. It should say it is in Manual mode (default), not auto. Then:
Describe what each top-level folder of this repository contains. Do not
change anything.
It should answer without asking to edit anything.
2. R is reachable.
Run Rscript -e "sessionInfo()" and show me the output.
Approve the command when asked: you should see your R version.
3. Settings and instructions load. /permissions should list 17 deny rules, and /memory should list AGENTS.md. On a Pro or Max account, also open /privacy-settings and decide whether your conversations may be used for model training. Type /exit.
4. The project is ready. Restart R (Session → Restart R), then in the R console:

renv::status()
testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

renv::status() should report no problems. The test summary should show FAIL 0 and PASS 8. The eight passing checks cover the protections, Manual mode, no command approved in advance, AGENTS.md, git and the raw-data checksum. The other tests skip: they wait for the block that creates their files.
5. The agent’s model answers. You did this in Step 7; if you skipped it, do it now, because Block 6 needs it.
6. The checkpoint branches are there. The Git pane’s branch menu should list checkpoint-skills, checkpoint-cleaning and checkpoint-refactor, among the remote branches (as origin/checkpoint-skills and so on). Stay on main.
7. The code-review folder. Block 9 reviews the Day 2 script in a folder of its own. In the R console:

review_dir <- usethis::create_project("~/ai-review", open = FALSE)
download.file("https://osf.io/download/3x6hb/",
              file.path(review_dir, "ANALYSIS.R"), mode = "wb")

It prints where it made the folder. Check that ANALYSIS.R is there. If the download fails, use your browser to download ANALYSIS.R from the OSF project into that folder.
You are done when the Git pane shows no changes, Claude Code starts in Manual mode, /permissions lists 17 deny rules, the tests run with no failures, the API key test replies, and ~/ai-review holds ANALYSIS.R. If anything differs, copy the output of steps 2 and 4 into a note outside the repository and bring it on the day.
If it goes wrong: Rscript not found, return to Step 2; no reply from the API key test, return to Step 7; empty /permissions list, start claude from the workshop repository’s Terminal tab; a changed file, Revert in the Git pane; package problems, run renv::restore() again and send the error to your instructor before the day.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


permission mode
The setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).


skill
A reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.


symbolic link
A file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler.

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
Activity: The context demonstration
Inline completion is the simplest kind of assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files.: grey “ghost text” appears as you type. You accept it with Tab, reject it with Esc, or carry on typing. By the end of this page you will know how to get useful suggestions more often. Load and name your data in the script above the cursor, then write a specific comment just before it. Claude Code has no inline completion, so this page uses GitHub Copilot instead.
Self-study: about 25 minutes, after the workshop day. Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, signed in to GitHub Copilot (if you are not, open the optional GitHub Copilot box in Setting up Claude Code first).

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
NoteSet-up routes, plans and data







RStudio: enable GitHub Copilot in RStudio’s options and sign in to GitHub.

Positron: choose GitHub Copilot as the completions provider (see Positron’s completions documentation).

VS Code: select Use AI Features from the Copilot icon in the Status Bar and sign in with GitHub.

Copilot Free allows a limited number of completions per month (2,000 at the time of writing); paid plans do not meter them. Completions send the code around your cursor to the provider, so the disclosure points in Block 4 apply here too. Use one completion provider at a time, so you know which tool made each suggestion.









TipUsing Posit Assistant





In RStudio and Positron you can use Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions instead: in RStudio, turn it on from the Posit Assistant toolbar button (it needs a Posit AI account); in Positron, choose it as the completions provider. Posit AI does not meter completions.

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
The context principle
A suggestion can only use what is in the model’s context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window. when it is made. Copilot fills that window mainly from the current file, and above all from the comment just before the cursor. In Positron it may also use other open tabs. It does not see your R session.

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Activity: The context demonstration


The context demonstration (10 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository is open, and the set-up check produced ghost text.
The data are voles_metabolism.csv: a synthetic trial in 72 voles, with columns subject_id, sex, treatment_arm, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g and metabolic_rate_post. The names were chosen so that no model has seen them before.
1. No context. Restart R, so you are in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., and open a blank R script. Type only this comment, and wait.
In the R script:

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment

Note the suggestion. With no data and no column names in view, the model has to guess.
2. Context in the file. In a new blank script, type the lines below down to glimpse(voles), and run them, so that voles is loaded. Then type the same comment on a new line, and wait.
In the R script:

# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
# 72 voles, three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose), two sexes
# Native pipe |>, tidyverse

library(tidyverse)

voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
glimpse(voles)

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment



A typical good result


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(
    mean_change = mean(mass_change_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = treatment_arm
  )

The exact form varies between people and sessions.

Compare the two suggestions. Did the second use real column names? Did it compute post minus pre?
You are done when you can say what the second suggestion had that the first did not.
If it goes wrong: if no suggestion appears, type the comment again on a new line; if the script stops running, Session → Restart R and run it from the top.








TipUsing Posit Assistant: context in the session





With Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions, keep voles loaded from step 2, then type only the comment from step 1 in a new blank script. If the suggestion now uses the real column names, it came from your session, not from the file.

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
Activity: Build a small analysis


Build a small analysis (10 minutes)


Goal: extend scratch/completions.R into a short analysis that reruns, deciding on every suggestion yourself, so that no suggestion enters your code unchecked.
Start state: scratch/completions.R with the step 2 code from the demonstration, and voles loaded.
For each step, write the comment first. Then accept, modify or reject the suggestion. Note which you did in a comment under the code, for example # modified: added n(). The note makes you notice any suggestion you accepted without checking.
0. Derived column. Add mass_change_g (mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g) to voles as a column. Steps 1 and 2 need it there, not only inside a summary.
1. Summary table. The mean and standard deviation of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with the number of observations per cell.
2. Plot. mass_change_g against metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm.
You are done when steps 0 to 2 each have a note (accepted, modified or rejected), and scratch/completions.R, saved and run from the top in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record. (Session → Restart R), produces the table and the plot without error.
If it goes wrong: delete the last suggestion you accepted, and write a more specific comment naming the data frame and its columns.


An example


# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

voles <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    subject_id = col_character(),
    sex = col_character(),
    treatment_arm = col_character(),
    mass_pre_g = col_double(),
    mass_post_g = col_double(),
    metabolic_rate_post = col_double()
  )
) |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g)

# mean and SD of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with n per cell
voles |>
  summarise(
    mean_change_g = mean(mass_change_g),
    sd_change_g = sd(mass_change_g),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(treatment_arm, sex)
  ) |>
  arrange(treatment_arm, sex)

# mass_change_g against metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm
ggplot(voles, aes(metabolic_rate_post, mass_change_g, colour = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Metabolic rate (post-treatment)", y = "Change in mass (g)")

The plot drops the one animal with no metabolic rate and says so in a warning: read it rather than ignore it.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: steer inline completion with a specific comment and the right code above the cursor, trusted because you decided on every suggestion and your script runs from a fresh R session.

Check: accept, modify or reject every suggestion deliberately.

Reproduce: good suggestions come from context in the file, so keep that context in your script, where it reruns.

Record: nothing to log for practice code in scratch/. When completions write code you keep, add a line to your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README., in the form from Block 3.

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
Check your understanding
The single most reliable way to improve inline suggestions in a new script is to:

Switch to a different underlying modelOpen more files in the editor as additional contextLoad the data in the script above the cursor, then write a specific comment naming the data frame and its columnsRestart the IDE so the assistant has a fresh context

You have voles loaded in your R session, but in an empty script Copilot’s suggestion uses made-up column names. The most likely reason is:

Copilot cannot read R codeCopilot sees the code in your editor, not the objects in your R sessionCopilot reads new objects only after R is restartedThe data frame has too many rows for Copilot to read

title: Block 2: Inline completions
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipThe full four-step analysis





The live activity uses two of four steps. The full sequence, again writing the comment for each step before accepting, rejecting or modifying the suggestion:

Filter to subjects with non-missing metabolic_rate_post and create a derived variable mass_change_g.
Produce a summary table of the mean and standard deviation of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with the number of observations per cell.
Fit a linear model of metabolic_rate_post on treatment_arm and sex. Inspect the coefficients.
Produce one plot relating mass_change_g to metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm.

When you have finished steps 2 and 4, post the code Copilot suggested for step 4 in the Zoom chat, with a note on whether you accepted, changed or rejected it. Then compare with what others posted: the comparison usually shows different suggestions, different acceptance decisions and, often, different bugs.

Glossary




term
definition



AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


context window
The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.

title: Block 2: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 1: A logic error
AI is a fast debugging partner for code you wrote yourself, because you can judge its answer against what you meant. You fix two bugs that raise no error: one the data reveal, and one that only your knowledge of the study catches.
⏱ ~20 minutes · Start on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 1: A syntax error


A syntax error (7 minutes)


Start state: voles is loaded in your R console, and Claude Code is open with a new conversation (/clear).
You wrote this in your script to count voles per treatment:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_barchart()

R returns:
Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart"
1. Ask for a fix. Paste the code and the error, and ask.
Prompt (Claude Code or a chat window):
This code gives an error:

  ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
    geom_barchart()

Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart"

What is wrong, and what is the fix?
Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
2. Explain it before you accept it. Write one sentence saying why the original failed. If you can write it, you understood the fix; that sentence is your check.






TipWith inline completion instead





Paste the code and the error into your script as a comment, add # Fix this code: on the next line, and let the assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. suggest a continuation.





Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_bar()

The function is geom_bar(); ggplot2’s geoms have no _chart suffix. “Could not find function” means no loaded package has a function of that name.

You are done when the corrected plot draws a bar for each treatment arm, and you have written your one-sentence explanation.
If it goes wrong: if the fix produces a different error, paste that error back in the same conversation; the assistant now has two clues.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Asking or acting
So far you have used AI that answers: you gather the evidence and paste it in. Exercise 2 ends with AI that acts, an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. that reads your files and runs code itself, so you check each command and its output.






TipBackground: AI that answers versus AI that acts













AI that answers
AI that acts



Examples
A chat window; Posit Assistant’s Ask mode (/ask); Claude Code given the answer-only line, with you refusing any approval
Claude Code allowed to read and run; Posit Assistant in Normal mode


Who gathers the evidence
You: you run distinct() and paste the output
It does, and shows you each command


What you check
That its reasoning fits the evidence you pasted
That each command is sensible, and what its output says



Use AI that answers when you want to learn, or when the data must not be touched. Posit Assistant’s Ask mode enforces it; with Claude Code, which has no ask mode, the answer-only line is a request and your No at each approval is what holds. Block 4 sets out the full range.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
Exercise 2: A logic error


A logic error (8 minutes)


Start state: voles is loaded in your R console, and Claude Code is open with a new conversation (/clear).
You wrote this in your script to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles:

high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

The code runs without error. R returns:
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_mass
      <dbl>
1       NaN
There is no error to paste: the bug is in what you asked for. The fix is to put the evidence in front of you first, and then in front of the assistant.
1. Inspect the data before asking for help.
In the R console:

voles |> distinct(treatment_arm)
voles |> count(treatment_arm)
nrow(high_dose)

The values are Control, Low_dose and High_dose, and nrow() is zero: you have found the bug yourself in seconds.
2. Ask with the evidence in hand. Paste the code and the diagnostic output together.
Prompt (Claude Code or a chat window):
I am trying to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles.
My code:

  high_dose <- voles |>
    filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

  high_dose |>
    summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

returns NaN. But voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) returns
"Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose". I think the filter fails because of
the capitalisation. Is that the only problem?
Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
3. Now let the agent gather the evidence. This is the one step in the block where it acts. Type /clear, then:
Prompt (Claude Code):
Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and run R code with Rscript to find why
filtering treatment_arm for "high_dose" returns no rows. Don't edit any files.
Show each command and its output.
It reads the file without asking, because reading needs no approval in Manual mode. Before it runs R it asks: read the Rscript command, and choose Yes if it only reads the data and prints results. Then compare its diagnosis with the one you found in step 1.


Solution


high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "High_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g, na.rm = TRUE))

The filter now matches the data. na.rm = TRUE is a precaution for real data, which usually have missing values.

You are done when nrow(high_dose) is 24 and the mean is a number, not NaN.
If it goes wrong: if nrow() is still zero, run voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) again and copy the value exactly as printed.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
section: Exercise 3: A correct-looking but wrong result
text:
Exercise 3: A correct-looking but wrong result


A correct-looking but wrong result (5 minutes)


Start state: voles is loaded in your R console, and Claude Code is open with a new conversation (/clear).
You wrote this to get the mean change in body mass by treatment arm:

voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

It runs. There is no error and no NaN. R returns something like:
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  treatment_arm mean_change
  <chr>               <dbl>
1 Control             -0.21
2 Low_dose            -1.49
3 High_dose           -3.19
The numbers look plausible, but the treatment was designed to increase mass, and this table says mass falls. Nothing in the data or the code reveals the error: only your knowledge of the study does. An AI can catch it too, but only if you tell it what the answer should be.
1. Write down what a correct result should look like, then compare. Here: positive values, rising from Control to High_dose. The mismatch is the diagnosis.
2. Ask for a second opinion, stating the expected direction.
Prompt (Claude Code or a chat window):
This should show mass gain increasing with dose, but the values are negative
and decreasing. What is wrong?

  voles |>
    mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
    summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.


Solution


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

mass_change_g is post minus pre: gain, not loss. The original ran without complaint because subtraction works in either direction.

You are done when your corrected means are positive and increase from Control to High_dose, as you predicted in step 1.
If it goes wrong: if the values are still negative, check which mass you subtract from which: post minus pre is gain.

title: Block 3: Debugging with AI
text:
The debugging checklist
Inspect the data first, ask the AI second.


Read the error in full: the function name and the phrase usually locate the bug.

Inspect the data: glimpse(), distinct(), summary(), and nrow() after a filter.

Check names exactly, including capitals and underscores.

Then ask, giving the code, the error and the diagnostic output together. Ask for an answer, not an action, until you have the evidence.

Explain the fix in one sentence before you accept it.

Before trusting a clean run, state what the result should look like (sign, size, order) and compare.







NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: use an assistant to diagnose and fix errors in your own code, trusted because you inspect the data first, explain each fix in a sentence, and compare every clean-running result with what you expected.

Check: inspect the data before asking, and write one sentence explaining each fix; state the expected sign and size of a result before trusting it.

Reproduce: rerun the fixed code in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., so the fix does not depend on an object left over from your experiments.

Record: nothing to log yet; the AI-use log starts in Block 4.

title: Block 2: Debugging with AI
text:
Check your understanding
A filter returns zero rows and the summary is NaN, with no error. What should you do before asking an AI?

Paste the NaN output into a chat window and ask what is wrongInspect the data, for example with distinct() on the filtered column, so you can give the assistant the evidenceReinstall dplyrAdd na.rm = TRUE and run it again

Code runs without error and returns plausible numbers. What is the most reliable first check?

title: Block 2: Debugging with AI
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipA misspelt function name (self-study)





Goal: fix an error with Claude Code’s help and explain the fix in one sentence, so that you accept only a fix you understand.
Start state: scratch/debugging.R is open with voles loaded, and Claude Code has a new conversation (/clear). During the workshop, wait until after Block 3, which reads Exercise 1’s conversation.
You wrote this in scratch/debugging.R to count voles per treatment:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_barchart()

R returns:
Error in geom_barchart() : could not find function "geom_barchart"
1. Ask for a fix. Paste the code and the error, then ask.
Prompt (Claude Code):
This code gives an error:

  ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
    geom_barchart()

Error in geom_barchart() : could not find function "geom_barchart"

What is wrong, and what is the fix?
Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
2. Explain it before you accept it. Write one sentence saying why the original failed. If you can write it, you understood the fix; that sentence is your check.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_bar()

The function is geom_bar(); ggplot2’s geoms have no _chart suffix. This is not a syntax error. R parses the code without complaint. It fails only when it looks for a function called geom_barchart() and finds none. “Could not find function” means no loaded package has a function of that name.

You are done when the corrected plot draws a bar for each treatment arm, and you have written your one-sentence explanation.
If it goes wrong: if the fix produces a different error, paste that error back in the same conversation; the assistant now has two clues.









TipAn aesthetic-mapping error





This error needs ggplot2’s grammar rather than the data. You wanted a scatter plot of post-treatment metabolic rate against post-treatment mass, coloured by treatment arm:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(color = treatment_arm) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

R returns an error saying that object treatment_arm was not found. The exact wording varies between ggplot2 versions.
1. Ask for a fix. Before accepting it, write one sentence on why ggplot2 could not find treatment_arm.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = treatment_arm)) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

treatment_arm is a column in the data, so the mapping must go inside aes(). An argument outside aes(), such as color =, expects a fixed value like "red" or "#0072B2". R looked for an object called treatment_arm in your environment, found none, and stopped. colour and color are interchangeable in ggplot2.

When ggplot2 reports that a column such as treatment_arm was not found, the most common cause is:

The data argument was supplied incorrectlyA column name was used outside aes(), where ggplot2 expected a fixed valueThe ggplot2 package is not loadedThe variable contains missing values

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Exercise 1: What can it see?
Two questions decide how far you can trust an AI assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files.: what can it see, and what can it do? First you trace what reached the model provider in Block 2. Then you hand an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. a routine change and check it.
⏱ ~30 minutes · Start on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.
What each tool can see. The routes are the same in every tool; what travels along them is not. The biggest difference is your R session: Claude Code cannot see it, and Posit Assistant works inside it.

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Exercise 1: Watch what it gathers


Watch what it gathers (8 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository, with a clean Git pane, and Claude Code open in the Terminal tab with a new conversation (/clear).
1. Ask without the answer-only line. This is a Block 3 question, but this time you let Claude Code look for itself:
Prompt (Claude Code):
My code

  voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g)

fails with "object 'mass_post' not found". voles is read from
data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv. What is wrong?
2. Read the transcript, not just the answer. Above its reply, Claude Code lists each action it took. When we tested this prompt, it ran a short command such as head -n 3 data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv (or Get-Content on Windows) without asking, because Claude Code treats a small set of read-only commands like reading a file. It then named mass_post_g as the real column. If it asks to run anything else, choose No: it can answer from the file.
3. Name the route. For each action in the transcript, find its route in the diagram below: a file it read is route 2; the output of a command it ran is route 4.
You are done when you can name every file or command output that reached the model provider, and the answer names mass_post_g.
If it goes wrong: if it read more than the header, or other files, note which: an agent reads what it judges useful, which is why the habits below matter for confidential data.






TipUsing Posit Assistant





Run the failing code in your R session, then ask only “Why did my last command fail?” Posit Assistant already has the names and types of your objects, so it may answer without fetching anything: that is route 3.





Disclosure: every route out of your machine
Everything an assistant sees is sent to a model provider, by four routes:



Route 1: what you paste


Errors, output and results you paste into a chat or prompt


any tool


Model provider




Route 2: files it reads


Copilot: open files. Claude Code and Posit Assistant: any project file they choose to read


read


Model provider




Route 3: session context the IDE injects


Your live R session: R version, and the names and types of your objects (not their values)


Posit Assistant only


Model provider




Route 4: output of commands it runs


The agent runs Rscript or head data.csv, and reads what it prints


Claude Code, Posit Assistant


Model provider



Everything before an arrow reaches the model provider. A data file in the project may already be disclosed; for a tibble loaded in your session, its names and types are, and its values as soon as code the agent runs prints them.








ImportantWorking with confidential data: five habits





Work on a copy. Put a synthetic or anonymised copy in the project, and run the final analysis on the real data yourself, outside the agent’s folder.

Know your account. Commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise, API) are not used for model training; on Pro or Max, set /privacy-settings. Check your institution’s approval, ethics approval and data agreements first.

Deny reads of sensitive folders in /permissions, for example Read(/data/confidential/**). It is best effort: commands can still read the file.

Stay in Manual mode, and refuse any command that would print records.

Describe, don’t show. names() gives column names and summary() the shape of the data; print(), glimpse() and str() show actual values.







TipBackground: tool-specific notes





There is no .claudeignore file, and /sandbox is not available on native Windows. Posit Assistant blocks .Renviron and .env by default, and shares the names and types of objects in your session, not their values; code it runs can still print values.





Context you hold in your head
A data file supplies column names, but not your question or your design. Your instructor may show this with two prompts; the demonstration is below, and you can try it yourself in Going further.






TipInstructor: demonstration





Your instructor asks a new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
and then, in another new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
The first gets a tour of options; the second can get a recommendation, because the design now exists outside your head. Treat it as a proposal to check: the primary analysis is your decision.

title: Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy
section: Part B: What can the assistant do?
text:
Part B: What can the assistant do?
The model is the same at every level below. What changes is its permission modeThe setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).: what it may do without asking. Each level is a rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. on an autonomy ladder. From rung 3 up, what changes is which tool calls run without your approval. The self-study page Build your own agent in R shows that approval step in code.








Rung
What happens
Claude Code
Posit Assistant



0. Suggest
Completes the line you are typing
—
Next Edit Suggestions


1. Ask
Answers; changes nothing
— (no ask mode; Block 3’s answer-only line is a request)
Ask mode (/ask)


2. Plan
Proposes steps; changes nothing until you approve
/plan
/plan


3. Act, with approval
Edits files and runs commands, asking first
Manual (default): the workshop’s starting mode
Normal mode


4. Act, partly unsupervised
Some actions without asking

acceptEdits; auto (a classifier approves actions; Claude Code’s own default since v2.1.283)
Auto mode (/auto)


5. Act, unsupervised
No prompts
bypassPermissions
YOLO mode (/yolo)



Your starting mode. Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in Manual, although its own default is auto since v2.1.283; keep Manual for confidential data. Claude Code has no ask mode, and /plan can still run commands, so read any it proposes. Use rungs 0 to 3 only; the quick reference has the rest.
Rung 3 is where routine work is safe, for example adding a derived column and a plot script. Three things make it safe: you start from a commit, so any change can be reverted; every edit and command is shown to you first; and a test checks the result, whatever the agent reports. Exercise 2 is exactly this.






Warning



Each rung up removes a moment when you would have seen the action. acceptEdits also auto-approves file commands such as cp and mv, so a cp over a raw data file needs no approval. auto suits routine work you will test anyway, not confidential data or anything unprotected. And an approval you click through without reading is rung 5 with extra steps: Block 6 covers the rules that hold however tired you are.


The higher the rung, the more an agent acts on its guesses about your conventions, which is why Block 5 writes them down.






NoteThe safe vibe-coding recipe





Commit, so you start from a clean Git pane.

Protect the inputs: /permissions shows the deny rules, or you add one.

Have the checks ready: tests in tests/ before the agent starts.

Ask in one prompt or skill, in Manual mode, reading each approval.

Run the checks: the test suite in a fresh R session.

Read the diff in the Git pane, then commit or revert.

You will use these six steps in Blocks 7 and 9; the template ships the protections and the tests, so most of it is checking they are there.


Exercise 2: The same task, rising autonomy


Ask, plan, act (15 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository on main, committed and clean (the Git pane shows no changed files). While Claude Code runs in the Terminal tab, check its work from the R console and the Git pane (checking work).
1. Plan (rung 2). In Claude Code, type /clear, then:
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a derived mass_change_g column (mass_post_g
minus mass_pre_g). Create a new script scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R
that plots mass_change_g by treatment_arm and saves the figure to outputs/
with ggsave(). Don't run anything; I'll check the scripts myself.
Before approving, check the plan names both files, leaves data/raw/ alone and saves the figure to outputs/. If anything is missing, choose No, keep planning and say what to change.
2. Act, with approval (rung 3). Choose Yes, manually approve edits, so it stays in Manual mode, and read each edit before you approve it. The repository’s AGENTS.md tells it to run new scripts, so it may still ask to run Rscript: choose No, because you check the result yourself next.
3. Check. Click Diff in the Git pane for each changed file and read it as you would a colleague’s work. Then Restart R (Session → Restart R) and run:
In the R console:

testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_explore.R"))

One test checks mass_change_g really is post minus pre; the other runs the plot script in a fresh R session and checks a figure arrived in outputs/.
4. Record and commit. Create docs/ai-log.md (usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")) and write the first line of your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README. yourself, on one line, in the form from Block 1. Use today’s date, written as YYYY-MM-DD:
2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); added mass_change_g and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff
Commit it together with both scripts. You will add a line after each block in which an agent works; tests/test_ai_log.R checks that each line has four parts separated by semicolons, and that the dates are real and in order.
You are done when both tests pass, you have read every line of the diff, and your first AI-use log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: select the unwanted change in the Git pane and click Revert, then ask again more clearly. If you run out of time, the block5-done checkpoint branch has this block’s files; switch to it from the Git pane’s branch menu at the end of Block 5 if you are still behind.






TipStretch: reflect on the rungs





At which rung did you decide the most? Where would you have missed an unwanted change without the diff?
Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?









TipUsing Posit Assistant





Use /plan for step 1 and Normal mode (/normal) for step 2. Steps 3 and 4 are the same: the Git pane and the R console.









NoteAt the command line





The same checks from a terminal (after /exit, or in a second Terminal tab): git status, git diff, and Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_explore.R')".











NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand an agent a routine multi-file change at rung 3, trusted because you read every diff and a test you did not write checks the result.

Check: the Git pane’s diff after every agent action; the agent’s report that something “still runs” is a claim until a test confirms it.

Reproduce: work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert.

Record: your AI-use log starts here, in docs/ai-log.md.

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Check your understanding
You paste nothing, yet Claude Code names your columns correctly. How could it know them?

It cannot; it must be guessingIt read a file in your project or ran code that printed the data, and that output entered its contextIt can see every file on your computerIt remembers your data from a previous conversation

Your project’s settings hold the deny rule Read(/data/confidential/**). Which of these can still read a file in that folder?

Nothing: a deny rule blocks every routeOnly Claude Code's own Read toolR code the agent runs with Rscript, or a search of the whole project such as grep -r, which runs without askingOnly you, from the R console

In Claude Code’s acceptEdits mode, what does the agent do without asking?

Nothing; acceptEdits only changes how diffs are displayedOnly edits to files you have namedIt edits files and runs common file commands such as cp and mv without asking, but still asks before other shell commandsEverything, including all shell commands

Which check still works whatever rung the agent ran at?

The agent's own report that the task succeededThe approval prompts you saw while it workedReading the diff in the Git pane (or with git diff), and running the code or its tests yourselfThe plan the agent proposed before starting

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipAccess and cost





Plans and prices change; check before the session.


Claude Code needs an Anthropic account, used through a subscription or an API key; see Anthropic’s documentation for current options.

Posit Assistant uses Posit AI Pass or your own provider key, including an Anthropic API key. In RStudio, providers are configured in the assistant’s settings.

GitHub Copilot bills in AI credits; check GitHub’s plans page for what your plan includes.

Your institution may have approved some of these tools and not others.










TipTrusting a repository’s configuration





Project settings and hooks are code that runs on your machine. A cloned repository can carry its own, so trust only repositories whose configuration you have read.









TipGitHub Copilot and the remote rung





Copilot offers the same ladder, plus a rung 6: its cloud agent works on your repository on GitHub, on its own branch, and returns a pull request. The self-study page Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent walks through it.









TipStretch: the same error at three levels of context





The code voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g) fails with “object ‘mass_post’ not found”. In three new browser chats, ask about it with more context each time. First give the error message alone. Then give the error plus the code. Last, give the error, the code and the output of glimpse(voles). With the code, a chat may guess mass_post_g by analogy with mass_pre_g, but only the glimpse() output lets it confirm the name. Column names you never supplied, or a famous dataset you never mentioned (penguins, mtcars), are signs it is guessing.

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


permission mode
The setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).


rung
One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 3, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.


tool call
A single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls.

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
text:
Activity 1: Make AGENTS.md yours
In this block you write your conventions down once, so that every conversation follows them. You use two kinds of file: an instruction fileA file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project’s standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees., which loads every time, and a skillA reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description., which loads only when needed. Both are requests that the model usually follows; Block 5 covers rules that always hold.
⏱ ~35 minutes · Start on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Instruction file: loaded into every conversation


AGENTS.md: your conventions


read directly by


Claude Code and Posit Assistant




Skills: loaded when invoked or judged relevant


.agents/skills/<your-skill>/ (the master copy)


you copy


.claude/skills/<your-skill>/


read by


Claude Code



Posit Assistant reads .agents/skills/ directly, so it needs no copy. The course’s own skills already ship in both folders.





one per line, and specific enough to check (“use the native pipe |>”, not “write clean code”);

true of your own code, or the model gets mixed signals;

short, because the file loads into every request;

added when a mistake repeats: a correction in chat is forgotten next conversation;

not guarantees: “never edit raw data” belongs here and in the enforced controls of Block 6.

Activity: Make AGENTS.md yours
Your workshop repository already contains a starter AGENTS.md. Make it describe your practice, then prove that Claude Code reads it.






NoteThe starter AGENTS.md





It includes a canaryA fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.: a fixed first line the assistant is asked to put in any R code it writes, so you can see the file was loaded. The “Tests” rules ask the agent to prove its own work after every edit, which later blocks rely on.


# Project conventions: voles analysis

## Canary
When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block:
# agents-md: active v1

## Structure
- Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified.
- Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/.
- Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/.

## R style
- Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment.
- Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F.
- Build every path with here::here() (or here() after library(here)). Never
  use setwd() or rm(list = ls()).
- Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types.

## Reproducibility
- Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before
  adding a package.
- Do not edit renv.lock.
- Set a seed immediately before any random step.
- Every script must run in a fresh R session.
- Every script must run with Rscript from the project root; after writing one,
  run it that way and report the exit status.
- Save figures with ggsave() to outputs/.

## Tests
- After editing any R file, run Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')" and
  paste the final summary line verbatim.
- Never edit anything in tests/fixtures/, an existing expectation or a
  tolerance to make a test pass.
- Every new function in scripts/functions/ gets a test with at least one
  known-answer case on a small tibble, including an NA; expected values are
  worked out by hand, never by running the code under test.

## Data integrity
- Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment.
- Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic.

## Statistics
- Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory.
- Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code.

## Version control
- Before you edit any file, run git status.
- If this folder is not a git repository, stop and ask me to set one up.
- If there are uncommitted changes, list them and ask whether I want to
  commit first.
- Never commit, push or change git settings unless I ask.

## Working with me
- Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval.
- Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/. The one
  exception: a skill may run tests/make_reference.R once, to capture a
  reference that does not exist yet.







Edit, check, verify (15 minutes)


Start state: your workshop repository open, a clean Git pane, and Claude Code running in the project’s Terminal tab (checking work).
1. Baseline.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot
of mass_post_g by treatment arm. Show the R code in your reply; do not
create any files.
Look for the canary, # agents-md: active v1, as the first line of the code. (Asking for the code in the reply gives the canary somewhere to appear.)
2. Make it yours. Type /memory, choose AGENTS.md, and in your editor:

delete one rule you do not actually follow;
add one convention you always follow.

Keep the canary and the “Tests”, “Statistics” and “Working with me” sections, which later blocks rely on. Save.
3. Verify. Type /clear and repeat the step 1 prompt. The canary shows the file was loaded; check the plot code against your new rule to see whether it was followed.
4. Check it with a test. In the R console, after Session → Restart R:

testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_controls.R"))

It confirms AGENTS.md is in place with its canary, the project still starts in Manual mode, and the deny rules are intact. Commit AGENTS.md from the Git pane.
You are done when the canary appears, the test passes, and your edited AGENTS.md is committed.
If it goes wrong: check there is no CLAUDE.md (the test checks this too) and that /memory lists AGENTS.md. Still stuck? Compare with the block5-done branch from the Git pane’s branch menu.






TipUsing Posit Assistant





Posit Assistant reads the same AGENTS.md. Open it from the gear menu (Open project memory), or describe your conventions and run /savememory. If the canary is missing, check that you trusted the workspace.

title: Block 5: Instructions and skills
text:
Part B: Skills
A skill is a folder holding a SKILL.md file, plus any scripts or templates it needs. Its front matterThe block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill’s name and description, or a Quarto document’s options., between two lines of three dashes at the top, gives a name and a description:


The description is the trigger. “Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report, poster or paper” loads when it should; “for plots” loads erratically. Invoking it by name (/skill-name) always works.

The body is a procedure: when to use it, the steps, hard rules and a final check. It loads only when used, so it can be longer than AGENTS.md.







TipBackground: skills that run only by name





For a skill that writes files, disable-model-invocation: true in the front matter makes it run only when you invoke it by name.



Keep the master copy in .agents/skills/ and copy it into .claude/skills/ for Claude Code (Posit Assistant reads .agents/skills/ directly). The deny rules protect .claude/ from the agent’s edit tools but not .agents/skills/, so check the master copy in the Git pane too. The course’s own skills already ship in both; type /skills to list them. For a skill you write, copy it once, and again whenever you change it:
In the R console:

fs::dir_copy(
  here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"),
  here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)

Activity: Write a skill and test it


A house figure style (20 minutes)


Start state: Claude Code in Manual mode in your project’s Terminal tab, with your AGENTS.md committed.
1. Baseline, before the skill exists.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_baseline.R.
Approve the edit. Doing this first guarantees the baseline was written without the skill.
2. Create the skill. In the R console, usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md") creates and opens the file. Paste in:
---
name: house-figures
description: >-
  Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear
  in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a
  figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots.
---

# House figure style

## Rules
1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation
   (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar
   with error bars ("dynamite plot").
2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette
   (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same
   variable to point shape so the figure works without colour.
3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)".
4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12).
5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure.
6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a
   fitted model and asks for them.

## Before returning code
List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why.
Copy it into .claude/skills/ with the fs::dir_copy() line above (you do this yourself, because .claude/ is protected from the agent). Type /skills: house-figures should be listed, with no restart.
3. With the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_house.R.
4. Grade it. Run both scripts in a fresh R session and look at the figures: callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "fig_baseline.R")), then the same for fig_house.R. Then record, for each rule:


Rule
Without skill
With skill



1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot




2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape




3. Units in axis titles




4. theme_classic(base_size = 12)





5. n per group shown




6. No unrequested p-values





5. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md in the same form as Block 4, with today’s date, naming the skill you tested and what you kept or changed in its output. Commit it with the skill and the two scripts.
You are done when the table is filled in from the figures you looked at, not from the agent’s list of rules it applied, and your log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if /skills does not list it, check that .claude/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md exists and its front matter starts and ends with three dashes. Out of time? Commit or discard your changes in the Git pane first, so the switch is not blocked, then switch to block5-done.
Payoff. What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and would you use it for the next figure?






TipStretch: test the trigger





In a new conversation (/clear), test the trigger: “Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm” should not load the skill; “Polish the figure in scripts/fig_baseline.R for the poster” should. Or test rule 6: ask it to “add significance stars between the groups in scripts/fig_house.R” and see whether it declines. Either way, what makes the output trustworthy is the grading in step 4, which you can repeat on every figure.









TipUsing Posit Assistant





Posit Assistant reads .agents/skills/ directly, so no copy is needed. Invoke the skill by name in the same way.











NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: state your conventions once for every conversation, and package a procedure as a skill you invoke by name, trusted because the canary and tests/test_controls.R show the files are connected, and you grade the output rule by rule.

Check: a canary shows a file was loaded, not followed; grade the output and run the figure code.

Reproduce: your AGENTS.md states the reproducibility rules (renv, fresh R session, seeds); Blocks 7 and 9 check the agent kept to them.

Record: add a line to docs/ai-log.md naming the skill you tested and what you changed in its output.
