title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipSkills you did not write





Claude Code ships built-in skills such as /code-review and /debug. Shared collections are also published online, for example Anthropic’s anthropics/skills repository. Read any skill before you install it: it can include scripts that the assistant runs on your machine. Install a skill bundle and compare, below, gives you one to practise on: pub-figures, which packages the ggplot chapter’s conventions as a skill.









TipLinking a skill instead of copying it





On macOS or Linux you can use a symbolic linkA file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler. instead of a copy, so there is only one version to keep up to date. First delete the copy with fs::dir_delete(here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures")). Then create the link with fs::link_create(here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"), here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures")). Claude Code follows the link. The link stores the full path, so recreate it if you move the project. On Windows, symbolic links need extra configuration, so copy the folder.









TipDraft an instruction file for a project of your own





Where an instruction file comes from in your own projects, in Activity 1, compares three routes. This task follows the third: the agent drafts, you decide.


From draft to your own file


Goal: give one of your own projects an AGENTS.md that holds only rules you would defend, so that the agent starts every conversation there from your conventions.
Work in one of your own projects, not the workshop repository, and commit or back it up first. Start Claude Code in the project’s folder.
1. Ask for a draft, not a file.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Look through this project: its folders, scripts, README and any existing
instruction files. Propose an AGENTS.md of conventions for working here,
one rule per line, under 60 lines. Mark each rule "seen in the code" or
"suggested". Show it in your reply; do not create any files.
2. Prune it. Create AGENTS.md yourself (usethis::edit_file("AGENTS.md")) and paste in only the rules you would defend. Go through What makes an instruction work line by line. A rule marked “seen in the code” may only describe a habit you want to break. A “suggested” rule may sound sensible but not be yours. Then add what the agent could not see: your statistics rules, and what must never be touched.
3. Add a canary and verify. Put a canary section at the top, as in the workshop file. Then type /clear, check /memory and ask for a small piece of R code.
Optional comparison. In a throwaway copy of the project, run /init and compare the CLAUDE.md it writes with your file. Delete that CLAUDE.md afterwards: while it exists, Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md.
You are done when the canary appears and every line in your AGENTS.md is one you would defend.











TipTurn a conversation into a skill





Skills in your own work, after Activity 2, describes the usual route to a skill: get an output right over several rounds, then distil the result.


Distil a skill


Goal: turn the corrections you make in one conversation into a skill, so that one request reaches the same result next time.
1. Get it right the long way. Start with /clear.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Make a summary table of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data,
for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/tab_summary.R.
Run the script yourself and correct the table at least twice, with your own preferences: decimal places, a column for n, units in the headers, the order of the arms.
2. Distil it.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Turn the decisions we reached in this conversation into a skill at
.agents/skills/summary-tables/SKILL.md. Keep the rules that would apply to
any summary table in this project; leave out details specific to this
variable. Write a description that says when to use it and when not to.
The deny rules keep the agent out of .claude/, but not out of .agents/skills/, so it can write this draft. Read it before you approve it. (Posit Assistant has a built-in create-skill skill for this step.)
3. Review it as you reviewed pub-figures:

Is the description specific enough to trigger only for summary tables?
Has every detail of this one table gone?
Does anything contradict AGENTS.md?

Edit the file until all three answers are yes.
4. Install and test. Copy it with the fs::dir_copy() line from Activity 2, changing house-figures to summary-tables. Type /clear, then ask in one line for a summary table of another variable in the voles data, starting with /summary-tables. Grade the table against the skill’s rules from the table itself, not from the agent’s report.
You are done when one request produces a table that meets the rules you reached in step 1, and you have committed the skill (both folders).
Payoff. How many rounds of correction did the skill save, and what did you still have to check?











TipInstruction and skill files in other tools












File or folder
Posit Assistant
GitHub Copilot




AGENTS.md (repository root)
Read as project memory
Read by the cloud agent, agent mode and the CLI


CLAUDE.md
—
Read by the cloud agent


.github/copilot-instructions.md
Offered for conversion by /import-instructions

Read by Copilot


Path-scoped rules
No equivalent found

.github/instructions/*.instructions.md with applyTo



.agents/skills/<name>/
Yes
Yes


.claude/skills/<name>/
—
Yes


.github/skills/<name>/
—
Yes



This course has no CLAUDE.md, so every tool reads the same AGENTS.md. Copilot reads both .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/; if it lists a skill twice, remove one route for Copilot.
Posit Assistant also includes built-in skills such as quarto-authoring and r-package-development.









TipA rule for Quarto files only





Some rules are right for one kind of file and wrong elsewhere. A chunk option such as #| echo: false is meaningful in a .qmd file and meaningless in an .R script. A path-scoped rule is an instruction file that loads only when the agent works on matching files. It differs from a skill: a rule states conventions, a skill sets out a procedure. (A skill can also be limited to matching files, with the same paths: field in its front matter.) The test for a scoped rule: would it be wrong, not merely irrelevant, in the files it excludes? If not, put it in AGENTS.md.


Create and test a scoped rule


Goal: make a rule that loads only for Quarto files and check that it does, so that a convention that is wrong elsewhere stays out of your R scripts.
1. Where the file goes. For Claude Code, a rule is one Markdown file in .claude/rules/:
your-project/
├── AGENTS.md                 loads in every conversation
└── .claude/
    ├── settings.json
    ├── skills/
    └── rules/
        └── quarto.md         loads only when the agent works on a .qmd file
2. What the file holds. The whole file is shown below. The front matter at the top, between the two lines of three dashes, says which files the rule applies to: paths: takes a list of patterns, and "**/*.qmd" means any .qmd file in any folder. The rules follow, one per line. (The “hashpipe” is the #| at the start of a chunk-option line.)


.claude/rules/quarto.md

---
paths:
  - "**/*.qmd"
---

# Quarto document conventions

- Set chunk options with the hashpipe (#|) inside the chunk, not in the
  {r} header.
- Give every chunk a label; prefix figure chunks with fig-.
- Every figure chunk sets #| fig-cap:, #| fig-width: and #| fig-height:.
- Refer to figures in the text with @fig-..., never by a typed number.
- Default to #| echo: false unless the document is a code walkthrough.
- Resolve paths with here::here(); never assume the working directory is the
  document's folder.

3. Create it. In practice you would describe the rule and let the agent draft the file. Try that first:
Prompt (Claude Code):
Draft a Claude Code rule file for .claude/rules/quarto.md that applies only
to .qmd files, with the front matter it needs and our Quarto chunk
conventions. Show it in your reply; do not create the file.
Compare its draft with the file above. The deny rules keep the agent out of .claude/, so you save the file yourself: run usethis::edit_file(".claude/rules/quarto.md"), paste in the version you prefer, and save.
4. Test. A rule loads only when the agent itself reads or edits a matching file; opening the file in RStudio does not count. So:

Create a short Quarto file yourself with usethis::edit_file("reports/rule_test.qmd"). A title and one line of text are enough. Save it.
Ask the agent to read reports/rule_test.qmd and add a chunk that plots mass_post_g by treatment_arm. A correct answer uses hashpipe options, a fig- label, a caption and here::here().
Type /clear, then ask for the same plot in a new script, scripts/rule_test.R. The Quarto rules should not appear.

If the rules do not appear in the .qmd either, the rule is not loading.
Other tools. Copilot uses a different folder and a different front-matter key:


.github/instructions/quarto.instructions.md

---
applyTo: "**/*.qmd"
---

# Quarto document conventions

(the same rules as above)

Posit Assistant has no path-scoped rules: its documentation describes only the project’s AGENTS.md and a personal one. Add the rules to AGENTS.md under a heading such as “When editing .qmd files”, or rely on its built-in quarto-authoring skill. Behaviour differs between tools, so test on yours.
You are done when you know whether the rules appeared for the .qmd chunk and stayed out of the .R script on your tool.


Every scoped rule is a second copy of a convention to keep in step, once per tool. Use scoped rules sparingly.









TipInstall a skill bundle and compare





house-figures is six rules that you wrote and can read at a glance. pub-figures is the opposite case. It packages the conventions from the ggplot chapter as a skill of about 200 lines, with R scripts that the assistant sources and adapts. Those conventions are the chart-type and audience tables, theme_project(), colorspace palettes, the colour-vision-deficiency check, the four-element legend and saving in two formats. You did not write this skill, so you read it before you install it.
The bundle contains:
pub-figures/
├── SKILL.md                when to use it, the rules, a pre-flight checklist
├── theme-project.R         theme_project() and palette functions
├── raincloud-template.R    figure skeleton, including saving
├── emmeans-bridge.R        model-based significance brackets
└── patchwork-template.R    multi-panel figure with one shared legend
In the ggplot chapter you wrote a simple theme_project(). The theme_project() in this bundle is the full version. It keeps the same name and base_size argument, and adds a font, colours for titles and gridlines, and an axis_type argument.


 Download pub-figures.zip




A skill bundle you did not write


Goal: install a skill you did not write, run it by name and check its output yourself, so that you know what it does before you rely on it.
1. Read before you install. Open SKILL.md and theme-project.R (both are also reproduced below). Find two places where pub-figures contradicts your house-figures rules. (There are at least two, both deliberate: the palette and the theme.) Find the line that tells the assistant what to do when information is missing.
2. Install. In the R console, run unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills")). It lets you pick the downloaded zip and unpacks it into .agents/skills/. Then copy the skill into .claude/skills/ for Claude Code: use the fs::dir_copy() line above, changing house-figures to pub-figures. The skill uses ggdist, colorspace, ragg, colorBlindness, emmeans and ggpubr. If your project uses renv and they are not in its lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., add them yourself before the test. Do not let the assistant install packages.
3. Same prompt, named skill. Both skills describe themselves as being for figures in reports, posters and papers, so a plain request could load either. Overlapping descriptions are a real hazard once you collect skills from several sources. So name the one you want. Type /skills to check that it is listed (skills reload without a restart). Then run this prompt:
Prompt (Claude Code):
/pub-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
data, for a lab report.
Did the assistant ask about the audience, or record a default?
4. Grade it against its own checklist. The skill ends with a pre-flight checklist. Check the script against each item yourself; do not accept the assistant’s report that it did. Then run the script: are both a PDF and a PNG in outputs/figures/? Run the colorBlindness::cvdPlot() line it left for you, then look at the result.
5. Test a rule under pressure. Ask it to “add significance stars between the groups” without fitting a model. The skill says it must insert a legend placeholder rather than invent p-values. Then give it a fitted model it can actually see. Claude Code cannot see objects in your R console, so a model you fit there does not count. Ask it to add model <- lm(mass_post_g ~ treatment_arm, data = voles) to the figure script itself, or paste the output of summary(model) into the prompt. Then ask for the stars again: it should now use the emmeans-bridge.R pattern with an adjusted p-value.
6. Compare. Which skill would you hand to a colleague? Which would you trust without rereading it after an update? A long skill encodes more of your standards, and hides more of them from view.
7. Keep one. Delete pub-figures from both .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/ in this repository; the checkpoints assume house-figures. With two figure skills installed, which palette you get depends on which one loads. In your own projects, keep one figure skill.
You are done when you have checked the figure script against the skill’s pre-flight checklist yourself, seen how it handles significance stars without and with a model, decided which skill you would hand to a colleague, and removed pub-figures from this repository.








Notepub-figures/SKILL.md







---
name: pub-figures
description: >-
  Use when producing a ggplot2 figure intended for sharing outside the
  immediate session, including manuscript figures, lab reports, posters, talk
  slides, and public engagement graphics. Do not invoke for diagnostic,
  exploratory, model-checking, or one-off plots.
---

# Publication figures

This skill governs production of figures that will be seen by an external audience. It is self-contained: the house rules below apply even if the project has no instruction file.

## House rules

- Tidyverse style, native pipe `|>`, `here::here()` for every path.
- British spelling in titles, labels, legends and comments.
- Never produce pie charts, dual y-axes, 3D effects, or bar charts with error bars ("dynamite plots") when the raw data exist.

## Missing information

If information you need is missing (the audience, a variable's unit, the fitted model), ask the user once, in a single message, before writing code. If the user tells you to proceed without it, or you are working unattended (for example as a cloud agent on a pull request), choose the safe default this skill gives, record the choice in a code comment and, if there is one, in the pull request description, and continue.

## Project toolkit

The packages this skill uses are listed below. Check that each one you need is
in `renv.lock`; if one is missing, stop and ask before installing anything:

- `ggplot2`, `patchwork`, `here`, `scales` for core plotting, composition, paths, and label formatting.
- `ggdist` for raincloud and half-eye distributions: `stat_halfeye()`, `stat_pointinterval()`.
- `ggbeeswarm` for moderate-n group displays: `geom_quasirandom()`.
- `colorspace` for palettes: `scale_*_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2")`, `scale_*_continuous_sequential(palette = "Viridis")`, `scale_*_continuous_diverging(palette = "Blue-Red")`, and the HCL generators (`sequential_hcl()`, `diverging_hcl()`) used by the brand-seeded scales in `theme-project.R`.
- `emmeans` for estimated marginal means and pairwise contrasts: `emmeans(model, specs = "var")`, `pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")`.
- `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()` as the rendering layer for emmeans-derived contrasts. Never `ggpubr::stat_compare_means()`, which performs unadjusted pairwise t-tests by default.
- `ggh4x` for nested or hierarchical faceting: `facet_nested()`, `facet_nested_wrap()`, `guide_axis_nested()`.
- `ragg` for raster output via `ggsave(device = ragg::agg_png)`.
- `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` for the colour-vision-deficiency check.
- `showtext` (optional) for the project font; without it `theme_project()` falls back to the device's default font.

Do not introduce additional plotting packages without amending this list. Do not reach for `cowplot` themes when `theme_minimal()` or `theme_project()` will do. Do not hand-write manual hex colour vectors as data scales: use the `colorspace` palettes or the brand-seeded constructors in `theme-project.R`, both of which keep palettes CVD-checkable. A single fixed colour for a single-group or highlight geom is permitted and is not a "data scale".

## Using the files in this skill

Source the theme and palette functions from the skill folder:

```r
source(here::here(".agents", "skills", "pub-figures", "theme-project.R"))
```

If the folder was copied into `.claude/skills/` rather than linked, use that path instead. `theme_project()` here is the full version of the simple `theme_project()` from the ggplot chapter: same name and `base_size` argument, plus a font, furniture colours and an `axis_type` argument.

## Audience must be determined first

Identify the audience as one of `journal-lab-report`, `poster`, `talk`, or `public-engagement` before writing any plotting code. Styling, annotation density, and title framing all depend on the answer.

If the audience is not specified, ask (see *Missing information*). If proceeding without an answer, default to `journal-lab-report` and record the assumption at the top of the script:

```r
# Audience not specified; defaulting to journal-lab-report.
# Re-run with explicit audience if poster, talk, or public-engagement intended.
```

Then state in one sentence each: the variables and their types (continuous, discrete, date/time), the scientific question, the chart type the variable structure calls for, whether raw data will be shown, and whether statistical annotations are required.

## Statistical annotations require a model object

Do not annotate test statistics, p-values, or confidence intervals unless a fitted model object exists: fitted by code in this project that you have run or can read, or present in the user's live R session where your tool can see it. Fabricating values from descriptive data is a serious error. If there is no model, omit annotations and insert this placeholder for the legend:

> LEGEND PLACEHOLDER. Model object required to supply the test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and adjustment method. Do not fabricate.

## Chart selection

| Variable 1 | Variable 2 | Variable 3 | Default chart |
|------------|------------|------------|---------------|
| Continuous | — | — | Raincloud (`ggdist::stat_halfeye` + boxplot + jitter) |
| Continuous | Continuous | — | Scatter plot |
| Continuous | Continuous | Discrete | Scatter, colour and shape mapped to discrete |
| Discrete | — | — | Bar chart of counts |
| Discrete | Continuous | — | Raincloud per group; boxplot if many groups; bar only if one summary value per group |
| Discrete | Discrete | — | Heatmap of counts |
| Discrete | Discrete | Continuous | Heatmap of the continuous variable |
| Date | Continuous | — | Line chart |
| Date | Continuous | Discrete | Line chart, one line per group |

If a chart not in this table is requested, select the closest matching entry, generate the code, and record both the request and the substitution in a comment at the top of the script (and in the pull request description, if there is one).

## Colour

The colour-vision-deficiency check (`cvdPlot()`, below) is the final arbiter: a palette that fails it must be replaced, regardless of brand intent.

**No brand specified (default).** Use `colorspace::scale_*` functions, matched to data structure.

**Brand specified.** When the request names a brand colour (for example, "use a brand colour of darkblue"), call `set_brand("darkblue")` once after sourcing `theme-project.R`. `set_brand()` accepts any R colour name or hex string. The brand colour then seeds:

- single-colour and highlight geoms, via `brand_base()`;
- sequential continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_seq()`;
- the **high** arm of diverging continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_div(midpoint = <value>)`. The low arm is the brand's complementary hue, so the two arms always contrast, unless you name a second brand colour with `set_brand(<brand>, div_low = <colour>)`.

**Categorical colour is never brand-seeded.** One seed colour cannot generate a coherent, CVD-safe set of distinct hues. For unordered groups, use `colorspace` "Dark 2"; `scale_*_brand_qual()` in `theme-project.R` is the same palette and takes no `base` or `n` argument. The brand colour can still mark one focal group, with the other groups in grey.

| Data structure | Palette type | colorspace default | With a brand set |
|----------------|--------------|--------------------|------------------|
| Discrete, unordered groups | Qualitative | `Dark 2` | `Dark 2` (`scale_*_brand_qual()` is identical) |
| Discrete, ordered groups | Sequential discrete | `Purples 3` | `Purples 3` (the brand scales are continuous only) |
| Continuous, one-directional | Sequential | `Viridis` | `scale_*_brand_seq()` |
| Continuous, midpoint-centred | Diverging | `Blue-Red` | `scale_*_brand_div()` |

If a brand-seeded scale fails the CVD check, replace it with the colorspace default in the same row and record the fallback in a comment.

Categorical groupings must use redundant encoding: shape for points, linetype for lines. Colour alone is not sufficient.

## Audience-specific styling

| Element | Journal / lab report | Poster | Talk | Public engagement |
|---------|---------------------|--------|------|-------------------|
| Title above figure | No | Yes (explanatory) | Yes (explanatory) | Yes (explanatory) |
| Figure legend below | Yes (four elements) | Optional, abbreviated | No | No |
| Direct labelling | Sparingly | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Highlighting (grey out non-focal) | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Reference lines | Sparingly | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Statistical annotations | Precise p-values | Abbreviated | One key result | None |
| Base font size | 12 pt floor | 16 to 20 pt | 14 to 18 pt | 14 to 18 pt |
| Raw data shown | Always where n permits | Always | Always | Where it clarifies |

`theme_project()` defaults to `base_size = 12`, the journal/lab-report floor. Raise it explicitly via `theme_project(base_size = ...)` for poster, talk, and public-engagement figures per this table.

Descriptive titles state what the figure shows. Explanatory titles state what it means. Journal figures put descriptive framing in the legend, not the title.

## Showing raw data

| n per group | Display |
|-------------|---------|
| Up to ~30 | Strip plot or raincloud, all points visible |
| ~30 to ~300 | Raincloud with jittered points, alpha 0.3 to 0.5 |
| ~300 to ~3000 | Beeswarm or 2D density |
| > ~3000 | Hexbin or 2D contour |

## Statistical annotations workflow

Pairwise contrasts come from `emmeans::emmeans()` and `emmeans::pairs()` with an explicit adjustment method (`tukey`, `holm`, or similar). Render brackets with `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()`, supplying a data frame of contrasts.

Filter to significant contrasts before drawing. Format p-values with `scales::label_pvalue()` so very small values appear as `<0.001` rather than `0.000`.

A worked example is in `emmeans-bridge.R`.

## Error bars

Three options, not interchangeable:

- **Standard deviation:** spread of individual observations. Use when describing population variability.
- **Standard error of the mean:** precision of the sample mean. Shrinks with sample size.
- **95% confidence interval:** the recommended default. Prefer model-based intervals via `emmeans` where a model exists, otherwise from `stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal)`.

The choice must appear in the y axis label.

## Multiple panels and shared legends

When composing panels with `patchwork` and `plot_layout(guides = "collect")`, collection merges only guides that are identical in aesthetic, scale, breaks, and title (`name`). It deduplicates by guide specification, not by visual appearance, and it never removes a guide it judges different. Two failures follow: panels that encode the same variable through different aesthetics (`fill` in one, `colour` plus `shape` in another) or different palettes produce one legend each; and a panel encoding a genuinely different variable produces its own legend, which is correct.

Resolve the layout from the plot specifications:

- **Same variable, same palette, across all panels:** produce one shared legend. Designate the panel with the richest encoding (e.g. colour plus shape) as the legend-bearer, because that legend is a complete key for the simpler panels but not the reverse. Apply the identical scale call and an identical `name` in every panel, then suppress the guide on every non-bearing panel with `guides(<aesthetic> = "none")`. Record the choice of bearer in a comment.
- **Panels encode different variables:** do not force collection into one key. Keep the separate legends; merging them would mislabel a panel.

A mismatched `name`, a differing aesthetic or scale, or a missing suppression line will silently leave more than one legend for the same variable. After composing, confirm exactly one legend appears per distinct variable. A worked skeleton is in `patchwork-template.R`.

## Saving

Always save to `outputs/figures/` via `here::here()` in both PDF and PNG formats. Specify `width`, `height`, `units`, and `dpi` explicitly; do not rely on `ggsave()` defaults. Use `ragg::agg_png` as the device for PNG output with `bg = "white"`. PDF uses the default device.

## Accessibility check

The agent cannot verify visual accessibility. Insert this line at the end of the script and flag it for the investigator to run and inspect:

```r
if (interactive()) colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1)
```

If the four-panel simulation shows groups becoming indistinguishable under deuteranopia, protanopia, or tritanopia, the palette or redundant encoding must be revised. For brand-seeded scales, a failed check requires falling back to the `colorspace` default named in the colour table; brand intent does not override accessibility.

## Pre-flight checklist (agent-verifiable items only)

Before declaring the script complete, confirm:

- Both axes labelled with name and unit, or just name for dimensionless variables.
- Bar chart axes start at zero; other axes cropped to the data range.
- Faceted panels share scale unless a comment justifies freeing it.
- Composite figures collect to one legend per distinct variable; non-bearing panels suppress their guide with `guides(... = "none")` and all retained scales share an identical `name`.
- Palette applied via `colorspace::scale_*` functions or the brand-seeded constructors in `theme-project.R`, never hand-written hex vectors as data scales. Single fixed colours for single-group or highlight geoms are permitted.
- Categorical colour uses `Dark 2` (directly or via `scale_*_brand_qual()`), not a brand-seeded palette.
- A brand-seeded scale that the colour-vision-deficiency check would fail is replaced by its `colorspace` default; the fallback is recorded in a comment.
- Categorical grouping carries redundant encoding (shape or linetype).
- Statistical annotations sourced from a fitted model object, never from descriptive data.
- None of the forbidden chart types in *House rules*.
- Default theme is `theme_project()`, `theme_minimal()`, or `theme_classic()`. Never `theme_grey()`.
- `theme_project()` base font size matches the audience floor (12 pt journal; 14 to 20 pt otherwise).
- File saved to `outputs/figures/` as both PDF and PNG with explicit dimensions.
- `cvdPlot()` call, wrapped in `if (interactive())`, inserted at the end of the script with a comment flagging it for the investigator.

## Supplementary files in this skill directory

- `raincloud-template.R`: figure skeleton with palette, theme, and saving.
- `emmeans-bridge.R`: worked emmeans-to-ggpubr annotation pattern.
- `theme-project.R`: project theme plus brand-seeded HCL palette constructors.
- `patchwork-template.R`: composite-figure skeleton with collected legend and guide suppression.

# ==============================================================================
# Project theme and palette construction for ggplot2.
#
# Colour policy (authoritative; see pub-figures SKILL.md):
#   * No brand set         -> use colorspace palettes directly.
#   * Brand set            -> set_brand("darkblue") sets the base colour (used by
#                             single-colour and highlight geoms) and reseeds the
#                             sequential ramp and the diverging HIGH arm. The
#                             low arm becomes the brand's complementary hue
#                             unless set_brand() is given div_low. Sequential
#                             and diverging are
#                             generated via colorspace HCL generators
#                             (CVD-robust, monotonic luminance).
#   * Categorical colour is NEVER brand-seeded: scale_*_brand_qual() delegate to
#                             colorspace "Dark 2", which sizes itself to the data.
#                             A single seed cannot make a coherent multi-hue set.
#   * Single-group / highlight geoms default to brand_base(), teal until reset.
#
# Manual hex palettes are NOT used as data scales. Only the base colour is used
# directly, and only for single-colour or highlight geoms.
#
# theme_project() here is the full version of the simple theme_project() taught
# in the ggplot chapter (Block 3: Themes and scales). It keeps the same name and
# base_size argument, and adds a font, furniture colours and axis_type.
#
# Dependencies: ggplot2 (>= 3.5), colorspace, scales; showtext + sysfonts for
#   fonts (optional: without them the device's default font is used);
#   colorBlindness for the accessibility check.
# ==============================================================================

library(ggplot2)
library(colorspace)

# ---- Brand state and setter --------------------------------------------------
# A single mutable brand state lets one call rebrand everything downstream.
# `set_brand("darkblue")` sets the base colour, which seeds the sequential ramp
# and the diverging high arm. Accepts any R colour name or hex string.

.brand_state <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.brand_state$base    <- "#09baba"  # teal default
.brand_state$div_low <- "#2c4977"  # navy default for the diverging low arm

#' Normalise a colour name or hex to a hex string
#' @keywords internal
.as_hex <- function(col) {
  rgb <- grDevices::col2rgb(col)  # accepts R colour names and hex
  grDevices::rgb(rgb[1], rgb[2], rgb[3], maxColorValue = 255)
}

#' Set the project brand colour
#'
#' Sets the base colour used by single-colour and highlight geoms, the
#' sequential ramp and the diverging high arm. Call once at the top of a
#' script: `set_brand("darkblue")`. Accepts any R colour name or hex string.
#'
#' @param base Brand colour (name or hex).
#' @param div_low Optional colour for the diverging low arm. If `NULL` (the
#'   default), the low arm uses the hue opposite the brand colour on the HCL
#'   colour wheel, so the two arms always contrast.
#' @return Invisibly, the resolved brand state as a list.
#' @export
set_brand <- function(base, div_low = NULL) {
  .brand_state$base <- .as_hex(base)
  .brand_state$div_low <- if (is.null(div_low)) {
    .complement_of(.brand_state$base)
  } else {
    .as_hex(div_low)
  }
  invisible(as.list(.brand_state))
}

#' Colour with the opposite HCL hue, for the diverging low arm
#' @keywords internal
.complement_of <- function(col) {
  hue <- (.hue_of(col) + 180) %% 360
  colorspace::hex(colorspace::polarLUV(L = 40, C = 60, H = hue), fixup = TRUE)
}

#' Reset the brand to the teal/navy default
#' @return Invisibly, the resolved brand state as a list.
#' @export
reset_brand <- function() {
  .brand_state$base    <- "#09baba"
  .brand_state$div_low <- "#2c4977"
  invisible(as.list(.brand_state))
}

#' Current brand base colour
#'
#' Returns the current brand base as a hex string. It is a function, not a value,
#' so it reflects the most recent `set_brand()` call. Use as `brand_base()`.
#' @return A hex colour string.
#' @export
brand_base <- function() .brand_state$base

# ---- Internal: font registration ---------------------------------------------

# Returns TRUE if `family` is available to showtext, FALSE otherwise, so the
# theme can fall back to the device's default font rather than warn on every
# text element.
.register_project_font <- function(family = "Open Sans") {
  if (!requireNamespace("showtext", quietly = TRUE)) {
    return(FALSE)
  }
  showtext::showtext_auto(enable = TRUE)
  if (!(family %in% sysfonts::font_families())) {
    try(sysfonts::font_add_google(family, family), silent = TRUE)
  }
  family %in% sysfonts::font_families()
}

# ---- theme_project() ---------------------------------------------------------

#' Project theme
#'
#' A composable ggplot2 theme controlling non-data aesthetics only. It sets no
#' data-encoding colours; pair it with a scale constructor (see below). Furniture
#' colours (title, axis labels, gridlines) are decorative and need not be
#' CVD-safe; the strip background is deliberately neutral grey so it is not
#' mistaken for a data signal when a fill palette is present. Furniture colours do
#' not track the brand by design; rebrand them by editing the literals below.
#'
#' @param base_size Base font size in points. Default 12 (journal/lab-report
#'   floor; raise to 14-20 for poster, talk, or public-engagement).
#' @param base_family Base font family. Default "Open Sans".
#' @param base_line_size Base line size. Default 0.5.
#' @param base_rect_size Base rectangle size. Default 0.5.
#' @param axis_type "categorical" or "continuous"; controls gridlines.
#' @return A ggplot2 theme object.
#' @export
theme_project <- function(base_size = 12,
                          base_family = "Open Sans",
                          base_line_size = 0.5,
                          base_rect_size = 0.5,
                          axis_type = c("categorical", "continuous")) {

  axis_type <- match.arg(axis_type)
  if (!.register_project_font(base_family)) {
    base_family <- ""  # device default font
  }

  title_col <- "#2c4977"  # decorative furniture only
  label_col <- "#41566f"
  muted_col <- "#5d6b7d"

  base <- ggplot2::theme(
    line = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "#000000", linewidth = base_line_size),
    rect = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", colour = "#000000",
                                 linewidth = base_rect_size),
    text = ggplot2::element_text(family = base_family, colour = "#000000",
                                 size = base_size),
    plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0,
                                       size = ggplot2::rel(1.4),
                                       margin = ggplot2::margin(8, 0, 6, 0),
                                       colour = title_col),
    plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0, size = ggplot2::rel(1.1),
                                          margin = ggplot2::margin(2, 0, 0, 0),
                                          colour = label_col),
    plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 1, size = ggplot2::rel(0.8),
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(6, 0, 0, 0),
                                         colour = muted_col),
    axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = muted_col, size = ggplot2::rel(0.9)),
    axis.title.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = label_col,
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 4, 0, 0)),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(colour = muted_col, size = ggplot2::rel(0.9)),
    axis.title.x = ggplot2::element_text(colour = label_col,
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(4, 0, 0, 0)),
    panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    strip.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#e9e9e9", colour = NA),
    strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#2c4977",
                                       size = ggplot2::rel(1.0)),
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    axis.line = ggplot2::element_line(linewidth = base_line_size, colour = "black"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

  grid_col <- "#dedddd"
  if (axis_type == "continuous") {
    grid_theme <- ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col),
      panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col)
    )
  } else {
    grid_theme <- ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col),
      panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank()
    )
  }

  base + grid_theme
}

# ---- Brand-seeded palette constructors ---------------------------------------
# These wrap colorspace HCL generators, seeded on the current brand colour, so
# the ramp is perceptually based with monotonic luminance. With no set_brand()
# call the seed is teal; callers may also pass `base`/`low`/`high` explicitly,
# which always overrides the brand state. If no brand is intended at all, use
# colorspace::scale_*_{qualitative,sequential,diverging} directly.

#' Hue (HCL) of a colour, for seeding colorspace generators
#' @keywords internal
.hue_of <- function(col) {
  hcl <- colorspace::coords(as(colorspace::hex2RGB(.as_hex(col)), "polarLUV"))
  unname(hcl[, "H"])
}

#' Brand-seeded sequential scale (colour)
#'
#' Single-hue sequential ramp seeded on `base`, generated in HCL so luminance is
#' monotonic. Light-to-dark by default.
#'
#' @param base Seed colour. Defaults to the current `brand_base()`.
#' @param n Number of interpolation stops. Default 7.
#' @param ... Passed to `ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_seq <- function(base = brand_base(), n = 7, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::sequential_hcl(
    n = n, h = .hue_of(base), c = c(70, 10), l = c(25, 95), power = 1.2,
    rev = TRUE
  )
  ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn(colours = cols, ...)
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_seq
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_seq <- function(base = brand_base(), n = 7, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::sequential_hcl(
    n = n, h = .hue_of(base), c = c(70, 10), l = c(25, 95), power = 1.2,
    rev = TRUE
  )
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(colours = cols, ...)
}

#' Brand-seeded diverging scale (colour)
#'
#' Two-hue diverging ramp seeded on `low` and `high`, generated in HCL with a
#' balanced neutral midpoint. Supply `midpoint` to centre on a meaningful value.
#'
#' @param low Seed colour for the low arm. Defaults to navy or, after
#'   `set_brand()`, to the brand's complementary hue (or its `div_low`).
#' @param high Seed colour for the high arm. Defaults to the current `brand_base()`.
#' @param midpoint Data value mapped to the neutral midpoint. Default 0.
#' @param n Number of interpolation stops (odd recommended). Default 11.
#' @param ... Passed to `ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_div <- function(low = .brand_state$div_low,
                                    high = brand_base(),
                                    midpoint = 0, n = 11, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::diverging_hcl(
    n = n, h = c(.hue_of(low), .hue_of(high)),
    c = 80, l = c(35, 95), power = 1.0
  )
  ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn(
    colours = cols, rescaler = ~ scales::rescale_mid(.x, mid = midpoint), ...
  )
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_div
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_div <- function(low = .brand_state$div_low,
                                  high = brand_base(),
                                  midpoint = 0, n = 11, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::diverging_hcl(
    n = n, h = c(.hue_of(low), .hue_of(high)),
    c = 80, l = c(35, 95), power = 1.0
  )
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = cols, rescaler = ~ scales::rescale_mid(.x, mid = midpoint), ...
  )
}

#' Qualitative scale (colour) for categorical groups
#'
#' Categorical palettes are NOT brand-seeded. A single brand colour cannot
#' generate a coherent, CVD-safe multi-hue set: spreading hues from one anchor
#' discards the seed's own chroma and luminance and walks through arbitrary
#' intermediate hues. This constructor therefore delegates to `colorspace`'s
#' `Dark 2` qualitative palette, which is built for mutual distinctness and is
#' CVD-tested, and which sizes itself to the number of groups (so it cannot raise
#' "Insufficient values in manual scale"). Reserve the brand colour for the
#' sequential ramp, the diverging high arm, and single-colour or highlight geoms,
#' where one seed genuinely works. Always pair with a redundant aesthetic (shape
#' or linetype).
#'
#' @param ... Passed to `colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_qual <- function(...) {
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", ...)
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_qual
#' @param ... Passed to `colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative()`.
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_qual <- function(...) {
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", ...)
}

# ---- Example usage -----------------------------------------------------------
# Set a brand once, then everything downstream follows:
#   set_brand("darkblue")
#   ... + scale_fill_brand_seq()          # darkblue-seeded sequential
#   ... + geom_point(colour = brand_base())# darkblue single-colour geom
#   ... + scale_fill_brand_div(midpoint = 0) # complementary low arm, darkblue high
#
# No brand (default path): colorspace directly.
#   ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = g, shape = g)) + geom_point() +
#     colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") +
#     theme_project(axis_type = "continuous")
#
# Per-call override (ignores brand state):
#   ... + scale_fill_brand_seq(base = "#2c4977")
#
# Accessibility check is mandatory; a brand-seeded palette that fails it falls
# back to its colorspace default (Viridis for sequential, Blue-Red for diverging):
#   colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1)

# raincloud-template.R
# Figure skeleton: raincloud for Discrete x Continuous, with palette, theme
# and saving.
# Audience not specified; defaulting to journal-lab-report.
# Re-run with explicit audience if poster, talk, or public-engagement intended.
#
# Colour policy (see pub-figures SKILL.md):
#   * Groups are categorical, so colour comes from colorspace qualitative
#     "Dark 2" whether or not a brand is set. Categorical colour is never
#     brand-seeded; scale_*_brand_qual() in theme-project.R is the same palette.
#   * If a brand is set with set_brand(), use brand_base() only for
#     single-colour or highlight geoms.


library(ggplot2)
library(ggdist)
library(colorspace)
library(here)
library(scales)


# The skill's single copy lives in .agents/skills/. If you copied the folder
# into .claude/skills/ instead of linking it, change this path to match.
source(here::here(".agents", "skills", "pub-figures", "theme-project.R"))

# data |> expects: group (factor), value (numeric)
fig1 <-
  data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = value, colour = group, shape = group)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    aes(fill = group),
    adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, justification = -0.2,
    .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.05, seed = 1),
    alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5
  ) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") +
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") +
  scale_shape_discrete() + # redundant encoding alongside colour
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Value (unit)") +
  theme_project()

# Save as PDF and PNG with explicit dimensions ----
fig_dir <- here::here("outputs", "figures")
dir.create(fig_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

ggsave(
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig1.pdf"), fig1,
  width = 160, height = 110, units = "mm"
)
ggsave(
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig1.png"), fig1,
  width = 160, height = 110, units = "mm", dpi = 300,
  device = ragg::agg_png, bg = "white"
)

# Accessibility check; investigator to run and inspect. Wrapped in
# interactive() so a run with Rscript does not write a stray Rplots.pdf.
if (interactive()) colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1)

# emmeans-bridge.R
# Worked emmeans-to-ggpubr annotation pattern.
# Requires a fitted model object: fitted by code in this project that you have
# run or can read, or present in the user's live R session where your tool can
# see it. Never fabricate test statistics from descriptive data.

library(emmeans)
library(ggpubr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# model <- lm(value ~ group, data = data)  # supplied upstream

# fig1 <- ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) + geom_boxplot()   # supplied upstream
#
# ADAPT: `fig1` is your existing ggplot. `panel_yrange()` reads layer 1 by
# default, which must be the geom whose data the brackets sit above (e.g. the
# boxplot). If layer 1 is a reference line or similar, pass the correct index,
# e.g. panel_yrange(fig1, layer = 2L).

emm <- emmeans::emmeans(model, specs = "group")

# lowest and highest y values drawn by one layer ----
panel_yrange <- function(p, layer = 1L) {
  d <- ggplot2::ggplot_build(p)$data[[layer]]
  # positional y columns ggplot may compute
  cols <- intersect(
    c("ymin_final", "ymin", "lower", "ymax_final", "ymax", "upper", "y"),
    names(d)
  )
  if (length(cols) == 0L) {
    stop("No y-position column found in layer ", layer, ".")
  }
  range(unlist(d[cols]), na.rm = TRUE)
}

y_range <- panel_yrange(fig1)
# step between brackets as a fraction of the data range, so positions work for
# negative values and for data far from zero
y_step <- 0.07 * diff(y_range)

contrasts_df <-
  pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    contrast, delim = " - ", names = c("group1", "group2")
  ) |>
  # emmeans wraps level names containing spaces or operators in parentheses
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(
    c(group1, group2), \(x) stringr::str_remove_all(x, "^\\(|\\)$")
  )) |>
  dplyr::filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    p.label = scales::label_pvalue()(p.value),
    y.position = y_range[2] + y_step * dplyr::row_number()
  )

# headroom so the top bracket isn't clipped: highest position + one more step
y_top <- y_range[2] + y_step * (nrow(contrasts_df) + 1)

fig1 +
  stat_pvalue_manual(
    contrasts_df, label = "p.label", tip.length = 0.01
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(NA, y_top))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Composite figure: panels sharing ONE collected legend.
#
# Precondition: every panel maps the SAME grouping variable to the SAME palette.
# If a panel encodes a different variable, do not use this pattern for it; give it
# its own scale and accept a separate legend (forcing one key would mislabel it).
#
# Colour policy (see pub-figures SKILL.md):
#   * The shared grouping variable is categorical, so every panel uses
#     colorspace qualitative "Dark 2", with or without a brand. Categorical
#     colour is never brand-seeded. Keep an identical `name` across panels so
#     the legend collects to one.
#
# Legend-bearer: chosen here by richness of encoding. If unclear, use the panel
# with the most aesthetics mapped to the group and record the choice.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Legend-bearing panel: richest encoding (colour + shape), legend retained.
# Redundant encoding (shape) is required by the skill, and conveniently makes this
# panel a complete key for the simpler ones.
p_keep <- data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x1, y = y1, colour = group_var, shape = group_var)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15), name = "Group") +
  labs(x = "X1", y = "Y1") 

# Other panels: identical palette and identical name, guide suppressed.
# Suppression is what collection cannot do for you. Repeat per additional panel.
p_other <- data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x2, y = y2, colour = group_var)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") +
  labs(x = "X2", y = "Y2") +
  guides(colour = "none")

# Letters refer to plots in the order added (A = p_keep, B = p_other).
layout <- "
AB
"

fig1 <- p_keep + p_other +
  patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

fig1

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
text:
Glossary




term
definition



canary
A fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.


front matter
The block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill's name and description, or a Quarto document's options.


instruction file
A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


skill
A reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.


symbolic link
A file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Three kinds of guardrail
Your instruction fileA file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project’s standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees. and skills are requests: nothing guarantees that the model follows them. In this block you watch the controls that do hold refuse something. You also find the route each one misses, so you know what your repository prevents and what it only detects.
⏱ ~25 minutes · Start on main (or checkpoint-skills), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.
Beyond the instruction file, there are three kinds of guardrail. Each catches what the others miss.
Prevent where you can, detect everything, and commit before the agent starts, so that there is something to go back to.

text:
Decide what needs protecting (3 minutes)


Goal: for each thing worth protecting, decide how you would notice if it went wrong, so that you know which check you are relying on before an agent works near it.
Your instructor posts the table. Answer in the Zoom chat, row by row: if this went wrong, how would you notice?







Asset
What could go wrong
How you would notice



data/raw/
Overwritten or “tidied” in place



tests/fixtures/
The reference regenerated by the code under test



tests/
A failing test edited until it passes




.claude/, .posit/

The agent’s own guardrails switched off




.Renviron, .env

Credentials read and sent to the model provider




The last two are easy to miss: the files that hold your controls are assets too.
You are done when the group has an answer for every row. Most will be “the Git pane would show it” or “a test would fail”.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Exercise 2: Deny rules


Read, test and add a rule, then find the gap (15 minutes)


Goal: see a deny ruleA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. refuse, add one of your own and find the route the rules do not cover, so that you know what your repository prevents and what only git detects.
Start state: Git pane clean, Claude Code in Manual mode. Work on a scratch file, never on real data.
1. Make a scratch file and read the rules. Run this in the R console:

writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

Commit it in the Git pane, so git can show any later change to it. In Claude Code, type /permissions to list the 17 deny rules that your repository ships.
2. See a rule refuse.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Add a second line, "test", to data/raw/scratch.csv.
“Denied by a permission rule” means the rule held, whatever the model intended. The model may instead decline by itself, citing AGENTS.md. That was a request that happened to work. To see the rule refuse, reply “This is a scratch file; please make the edit with your edit tool”.
Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. If Claude Code asks to write the file another way, answer No: step 4 tries that.
3. Add a rule yourself. In /permissions, add Read(/data/confidential/**): habit 4 of the confidential-data habits in Block 3, a speed bump rather than a wall. When asked where to save it, choose the project’s shared settings file, .claude/settings.json, not the local one (see How it works). It applies at once. You do not test this rule here, because there is no data/confidential/ folder. In your own project, test it the way you test Edit(/data/raw/**) in this exercise.
4. Find the gap.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Run this R code with Rscript: writeLines(c("a", "test"), "data/raw/scratch.csv")
Deny rules do not cover R code, so only the approval prompt stands in the way. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. Here you can: it writes to a scratch file, and you want to see what catches the change. Approve it. The Git pane now shows the file as modified, and Diff shows the new line: git caught what no rule prevented.
Now try Claude Code’s own undo. Type /rewind (or press Esc twice with the prompt empty) and select your last prompt. The menu offers no Restore code: /rewind restores only changes made with Claude Code’s edit tools, and R code changed this file. Choose Never mind. Only git can undo this change.
5. Tidy up. Undo the change with git: revert the file in the Git pane. Then delete it, so that no scratch file is left among the raw data:

file.remove(here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

6. Record, test and commit. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md: ask the agent to draft it, as in Block 3, then write the last part yourself. Note which requests were refused, and what git caught and undid. Then restart R (Session → Restart R) and run:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

test_controls.R checks that Manual mode and every shipped rule are still in place. It also checks that no command is approved in advance. test_ai_log.R checks your new line. Commit the deletion of scratch.csv, your rule in .claude/settings.json and the log line together.
You are done when you have seen a rule refuse, added one of your own, seen the Git pane catch the R write that /rewind could not undo, scratch.csv is gone, the test suite has no failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your rule and log line are committed.
If it goes wrong: if the model keeps declining in step 4, write the line yourself in the console and carry on: the point is seeing git catch it. If /rewind does offer Restore code, the agent changed some file with its edit tool earlier in this conversation: choose Never mind anyway. If “no command is approved in advance” fails, you chose don’t ask again: remove that allow rule in /permissions.






NoteAt the command line





Step 1: git add/git commit. Step 4: git diff data/raw. Step 5: git restore, then git rm data/raw/scratch.csv. Step 6: Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')", then git add/git commit. See checking work.











NoteWhere each control acts








Route 1: the agent’s edit tool


Agent asks to edit data/raw/scratch.csv


edit tool


Deny rule refuses




Route 2: R code the agent runs


Agent runs writeLines() on the same file


approval prompt only


File changed


detected by


git status (and, from Block 7, a checksum test on the raw data)


undone by


The Git pane’s Revert. Not /rewind: it tracks only the edit tool’s changes




Requests, on every route


AGENTS.md and skills: the model may or may not follow them



With no hook registered, only the approval prompt stands between R code and the file, and only git can undo what it writes. Prevent where you can, detect everywhere, and commit first. And test every control: one you have not seen refuse something is one you are assuming.











NoteHow it works: where the rules live





Your repository’s .claude/settings.json starts the project in Manual mode ("defaultMode": "default": it asks before every edit and command). It also holds 17 deny rules. They protect the raw data, the data provider’s note, the codebook, the checks, the references, the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment. and the settings themselves. You never need to edit the file: /permissions shows the rules and adds new ones.


{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Read(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}


A leading / anchors a pattern to the project root. Read and Edit rules cover Claude Code’s own file tools, simple file commands it recognises (such as cat, head, tail, sed and tee) and shell redirects (> file). They do not cover R code that it runs, or a command that never names the file, such as a search of the whole project with grep -r. The documentation does not list rm, mv or cp. The rules protect named files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write its scripts and tests in Blocks 7 and 8. Edit(/renv.lock) keeps renv::status() a real check.
Why the shared settings file. /permissions can save a rule to .claude/settings.json, which is committed with the project, or to the local .claude/settings.local.json, which git ignores. Only a rule in the shared file reaches a commit, and so reaches everyone who clones the repository. Answering don’t ask again saves an allow rule, usually in the local file. That is why test_controls.R checks that no command is approved in advance.









TipUsing another tool





The exercises use Claude Code. Posit Assistant sets permissions per tool in .posit/assistant/settings.json (for example "bash": {"rm *": "deny"}). deny rules hold in every mode, including auto and YOLO. It has no documented path rules for file edits, so rely on the Git pane in step 4 of Exercise 2. It blocks reading .env and .Renviron by default.









TipInstructor: demonstration of a guard hook





A hookA command the assistant runs automatically at a fixed point, for example before every tool call. A hook can block the call, but it matches text, so a differently written command can get past it. is a command that Claude Code itself (the harnessThe software around a model that keeps the conversation, sends it to the model, runs the tools the model asks for and sends back their results. Claude Code is a harness; so is a chat object made with ellmer., not the model) runs before every tool callA single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls.. So it does not depend on the model following a request. Your instructor saves the guard hook from Going further as hooks/guard_protected_paths.R (the template does not ship hooks/). They register it, run Test the hook before you trust it on the demonstration machine, and repeat step 4. The hook, written in R, blocks any call that mentions data/raw, so it blocks this one before any approval prompt. Then they try the same write using here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"). The text data/raw never appears, so the hook lets it through. A text-matching hook is a tripwire, not a wall; the Git pane still shows the change. The GitHub review gate (CODEOWNERSA GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review., branch protectionGitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.) is set up in the self-study page on GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent.









NoteDo you need a hook?





The workshop ships no hooks. Before you add one to your own project, ask these questions in order:


Can a deny rule say it? If the danger is a named file or a named command, use a rule: it needs no code and nothing to maintain.

Must it hold whatever route the agent takes? Then neither a rule nor a hook is enough. Keep the thing out of reach (outside the project, or behind the sandbox where it is available), and detect changes with git or a checksum.

Is it “every time X happens, do Y”? For example: run lintr or styler after each edit, run the tests before the agent says it is finished, notify you when it is waiting, or log every call. That is what hooks are for.

Is it a judgement call? For example, “prefer a mixed model when animals are measured twice”. Then write an instruction or a skill (Block 4).

A hook has costs:


It is code. It needs testing (Test the hook before you trust it, in Going further) and keeping up to date.

It runs on every matching call. A hook written in R adds R’s start-up time to each one.

It fails open by default. If it crashes, the call goes ahead. From Claude Code v2.1.295, adding "onFailure": "block" to the hook makes a crash block the call instead.

It must match every route. On Windows, Claude Code often runs commands through its PowerShell tool, so a hook that checks commands must match PowerShell as well as Bash.

It never approves anything. A hook can only add a check: a call it lets through still faces your usual approval prompt.

Ways to set one up:

Add a hooks block to .claude/settings.json yourself, as in A guard hook, in Going further.
Ask Claude to draft the script and the settings for you, then read them and paste them in yourself. In the workshop repository, the deny rules keep it out of .claude/ and hooks/.
Set the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1 before you run /init. Claude Code then asks which of instruction files, skills and hooks to set up, explores the project, and shows you a proposal before it writes anything. Two cautions:

if you let it set up instruction files, it writes a CLAUDE.md, which hides an existing AGENTS.md (Block 4);
once Edit(/.claude/**) is in place, its writes to the settings are refused, so run it before you add that rule.



To see which hooks are registered, type /hooks.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: let an agent work in Manual mode in a repository where raw data, references and checks are protected, trusted because you have seen a deny rule refuse, seen git catch and undo the route it misses, and have a test that fails if the rules are weakened.

Check: watch every control refuse something, and find the route it does not cover. What gets past the rules shows in the Git pane, Block 7’s checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. test or test_controls.R.

Reproduce: the rules live in .claude/settings.json, committed with the project, so everyone who clones it gets the same protection. Commit before each agent task: git can undo any change since then, and /rewind cannot undo what R code wrote.

Record: your log line from step 6 notes which requests were refused and what git caught.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipA guard hook





Claude Code itself, the harness rather than the model, runs a PreToolUse hook before each tool call. It passes the hook the pending call as JSON on standard input (stdin). If the hook exits with status 2, the call is denied and its message is passed to the model. Exit status 0 does not approve the call: it goes on to your usual approval prompt. Claude Code and Posit Assistant use the same shape for this, so one script can serve both.
The guard below is written in R. It denies any edit, shell command or R code that mentions a protected path.

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# hooks/guard_protected_paths.R ----
# PreToolUse guard for Claude Code and Posit Assistant.
# Reads the pending tool call from stdin and exits 2 (deny) if the call
# mentions a protected path. A tripwire, not a wall: see "Break your own
# guard".

protected <- c(
  "data/raw",
  "tests/fixtures",
  "make_reference.R",
  ".github/workflows"
)

payload <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  paste(readLines(file("stdin"), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"),
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

# search the whole tool input as text, so the same rule covers file edits,
# shell commands and R code whatever the tool calls its fields
call_text <- as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(payload$tool_input, auto_unbox = TRUE))
hits <- protected[vapply(protected, \(p) grepl(p, call_text, fixed = TRUE), logical(1))]

if (length(hits) > 0) {
  message(
    "Blocked by project guard: this ", payload$tool_name,
    " call refers to a protected path (", paste(hits, collapse = ", "), "). ",
    "Do not modify protected files; ask the user to do it."
  )
  quit(save = "no", status = 2)
}

quit(save = "no", status = 0)

The template does not ship hooks/: save the script yourself as hooks/guard_protected_paths.R, for example with usethis::edit_file("hooks/guard_protected_paths.R"). It runs with Rscript --vanilla, so it does not start renv. jsonlite must be installed in your user library.
Register it with Claude Code by adding a hooks key to .claude/settings.json, alongside the existing permissions key. The deny rules protect .claude/, so make this edit yourself, not through the agent.
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|Bash|PowerShell",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "Rscript --vanilla \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/hooks/guard_protected_paths.R",
            "onFailure": "block"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
The matcher lists the tool names the hook runs for. On Windows, Claude Code often runs commands with its PowerShell tool rather than Bash, so a guard that matches only Bash would never see them. "onFailure": "block" makes the call fail if the hook itself crashes (Claude Code v2.1.295 or later; on older versions, delete that line and rely on the test below). Type /hooks to check that Claude Code has registered it.
Register it with Posit Assistant in .posit/assistant/settings.json. The tool names differ: edit, bash, and executeR for R code run in your session.
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "edit|bash|executeR",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
Posit Assistant runs project hooks only in a workspace you have trusted.


Test the hook before you trust it


Goal: check that the guard denies a protected path and allows a harmless call, so that you know it works before you rely on it.
Hooks fail open by default. If the script crashes, for example because jsonlite is not installed, both tools continue as if the hook had allowed the call, unless you set "onFailure": "block" in Claude Code. Even then, a hook that runs but checks the wrong thing allows everything. So test the script directly, without the agent. The R below runs the hook exactly as Claude Code does: as a fresh Rscript --vanilla process, given the tool call on standard input. It works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.
In the R console:

rscript <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript")
hook <- shQuote(here::here("hooks", "guard_protected_paths.R"))

run_hook <- function(json) {
  status <- system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", hook), input = json,
                    stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)
  status
}

# can the hook's own R session load jsonlite? 0 means yes
print(system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", "-e", shQuote("library(jsonlite)")),
              stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE))

# a call naming a protected path: expect 2
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript tests/make_reference.R"}}')

# a harmless call: expect 0
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript scripts/05_analysis.R"}}')

Any result other than 2 for the first call and 0 for the second means the hook is broken and is silently allowing everything.
Now repeat the request from step 4 of Exercise 2. The R code mentions data/raw, so the guard should deny it before you see an approval prompt.
To see exactly what each tool sends to hooks, add a temporary PostToolUse hook with no matcher. Make it append its input to a log file, then read the log. Posit Assistant’s hooks documentation gives an example.
You are done when the protected call returns 2, the harmless call returns 0, and the request from step 4 of Exercise 2 is denied before you see an approval prompt.











TipBreak your own guard







Red-team the tripwire


Goal: get a write past the guard hook, so that you see where a text-matching guard stops.
The live block removed the scratch file at the end. Recreate it first in the R console, then commit it from the Git pane:

writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

Prompt (Claude Code):
Run this R code:
writeLines(c("a", "test"), here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
The guard searches for the text data/raw. This call never contains it, because here::here() assembles the path from separate pieces, so the guard allows the call. A Windows path written with backslashes would also slip past.
This is the general limit of hooks that match text: they catch the obvious form of a dangerous action, not every way of expressing it. Claude Code’s documentation makes the same point about command patterns. A guard hook is a tripwire that stops accidents and makes intent visible; it is not a wall. The Git pane still shows the change. Revert the file there, then delete it and commit the deletion, as in steps 5 and 6 of Exercise 2.
You are done when the here::here() write has got past the guard, the Git pane has shown the change, and you have deleted scratch.csv again.


Why did here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv") get past the guard hook?

Hooks do not run for R codeThe guard matches the text 'data/raw', and the call never contains that texthere::here() runs with administrator rightsThe hook was registered for the wrong event

Your guard hook depends on jsonlite, which is not installed, and you have not set onFailure. What happens when the agent tries to edit a protected file?

The edit is blocked, because the hook could not approve itThe edit goes ahead: hooks fail open by default, so a crashing hook is treated as allowing the callThe agent stops and waits until jsonlite is installedThe edit is blocked only in plan mode










TipThe review gate on GitHub





Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely. There, the controls are on the repository itself: CODEOWNERS, branch protection and a CI check. The self-study page Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent sets them up.









TipFeedback hooks: useful, with a warning





Hooks can do more than block. A PostToolUse hook can run lintr on each R file the agent edits and pass the result back to it. A Stop hook can run the test suite and refuse to let the agent finish while tests fail. The second is powerful and dangerous: an agent that is told it cannot stop until tests pass may try to change the tests. Use it only when the deny rules and guard hook protect tests/.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Glossary




term
definition



branch protection
GitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.


checksum
A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.


CODEOWNERS
A GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


harness
The software around a model that keeps the conversation, sends it to the model, runs the tools the model asks for and sends back their results. Claude Code is a harness; so is a chat object made with ellmer.


hook
A command the assistant runs automatically at a fixed point, for example before every tool call. A hook can block the call, but it matches text, so a differently written command can get past it.


instruction file
A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


tool call
A single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Before you start
Cleaning mistakes are silent: a missing-value code treated as a measurement, the same animal kept twice, a row quietly dropped. Your instructor planted errors of these kinds in data/raw/voles_raw.csv. In this block an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. writes and runs the whole cleaning script from one command, working from a codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI. that you own. In Step 5 you find out which planted errors your cleaning caught, and how you know.
How you know is the point of the block. The cleaning script, the tests and the validation rules all come from your codebook, never from each other, so a misunderstanding in one of them cannot pass the others.
⏱ ~55 minutes · Start on main (or checkpoint-skills), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.
The steps follow the safe vibe-coding recipe from Block 3: the protections and the tests are in place first, then one command does the work, then you run the tests and the validation yourself.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Check the protections and the tests (2 minutes)


Goal: confirm that the protections and the tests are in place before any cleaning starts, so that a mistake by the agent is blocked or caught rather than found later.
1. Start state. The Git pane is clean, on main. If you are behind, switch to checkpoint-skills in the Git pane’s branch menu.
2. The protections. In Claude Code, type /permissions. Among the deny rulesA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files., find these four:


Edit(/data/raw/**): the raw data;

Read(/docs/data_note.md): the data provider’s note (Step 2 shows why);

Edit(/docs/codebook.csv): your codebook;

Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R): the tests.

3. The tests. In the Files pane, open tests/ and find test_cleaning.R and fixtures/raw_checksum.txt, a checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. of the raw file. The course team wrote the tests from the agreed codebook (the answer to Step 2) before any cleaning code existed. You run them in Step 4.
For every guardrail in the repository and what each one does, see How your workshop repository is guarded in Block 5.
You are done when you have seen the four rules and the two files.
If it goes wrong: if /permissions lists no rules, check that you started claude from the Terminal tab of the workshop repository. If the files are missing, ask your instructor: your fork may be older than the current template.
