title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 1: Profile the raw data
A model that reads a file gives you its impression of it. R gives you exact counts, and the codebook draft in Step 2 starts from them.


Profile (5 minutes)


Goal: count what is in the raw file with R, and make your own list of what looks wrong before the agent gives its view.
1. Run the profile. In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "00_profile.R"))

The shipped 00_profile.R only counts: it changes nothing and decides nothing. It reads data/raw/voles_raw.csv with every column as text, so codes such as 9999 and -1 stay exactly as entered. It prints three tables in the Console and saves each one to docs/:







File
What it lists
Look for



profile.csv
One row per column of the raw file: rows (n_rows), missing values (n_missing), distinct values (n_distinct), values that read as numbers (n_numeric), and the smallest and largest of those (min_numeric, max_numeric)
A minimum or maximum far from the rest, or from what the column could hold


profile_labels.csv
Every spelling of a sex or treatment_arm label, with its count (n)
Labels that differ only in spelling or case


profile_ids.csv
Each subject_id that occurs more than once (n), or whose length differs from the usual one (unusual_length)
For each ID: what would it be if typed correctly, and does that ID exist already?



2. Make your list. Write down at least three things that look wrong. Keep the list: you compare it with the agent’s draft in Step 2, with its plan in Step 3 and with the validation in Step 5.
3. Commit the three profile files, so that Step 2 starts from a clean Git pane.
You are done when the three profile files are committed and you have your list.
If it goes wrong: restart R (Session → Restart R) and run the line again.








NoteThe shipped scripts/00_profile.R






# scripts/00_profile.R ----
# Purpose: describe the raw file as entered, before any decision is made.
# Every column is read as character so codes such as 9999 or -1 appear
# exactly as entered.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

raw_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# one row per column: missingness, distinct values, numeric range ----
profile_df <- raw_df |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |>
  # suppressWarnings: text values become NA here by design
  mutate(value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))) |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    n_distinct = n_distinct(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_numeric = sum(!is.na(value_num)),
    min_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else min(value_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else max(value_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = column
  )

# every distinct label in the categorical columns ----
labels_df <- raw_df |>
  select(sex, treatment_arm) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |>
  count(column, value, sort = TRUE)

# identifiers that appear more than once, or whose length differs from the
# usual one (a possible formatting slip) ----
usual_length <- as.integer(names(which.max(table(nchar(raw_df$subject_id)))))
ids_df <- raw_df |>
  count(subject_id) |>
  mutate(unusual_length = nchar(subject_id) != usual_length) |>
  filter(n > 1 | unusual_length)

# print in full, and save each table so it can be opened, pasted or diffed ----
print(profile_df, n = Inf, width = Inf)
print(labels_df, n = Inf, width = Inf)
print(ids_df, width = Inf)
write_csv(profile_df, here("docs", "profile.csv"))
write_csv(labels_df, here("docs", "profile_labels.csv"))
write_csv(ids_df, here("docs", "profile_ids.csv"))

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
section: Step 2: Draft the codebook with the agent, then audit it
text:
Step 2: Draft the codebook with the agent, then audit it
The codebook is Day 2’s data dictionary (README chapter), with rules that code can read. Its facts come from docs/data_note.md, which stands in for the methods sheet or email you would get from the people who collected the data. A deny rule stops the agent reading the note, so it drafts from your profile alone, like an analyst who never asked. When you compare its draft with the note, the difference shows what the data alone cannot tell you.


Draft and audit the codebook (12 minutes)


Goal: a codebook you own, drafted by the agent, corrected by you against the data note and committed, so that every cleaning rule traces to a fact you can defend.
Predict first. The agent can see the counts but not the note. Which items on your Step 1 list do you expect it to get wrong?
1. Draft. The source column shows which entries are the agent’s own assumptions, so you know where to look first.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Draft a codebook for the raw voles data from docs/profile.csv,
docs/profile_labels.csv and docs/profile_ids.csv only, with the columns
column, type, rule, min, max, missing_codes, unit, source. In the source
column, say for every entry whether it comes from the profile or is your
assumption. Do not read any other file. Write it to
scratch/codebook_draft.csv and no other file.
Claude Code asks before it writes a file or runs a command. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Approve the write to scratch/codebook_draft.csv. Approve a command only if you can say what it does, and refuse any that would open docs/data_note.md: the deny rule stops Claude Code’s own tools reading the note, not R code it runs. Refusing is always safe.
2. Copy the draft into place. A deny rule stops the agent editing docs/codebook.csv, so it wrote its draft to scratch/, which git ignores. In the R console, copy the draft into docs/ and open it:

fs::file_copy(here::here("scratch", "codebook_draft.csv"),
              here::here("docs", "codebook.csv"))
usethis::edit_file(here::here("docs", "codebook.csv"))

From now on only you edit the codebook. Edit it in RStudio or Positron, not Excel: Excel can silently change separators, quotes and numbers when it saves a CSV.
3. Audit the draft. Before you open docs/data_note.md, check your prediction:

Did the draft list 9999 as a missing-value code, or treat it as a large measurement?
Did it notice that -1 is a code?
Where did its min and max come from? A range read off the data includes its errors. Valid ranges must come from the biology or the protocol.

4. Correct it against the note, and commit. Open docs/data_note.md (also shown below the task). Edit docs/codebook.csv until every line traces to the note or to a decision you can defend, and make its source say which. Where the note gives no unit (metabolic rate), write <unit>, not a guess: a guessed unit is an invented fact. Save the file and commit it, so that the cleaning starts from a recorded version of your rules.
You are done when the codebook is committed, and every rule traces to the note or to your own decision.
If it goes wrong: if file_copy() says the file already exists, you copied a draft earlier: edit that one, or add overwrite = TRUE to replace it and lose your edits. Short of time? Paste the codebook below into docs/codebook.csv and commit it. It is what most groups end up with.








NoteIf the draft knows too much





Suppose the draft states a fact that the profile cannot give, such as the 15–60 g range. Then the agent read more than the profile. Two routes run without asking:

a search of the whole project as a shell command, such as grep -r, which the read rule on the note does not cover;
the tests and the validation rules (tests/test_cleaning.R, scripts/functions/validate_voles.R), which contain the agreed rules. The deny rules stop the agent editing them, not reading them.

Either way, the draft no longer shows what the data alone reveal. Mention it in the debrief.









NoteThe shipped docs/data_note.md (open after item 3 of the task)







# Data note: vole metabolism experiment

From the colony manager who collected the data. One row per animal.

- **subject_id**: `V` followed by three digits (for example `V007`). Each
  animal appears once.
- **sex**: `M` or `F`.
- **treatment_arm**: `Control`, `Low_dose` or `High_dose`.
- **mass_pre_g**, **mass_post_g**: body mass in grams, before and after
  treatment. Adults in this colony weigh between 15 and 60 g. We entered
  `9999` when an animal could not be weighed.
- **metabolic_rate_post**: metabolic rate after treatment, from the
  respirometer. Valid readings lie between 5 and 30. We entered `-1` when the
  respirometry run failed.











NoteWhy a CSV, not a table in the README?





Code reads it. 01_clean.R reads docs/codebook.csv every time it runs, so nobody copies the rules into the script by hand. The over-cleaning test also reads its min, max and missing_codes columns. A Markdown table is for people; a CSV is for people and code.





A codebook you could agree on

column,type,rule,min,max,missing_codes,unit,source
subject_id,character,"pattern ^V[0-9]{3}$; unique; pad digits to three",,,,,data note; padding is a decision
sex,character,"allowed M, F; recode male to M, female to F",,,,,data note; recodes are a decision
treatment_arm,character,"allowed Control, Low_dose, High_dose; match case-insensitively",,,,,data note; case-insensitive matching is a decision
mass_pre_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note
mass_post_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note
metabolic_rate_post,double,,5,30,-1,<unit>,data note; no unit given
The note states the ID pattern, that each animal appears once, the allowed labels, the ranges and the missing-value codes. Padding short IDs and mapping other spellings onto the allowed labels are your decisions. The source column says so. The note gives no unit for metabolic rate, so <unit> stays until you find it out.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 3: Clean with one command
The shipped skillA reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description. clean-with-codebook holds the procedure; your codebook holds the facts. The skill writes scripts/01_clean.R, the only new script in this block.


Plan, review, then execute (15 minutes)


Goal: the skill writes and runs scripts/01_clean.R from your codebook, after you have approved its plan, so that every change to the data is made by a script you can rerun and is logged against a codebook rule.
Start state: the codebook and profile files committed, Git pane clean.
1. Invoke the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/clean-with-codebook Clean data/raw/voles_raw.csv using docs/codebook.csv.
2. Review its plan. The skill shows its plan first and waits for your reply. If the agent asks to write or run anything before you have seen a plan, refuse and ask for the plan. When the plan arrives, check that:

every rule cites a codebook row;
each problem on your Step 1 list is dealt with by one of those rules;
out-of-range values are set to NA and queried, not “corrected”;
no file outside scripts/01_clean.R and data/derived/ will be written;
duplicates are handled by a stated rule, with each exclusion logged.

Then reply in Claude Code: Yes, go ahead, or say what to change. This is the cheapest place to catch a wrong rule, before any file is written.
3. Read each request. Claude Code still asks before each write and each run. Approve what the plan described, and nothing else. New files should appear in the Git pane only in scripts/ and data/derived/. The skill runs the script twice, then runs the tests and reports the output.
While it works, predict where each problem on your Step 1 list will end up: changed and recorded in the cleaning log, set to NA and queried, or removed and recorded in the exclusion log. You check your predictions in Step 5.
You are done when data/derived/ contains voles_clean.csv, cleaning_log.csv and exclusion_log.csv, and the agent has reported the test output.
If it goes wrong: if it stalls, loops or writes elsewhere, press Esc (or Ctrl+C once) to stop it. In the Git pane, revert any file it changed. In the Files pane, delete any file it created (scripts/01_clean.R and anything in data/derived/): git has no earlier version of a new file to go back to, and /rewind cannot undo what the script’s R code wrote (Block 5). Then switch to checkpoint-cleaning, which has a working 01_clean.R and its outputs.








NoteWhat the skill tells the agent (clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md)





The skill ships in .agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/, with a copy in .claude/skills/. It runs only when you invoke it by name.


---
name: clean-with-codebook
description: >-
  Writes or revises a reproducible R cleaning script that applies a
  human-authored codebook (docs/codebook.csv) to raw tabular data. Use when
  asked to clean, recode or prepare raw data in a project that has a codebook.
  Not for exploratory analysis or modelling.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Clean data against a codebook

## Hard constraints
1. Never modify anything under data/raw/. Read raw files with explicit
   column types.
2. The codebook is the only source of rules. Do not infer units, ranges,
   missing-value codes or label mappings that the codebook does not state.
3. Do not edit docs/, scripts/functions/, scripts/02_validate.R,
   scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R or anything under tests/. If a check fails,
   report it; never change a check to make it pass.
4. Never drop a row silently. Every excluded row goes in the exclusion log
   with a reason.
5. Every changed cell goes in the cleaning log.
6. A value outside a codebook range that no codebook rule explains is set to
   NA, logged with rule "out_of_range_query", and listed in the final report.
   Never correct it by guessing a unit or decimal error.
7. No imputation.
8. Tidyverse style, native pipe, here::here() for all paths.

## Procedure
1. Present a plan before writing anything: every rule you will apply, the
   codebook row it comes from, and the order. Wait for the user to confirm.
2. If the data contain a value the codebook does not cover, stop and ask.
3. Write scripts/01_clean.R. It reads docs/codebook.csv when it runs; do not
   copy rules into the script by hand. Run it in a fresh R session
   (Rscript scripts/01_clean.R), then run it a second time and confirm the
   outputs are identical.
4. Run every test: Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')". Report the
   output verbatim, including skips.

## Outputs (exact columns)
- data/derived/voles_clean.csv: raw_row, then the codebook columns. raw_row
  is the 1-based row number in the raw file, not counting the header.
- data/derived/exclusion_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id (as it appears in the
  raw file), reason.
- data/derived/cleaning_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value,
  new_value, rule.
- rule is one of: missing_code, label_recode, id_format, out_of_range_query.

## Final report
Row counts in, out and excluded; every value set to NA for query; any gaps
in the codebook you found.











TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant. Invoke the skill with the same prompt in Normal mode, so it asks before each change. The skill presents its plan first, as it does in Claude Code.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 4: Run the tests yourself
The agent says its tests pass: that is a claim. One command, in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., turns it into evidence.


Run the tests (6 minutes)


Goal: run the tests yourself in a fresh R session, then commit, so that the agent’s “tests pass” becomes evidence you have seen.
1. Run every test. Restart R (Session → Restart R), so that nothing left in your session can make a test pass. Then run this in the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

The seven tests in test_cleaning.R check that the raw file is unchanged, every raw row is accounted for, the cleaning log is truthful and complete, nothing was over-cleaned, a fresh run writes identical files, and the clean data obey the agreed codebook. The table below the task says what each pass proves.
2. Read the change and record it. In the Git pane, click Diff on scripts/01_clean.R and look for anything the plan did not mention. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md (date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed): ask the agent to draft it, as in Block 3, then write the last part yourself. Then commit the script, its outputs and the log.
You are done when every cleaning test passes (other blocks’ tests may skip) and the work, with its AI-log line, is committed.
If it goes wrong: a failing test names the problem. Ask the agent to fix 01_clean.R, and quote the test. Never ask it to fix the test itself (a deny rule protects it). One failure may not be the script’s fault: the last test checks the agreed codebook from Step 2, while the over-cleaning test reads your own. If your ranges differ from the agreed ones, compare the two codebooks before you ask for a fix. Short of time? Switch to checkpoint-cleaning.








NoteWhat each test proves, and where the tests come from











Test in test_cleaning.R

A pass proves



raw data are unchanged
The raw file still matches its checksum: nothing changed it, by any route


every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log
No row was dropped silently, and every exclusion has a reason


every log entry is truthful: old value from raw, new value in clean
Each logged old value is the raw value, and each new value is the one in the clean file


every changed cell appears in the log
No change went unrecorded


no more values were set to NA than the codebook explains
Nothing was over-cleaned


cleaning is reproducible: a fresh run writes identical files
A fresh run writes byte-identical files


clean data pass every rule in the agreed codebook
IDs, labels and ranges obey the agreed codebook (a missing value is allowed)



The course team wrote tests/test_cleaning.R from the agreed codebook, before any cleaning code existed. So it checks what the cleaning should do, not what one script happens to do. The agent did not write it and cannot edit it: Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R) is one of the deny rules you checked before you started. In your own projects, write these tests yourself, from your codebook, before you ask an agent to clean.





The shipped tests/test_cleaning.R


# tests/test_cleaning.R ----
# Block 7: the raw data are untouched, every row is accounted for, every
# change is logged truthfully, nothing was over-cleaned, and the clean data
# pass every codebook rule. Written from the agreed codebook, before any
# cleaning code existed. Raw values are read as text, exactly as entered, so a
# logged old value can be compared character for character.
library(testthat)
testthat::local_edition(3)

read_chr <- function(...) {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here(...),
    col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())
  )
}

to_long <- function(data, value_name) {
  data |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-raw_row, names_to = "column", values_to = value_name)
}

same <- function(x, y) (is.na(x) & is.na(y)) | (!is.na(x) & !is.na(y) & x == y)

clean_path <- here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")

cleaning_inputs <- function() {
  raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") |>
    dplyr::mutate(raw_row = as.character(dplyr::row_number()))
  clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
  list(
    raw = raw_df,
    clean = clean_df,
    excluded = read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv"),
    log = read_chr("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"),
    raw_long = to_long(raw_df, "raw_value"),
    clean_long = to_long(clean_df, "clean_value")
  )
}

test_that("raw data are unchanged", {
  checksum_path <- here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")
  skip_if_not(file.exists(checksum_path), "no checksum file: tests/fixtures/raw_checksum.txt is missing")
  recorded <- readLines(checksum_path)
  current <- unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")))
  expect_identical(current, recorded)
})

test_that("every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  x <- cleaning_inputs()

  expect_equal(nrow(x$raw), nrow(x$clean) + nrow(x$excluded))
  expect_setequal(c(x$clean$raw_row, x$excluded$raw_row), x$raw$raw_row)
  expect_false(any(is.na(x$excluded$reason) | x$excluded$reason == ""))
})

test_that("every log entry is truthful: old value from raw, new value in clean", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  x <- cleaning_inputs()
  wrong_old <- x$log |>
    dplyr::left_join(x$raw_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::filter(!same(old_value, raw_value))
  wrong_new <- x$log |>
    dplyr::inner_join(x$clean_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::filter(!same(new_value, clean_value))
  expect_equal(nrow(wrong_old), 0)
  expect_equal(nrow(wrong_new), 0)
})

test_that("every changed cell appears in the log", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  x <- cleaning_inputs()
  numeric_cols <- c("mass_pre_g", "mass_post_g", "metabolic_rate_post")
  changed <- x$clean_long |>
    dplyr::left_join(x$raw_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      # numbers are compared as numbers, so 28.30 and 28.3 count as unchanged
      differs = dplyr::if_else(
        column %in% numeric_cols,
        !same(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(clean_value)),
              suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw_value))),
        !same(clean_value, raw_value)
      )
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(differs)
  unlogged <- dplyr::anti_join(changed, x$log, by = c("raw_row", "column"))
  expect_equal(nrow(unlogged), 0)
})

test_that("no more values were set to NA than the codebook explains", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  x <- cleaning_inputs()
  codebook <- read_chr("docs", "codebook.csv")
  numeric_rules <- dplyr::filter(codebook, !is.na(min) | !is.na(max) | !is.na(missing_codes))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(numeric_rules))) {
    col <- numeric_rules$column[[i]]
    codes <- trimws(strsplit(dplyr::coalesce(numeric_rules$missing_codes[[i]], ""), ";")[[1]])
    lo <- as.numeric(numeric_rules$min[[i]])
    hi <- as.numeric(numeric_rules$max[[i]])

    kept_raw <- x$raw[[col]][match(x$clean$raw_row, x$raw$raw_row)]
    value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(kept_raw))
    explained <- !is.na(kept_raw) & (
      kept_raw %in% codes |
        (!is.na(lo) & !is.na(value) & value < lo) |
        (!is.na(hi) & !is.na(value) & value > hi)
    )
    newly_na <- !is.na(kept_raw) & is.na(x$clean[[col]])

    expect_equal(sum(newly_na), sum(explained),
                 label = paste("values newly set to NA in", col))
  }
})

test_that("cleaning is reproducible: a fresh run writes identical files", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  derived <- here::here("data", "derived",
                        c("voles_clean.csv", "cleaning_log.csv", "exclusion_log.csv"))
  before <- unname(tools::md5sum(derived))
  callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "01_clean.R"), wd = here::here(),
                 show = FALSE)
  expect_identical(unname(tools::md5sum(derived)), before)
})

test_that("clean data pass every rule in the agreed codebook", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  clean_df <- readr::read_csv(
    clean_path,
    col_types = readr::cols(
      subject_id = readr::col_character(),
      sex = readr::col_character(),
      treatment_arm = readr::col_character(),
      mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(),
      mass_post_g = readr::col_double(),
      metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(),
      .default = readr::col_character()
    )
  )
  expect_equal(nrow(readr::problems(clean_df)), 0)

  # identifiers and labels
  expect_true(all(grepl("^V[0-9]{3}$", clean_df$subject_id)))
  expect_false(anyDuplicated(clean_df$subject_id) > 0)
  expect_true(all(clean_df$sex %in% c("M", "F")))
  expect_true(all(clean_df$treatment_arm %in% c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")))

  # ranges; a missing value is allowed, an out-of-range one is not
  in_range <- function(x, lo, hi) all(is.na(x) | (x >= lo & x <= hi))
  expect_true(in_range(clean_df$mass_pre_g, 15, 60))
  expect_true(in_range(clean_df$mass_post_g, 15, 60))
  expect_true(in_range(clean_df$metabolic_rate_post, 5, 30))
})

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 5: Validate, then grade
The tests give one pass or fail for each promise, but they do not show you the problems themselves. Validation does: it lists which raw rows break which codebook rule. Those are the rows your logs should account for. It uses assertr, as on Day 1, with this codebook’s rules. A person copied the rules into scripts/functions/validate_voles.R from the agreed codebook; the agent that cleaned did not write them.


Validate (4 minutes)


Goal: see each problem in the raw data, and find what your cleaning did with it.
1. Run the validation. In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "02_validate.R"))

Expect, in order:

an empty table (# A tibble: 0 × 5): every value in a number column was read as a number, so none slipped past the range rules as NA;

Raw data (expected to FAIL), then each broken rule with its rows and values. index is the row in the raw file, the same number as raw_row in your logs. Very small or large masses may print in scientific notation: 3.4e-02 is 0.034;

Clean data (expected to PASS), then All rules pass.;
last, the warning assertr encountered errors. It comes from the raw data, which should fail. R holds a warning until the whole script has run.

2. Find each row in your logs. Open cleaning_log.csv and exclusion_log.csv in data/derived/ (click them in the Files pane, or use View()). For each row the validation listed, find what your cleaning did with it, and check your predictions from Step 3. A duplicate is listed twice: one copy is kept and the other is in the exclusion log.
You are done when you have found what happened to every row the validation listed.
If it goes wrong: if the output mentions pointblank, or does not match the list above, your fork is older than the current template. Follow your instructor’s screen for now. Afterwards, copy both files from How the validation works, below, and run renv::install("assertr").


Grade against the answer key. Instructor-led, about 4 minutes. Before the course, your instructor made voles_raw.csv by planting the errors below in a copy of the clean voles_metabolism.csv, so they were in the raw file from the start. Your instructor now walks through each one. Open the list, and for each error mark whether your logs record it.


The planted errors



Planted error
In your logs?



9999 in mass_post_g (two animals)




-1 in metabolic_rate_post





treatment_arm label in lower case




treatment_arm label in upper case




sex spelled out




mass_pre_g recorded in kilograms




mass_pre_g ten times too large



Exact duplicate row



Near duplicate with a malformed ID




For the two duplicates, look in the exclusion log as well: a removed row is recorded there, not in the cleaning log.

For discussion:

The validation flagged the mass recorded in kilograms and the one ten times too large only as out of range: it cannot say why. What did the cleaning do with them? If it “corrected” them, on whose authority?
Did any planted error get past every rule in your codebook? A planted error that no codebook rule catches is a hole in the codebook, not in the cleaning.







NoteHow the validation works





Each assert() in validate_voles.R is one codebook rule. chain_start() and chain_end() run every rule before reporting, and error_fun = just_warn reports broken rules with a warning instead of stopping, so 02_validate.R goes on to check the clean data after the raw. The empty table at the start lists any value that could not be read as a number: such a value would become NA and slip past the range rules.

# scripts/functions/validate_voles.R ----
# Rules transcribed from docs/codebook.csv by a human, not by the agent
# that writes the cleaning script.

voles_col_types <- function() {
  readr::cols(
    subject_id = readr::col_character(),
    sex = readr::col_character(),
    treatment_arm = readr::col_character(),
    mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(),
    mass_post_g = readr::col_double(),
    metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(),
    .default = readr::col_character()
  )
}

# subject_id is V followed by three digits
is_vole_id <- function(x) grepl("^V[0-9]{3}$", x)

# One assert() per rule. chain_end() lists every rule the data break, with
# the row and the value, then warns rather than stops (just_warn), so a script
# can go on to check other data.
validate_voles <- function(data, label) {
  cat("\n", label, "\n", sep = "")
  data |>
    assertr::chain_start() |>
    assertr::assert(assertr::not_na, subject_id, sex, treatment_arm) |>
    assertr::assert(is_vole_id, subject_id) |>
    assertr::assert(assertr::is_uniq, subject_id) |>
    assertr::assert(assertr::in_set("M", "F"), sex) |>
    assertr::assert(
      assertr::in_set("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"),
      treatment_arm
    ) |>
    # a missing value passes: allow.na = TRUE is the default
    assertr::assert(assertr::within_bounds(15, 60), mass_pre_g, mass_post_g) |>
    assertr::assert(assertr::within_bounds(5, 30), metabolic_rate_post) |>
    assertr::chain_end(
      success_fun = \(data) {
        cat("All rules pass.\n")
        data
      },
      error_fun = assertr::just_warn
    ) |>
    invisible()
}


# scripts/02_validate.R ----
# Runs the codebook rules on the raw data (expected to FAIL) and, once
# 01_clean.R has run, on the clean data (expected to PASS). Each broken rule
# is listed with its rows and values; assertr then warns rather than stops,
# so both checks run.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

raw_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types())
# values that could not be read as numbers become NA and would pass the
# range rules, so list them
print(problems(raw_df), width = Inf)
validate_voles(raw_df, "Raw data (expected to FAIL)")

clean_path <- here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
if (file.exists(clean_path)) {
  clean_df <- read_csv(clean_path, col_types = voles_col_types())
  validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data (expected to PASS)")
}







Warning



within_bounds() and in_set() let a missing value pass (allow.na = TRUE, the default), as the tests’ range checks do. That lets genuine missing values through, but it would also pass a cleaning script that replaced every mass with NA. Validation alone cannot catch over-cleaning; the over-cleaning test in Step 4 can. That is why you run both.











TipInstructor: debrief (3 minutes)






Which planted errors did the agent’s first draft of the codebook miss before you corrected it against the note? What does that say about who should own the codebook?
Did any first draft contain a fact the profile cannot give, such as the 15–60 g range? If so, the agent read beyond the profile: the note, by a route the read rule does not cover, or the tests or validation rules, which it may read (If the draft knows too much, in Step 2).

Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: have an agent clean a raw file against a codebook you own, with one command, trusted because one test run proves the raw data are untouched, every row is accounted for, every change is logged truthfully, and a second run gives the same files.

Check: tests written from the codebook, not the cleaning code; validation that lists each broken rule by row; the Git pane diff; the answer key.

Reproduce: the reproducibility test reruns the cleaning in a fresh R session; Block 8 shows how to freeze a result as a reference.

Record: the codebook, both logs, and a line in docs/ai-log.md.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Check your understanding
Why must the codebook be written or confirmed by the analyst rather than inferred by the AI from the data?

Because AI tools cannot read CSV filesBecause missing-value codes, units and valid ranges are facts about how the data were collected; ranges read off the data include the errors they should catchBecause codebooks must be written in a specific file formatBecause the AI would take too long to profile the data

The agent reports “all tests pass”. What should you do next?

Nothing; the agent ran the testsRun the tests yourself in a fresh R session and read the diff; the agent's report is a claimAsk the agent to run them againDelete the tests, since they have done their job

The tests pass. What does running 02_validate.R add?

Nothing; it repeats the testsIt lists which raw rows break which codebook rule, so you can check what the cleaning did with each oneIt corrects the rows that break a ruleIt proves that nothing was over-cleaned

How does the checksum test differ from the deny rule?

They are equivalent; one is redundantThe deny rule blocks one route (the agent's editing tools) before a change happens; the checksum detects a change by any route, after it happensThe checksum prevents edits; the deny rule only reports themThe deny rule works on GitHub; the checksum works only locally

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipWrite the validation rules independently





Instead of using the shipped validate_voles.R from Step 5, you can ask an AI that has never seen the cleaning code to write the rules. For example, use a browser chat window and give it only the codebook:
Prompt (browser chat):
Using only the codebook below, write an R file containing a function
validate_voles(data, label) that checks every codebook rule with the assertr
package: one assert() per rule, between chain_start() and
chain_end(error_fun = just_warn). Also write voles_col_types(), returning
readr column types for the codebook columns, with character as the default
for anything else.

[paste docs/codebook.csv]
Compare what it writes with the shipped version. Look for a rule it missed, or a range it took from the data rather than the codebook. The separate conversation is there to expose errors of this kind.









TipRead the log yourself





The tests prove the log is truthful and complete. They cannot tell you whether a change was the right decision. The shipped scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R counts the changes by column and rule. It also picks up to ten logged changes at random for you to check by eye against the raw file (View(), or Positron’s Data Explorer).

source(here::here("scripts", "03_audit_cleaning.R"))


# scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R ----
# Purpose: read the cleaning log yourself. tests/test_cleaning.R already checks
# that the log is truthful and complete; it cannot tell you whether each change
# was the right decision. That is your job.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

cleaning_log_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# 1. What kinds of change were made ----
cleaning_log_df |> count(column, rule, sort = TRUE) |> print()

# 2. Up to ten logged changes to check by hand against the raw file ----
set.seed(2026)
cleaning_log_df |> slice_sample(n = 10) |> print(width = Inf)










TipThe fresh-run checks, one by one





The test suite already reruns the cleaning in a fresh R session. To do the same checks by hand, commit the outputs. Then run these lines in the R console:

renv::status()
callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "01_clean.R"))

renv::status() should report a consistent state. The agent may have used a package that is not in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.. If so, decide whether you want it, and record it yourself with renv::snapshot(), as on Day 1. (A deny rule stops the agent editing renv.lock.) After the callr::rscript() run, the Git pane should show no changes.






NoteAt the command line





Run Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')", Rscript -e "renv::status()", Rscript scripts/01_clean.R and git status --short data/derived after /exit, or in a second Terminal tab. See checking work.












TipHow the template’s safeguards were made





The checksum. The template’s tests/fixtures/raw_checksum.txt was written once, from the shipped raw file, like this:

fs::dir_create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"))
writeLines(
  unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"))),
  here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")
)

Do the same for your own raw data, then commit the checksum file. The template’s .gitattributes contains two lines, data/raw/** -text and data/derived/** -text. They stop git changing the line endings of the data files when it checks them out. The tests compare those files byte for byte: the raw file against its checksum, and the clean files against a fresh run of the cleaning. If git converted the line endings, as can happen on Windows, both tests would fail with no real change to the data.
The deny rules. This is the .claude/settings.json in your workshop repository, the same file you read in Block 5:


{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Read(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}


A leading / ties each pattern to the project root. The rules protect specific files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write scripts/01_clean.R and data/derived/. To protect files of your own, add rules with /permissions. Posit Assistant has no documented path rules for file edits. Use the guard hook from the Going further section of Block 5 instead.






Warning



What each control covers. The deny rule blocks the agent’s own file tools, simple file commands it recognises (such as cat, sed and tee) and shell redirects such as > file. It does not cover R code the agent runs: an R script that writes to data/raw/ is a different route. Nor does a read rule cover a search of the whole project with grep -r. The checksum test catches a change made by any route, but only after the fact. Use both: one prevents, the other detects. See Block 3 for reading, and Set up guardrails in your own project in Block 5 for a starting set of rules.


The skill. The skill ships in .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/. To use it in another project, download it with the button below. Unzip it into that project’s .agents/skills/ with unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills")). Then copy the folder into .claude/skills/: fs::dir_copy(here::here(".agents", "skills", "clean-with-codebook"), here::here(".claude", "skills", "clean-with-codebook")).


 Download clean-with-codebook.zip

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


checksum
A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.


codebook
A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


sentinel value
A number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for "not recorded" or -1 for "run failed". It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.


skill
A reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.

title: Block 9: AI-assisted code review
text:
Task 1: run the review
On Day 2 you reviewed ANALYSIS.R by hand, and the answer key listed twelve problems (P1–P12). Now an AI reviews the same script. You grade it against that key, so that you measure the machine rather than trust it.
⏱ ~30 minutes · Start: your workshop repository open, and the ~/ai-review folder you made before the day (Setting up Claude Code, step 7). Claude Code runs in that folder, not in your workshop repository.

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
TipBackground: what the evidence says





Used that way, AI review is reliably good for:

summarising what an unfamiliar script does;
flagging missing documentation, unexplained filters and hard-coded paths;
finding run errors, when it can actually execute the code;
a second pair of eyes that never tires on line 300.

In software engineering, developers acted on about three-quarters of an AI reviewer’s comments but saw only minor gains in quality, and the reviewer did worse when it was not told what the code was meant to do (Cihan et al., 2025; Cihan, 2025). Nobody has measured it on analysis scripts like this one, which is what you will do.









Note



Opening poll (type in chat)
“If an AI code reviewer told you your analysis was clean, would you trust it enough to submit?”
A: Yes, it read every line B: Only if I had also read it myself C: No, I would trust my own review over the AI’s D: I would trust it for Run, not for Reliable
Keep the result visible; we return to it at the end.

title: Self-study: AI-assisted code review
text:
Write the review prompt (7 minutes)


Goal: a review prompt with all four parts, saved in your workshop repository, so that you can reuse it on your own scripts after the course.
1. Start from the draft below and check it has all four parts. “Review my code” alone gets a vague, generous review; a good review prompt has:






Part
Why




A role and a standard: “a critical reviewer applying the four Rs”
Gives the output a structure you can check



The intended analysis: the model from the OSF page, with TO a count and block B a random effect
Without it, the AI cannot see that a Gaussian lmer() is the wrong family (P10)



No flattery: line number, which R, severity, a fix
Keeps it to findings you can act on



Honest uncertainty: “NEEDS HUMAN CHECK” instead of guessing
Shows you where to look yourself



2. Choose your version. The line about the 9999 sentinel valueA number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for “not recorded” or -1 for “run failed”. It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis. tells the reviewer something the script alone cannot. Keep it, or delete it to see what the reviewer finds unaided; doing both, as two runs, shows the difference the line makes. Everything else stays the same.
3. Keep it. In your workshop repository, run usethis::edit_file("docs/review-prompt.md") in the R console, paste your prompt, save, and commit it from the Git pane. You will reuse it after the course.
You are done when your prompt has all four elements and is committed as docs/review-prompt.md.


Working draft

Prompt (Claude Code):
You are a critical code reviewer for an evolutionary-biology journal.
Review ANALYSIS.R using the four Rs: Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible.

The intended analysis (from the pre-registration) is:
  total offspring (TO, a count: non-negative integer, often overdispersed)
  modelled as TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B), with block B as a random effect.

Rules:
- Do NOT praise the code. Report only problems.
- For each issue: line number(s), which R it violates, severity
  (critical / high / medium), and a concrete one-line fix.
- The raw data use 9999 as a "not recorded" code. Check whether this is
  handled.                                <- delete for a run without it
- Flag anything you CANNOT determine by reading alone as "NEEDS HUMAN
  CHECK" rather than guessing.
- If you are uncertain about a finding, say so explicitly.
Organise your output by the four Rs.

title: Block 9: AI-assisted code review
text:
Run the review (10 minutes)


Goal: an AI review of ANALYSIS.R, made from the script alone, so that you can grade it against problems you already know.
Start state: ~/ai-review holds ANALYSIS.R, and your instructor has told you whether you are in the with or the without group.
1. Start Claude Code in the review folder. Open a new Terminal tab; Claude Code for your workshop repository keeps running in the first. Then run:
cd ~/ai-review
claude
This folder has none of your workshop settings, so it may start in auto. Check that the mode shown is Manual (default). If it is not, press Shift+Tab until it is. Then type /memory: nothing from your workshop repository should be listed. A personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, if you keep one, still loads in every folder, so note it if it is there.
2. Send the review. Paste the prompt below. If you are in the without group, delete the line that begins - The raw data use 9999 before you send it. Comparing the two groups then shows what that one line changes. In Manual mode the agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. reads the script without asking, but must ask before it edits a file or runs a command. Answer No to every request: this is a review from reading alone. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on.
Prompt (Claude Code):
You are a critical code reviewer for an evolutionary-biology journal.
Review ANALYSIS.R using the four Rs: Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible.

The intended analysis (from the pre-registration) is:
  total offspring (TO, a count: non-negative integer, often overdispersed)
  modelled as TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B), with block B as a random effect.

Rules:
- Do NOT praise the code. Report only problems.
- For each issue: line number(s), which R it violates, severity
  (critical / high / medium), and a concrete one-line fix.
- The raw data use 9999 as a "not recorded" code. Check whether this is handled.
- Flag anything you CANNOT determine by reading alone as "NEEDS HUMAN
  CHECK" rather than guessing.
- If you are uncertain about a finding, say so explicitly.
- Do not edit or run anything: review the script by reading it.
Organise your output by the four Rs.
3. Keep it on screen. You grade it in Task 2, straight from the terminal.
You are done when the review is on screen, organised by the four Rs.
If it goes wrong: if there is no ~/ai-review, run the commands in This block’s files (expand it) above. If Claude Code mentions AGENTS.md or the voles data, you started it in your workshop folder. Type /exit, run cd ~/ai-review and start again. If you have no agent, use the chat route in Using another tool.








NoteHow it works: what makes a review prompt work





“Review my code” alone gets a vague, generous review. The prompt above has four parts, each for a reason:






Part
Why




A role and a standard: a critical reviewer, using the four Rs
Gives the output a structure you can check



The intended analysis: the model from the OSF page, with TO a count and block B a random effect
Without it, the AI cannot see that a Gaussian lmer() is the wrong family (P10)



No flattery: line number, which R, severity, a fix
Keeps it to findings you can act on



Honest uncertainty: “NEEDS HUMAN CHECK” instead of guessing
Shows you where to look yourself



The review must see the script and nothing else: with the data, the agent would find the 9999 code by itself, and the two groups would no longer differ.
Why Manual mode, not /plan. Plan mode stops the agent editing files, but on recent versions of Claude Code it may run some commands without asking you (Block 3). In Manual mode (rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 3, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. 3), every edit and every command except read-only ones asks first, and you refuse them all. The prompt’s last rule asks the same of the model, but your No is what holds.









TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant. Open ~/ai-review in RStudio or Positron. Switch Posit Assistant to Ask mode, so it can read but not change anything. Then give it the prompt. For the stretch below, use Normal mode, so it asks before running anything.
Chat window. Paste the whole of ANALYSIS.R into any chat window, followed by the prompt. Paste the script only, not the data. A chat window cannot run anything, but its answer to “does this run?” can read as though it did. Ask “what would prevent this running?” instead.









TipStretch: let it run the script





An agent that can run R turns the Run question from a prediction into evidence. In the same Claude Code session, still in Manual mode, it asks before running anything. The folder has no data, and the agent needs none for this: the run stops before the script reads any. Where it stops, and why, is the finding.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Run ANALYSIS.R from a fresh R session with Rscript and report the exact
output and any errors. Do not install packages; if a package is missing,
report which one. Do not edit any file.
Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now. Refusing is always safe. “The script runs” counts only if you can see the command and its output in the conversation. Without them, it is a claimed executionA statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.. A missing package is a finding about your machine, not about the code.

title: Block 9: AI-assisted code review
text:
Check your understanding
An AI reviewer reports that ANALYSIS.R “runs without errors”. What do you need before treating that as evidence?

Nothing; the model has read every lineA second AI reviewer's agreementThe command it ran and the output it saw, from a fresh R session; without them the statement is a predictionA statement of confidence from the model

Why is P8 caught more often when the review prompt keeps the line about the 9999 code?

A longer prompt makes any reviewer more thoroughNothing in the script reveals that 9999 is a code; the AI could only check for it when the prompt said soThe line lets the reviewer open the data fileP8 is a syntax error that only some models detect

title: Block 8: AI-assisted code review
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipCopilot code review on a pull request





If your repository is on GitHub, open a pull request containing ANALYSIS.R and request Copilot as a reviewer. Its comments appear on the changed lines, like a colleague’s. It reads the repository’s instruction files (.github/copilot-instructions.md, or AGENTS.md as in Block 5), but none of those exist in the OSF folder yet. To have Copilot apply the standard from Part 2, add your review rules (the four Rs, the intended analysis, no praise, NEEDS HUMAN CHECK) to .github/copilot-instructions.md in that repository before you request the review.









TipGenerating the README with AI





Self-study: about 20 minutes.
The second deliverable is the documentation that makes Reported and Run answerable: a README. You are provided with the research-readme skill: a SKILL.md, two helper scripts and a template.
Install the skill before you start. Download the bundle and unzip it into the OSF project folder at .agents/skills/, so that the folder .agents/skills/research-readme/ contains SKILL.md, scripts/ and references/.


 Download research-readme.zip




Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot read .agents/skills/ directly.

Claude Code reads .claude/skills/. Link or copy the folder there, as described in Block 5.

Chat window: you do not need to install anything. You will run the two scripts yourself and paste the template into the chat.

Check that the skill is visible before going on. In Claude Code, type / and look for research-readme. In any tool, the test is behaviour: when you invoke /research-readme in Pass 2, its first reply should be the numbered plan that the skill’s “Before executing” section requires. If it is not, the skill did not load.
Put the folder under version control first. A folder downloaded from OSF is not a git repository, so there would be nothing to compare the README against. With the OSF project open in RStudio or Positron, run usethis::use_git() in the R console and let it make the first commit.
You run this in two passes. The first shows the failure; the second shows the fix.
Pass 1: README from the AI alone (self-study: about 4 minutes)
Give the AI only ANALYSIS.R and the data, and ask for a README with no constraints. The result reads as complete. It will assign plausible units, describe variables it cannot have verified, and may state package versions it has no way to know. Note what it asserts about the variables and dependencies; Pass 2 replaces each guess with a fact you generate.
Pass 2: README from verifiable inputs
The skill’s rules are that the AI must not fabricate metadata, and that automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. So you generate the facts mechanically, and the AI only assembles and phrases them.
Step 1: Generate the inputs yourself (R, not AI)
In the R console, with the OSF project open in RStudio or Positron (so that here::here() points at it, not at your workshop repository):

skill_dir <- here::here(".agents", "skills", "research-readme", "scripts")

source(file.path(skill_dir, "describe_csv.R"))
# type, missing count and range per column, printed in full for pasting
describe_project_csvs(here::here()) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

source(file.path(skill_dir, "scan_packages.R"))
print_lockfile(here::here("renv.lock"))  # R and package versions, or a finding

This project has no renv.lock. scan_packages.R reports that as an explicit finding rather than an error, and the README must say so. You cannot pin versions you never recorded.
Look at the offspring column in the summary: its range will read something like 2 to 9999. The 9999 code (P8) is a real number in the file, and the summary reports it without judgement. Judging plausibility is your job. That honest, uninterpreted range is the visible trace of the sentinel.
Step 2: Hand the AI the specification and the inputs
Agent path: invoke /research-readme and let its five stages run. It will ask you for what it cannot find.
Chat path: paste the structure from references/readme_template.md and the output you just generated, with this prompt:
Prompt (chat window):
Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository, using exactly the
sections in the template I paste below, in order.

Use ONLY the facts I provide. Do not invent DOIs, ORCIDs, units or package
versions. Where a value is missing, insert a visible placeholder:
  **TODO: supply [field]: not provided**

Per-column summaries: [paste describe_project_csvs() output]
Dependencies: [paste print_lockfile() output]
Run order: ANALYSIS.R (the only analysis script in the folder).

Add an AI declaration stating that an AI assisted in drafting this README,
naming the model and today's date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere.


Audit the README (10 minutes)


Audit the draft against three of the skill’s rules:


No fabrication. Pick three facts. Can you trace each to an input you gave? If not, it is invented.

Describe, do not interpret. Did the AI assign units or meanings you did not supply? Did the 2 to 9999 range survive, or was it “tidied” into something plausible and wrong?

README only. The Git pane should show that nothing except README.md changed since the commit you made before Pass 1.

Note the worst fabrication or interpretation you caught, and whether the README’s offspring range alone would have led you back to P8. The AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. should say no more than you told it.


The skill bundle
The bundle you downloaded above is reproduced here for reference; you do not need to edit it. Read it before you use it, as you would any skill you did not write.
research-readme/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   ├── describe_csv.R
│   └── scan_packages.R
└── references/
    └── readme_template.md






Notescripts/describe_csv.R






# describe_csv.R ----
# Purpose: one row per column of a CSV file: name, the type readr assigns,
# missing-value count, and a brief range (numeric) or distinct-value count
# (other). Describes; does not interpret.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 2.

describe_range <- function(x) {
  if (all(is.na(x))) {
    return("all values missing")
  }
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    return(paste(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), "to", max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
  }
  paste(dplyr::n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE), "distinct values")
}

# one-row-per-column summary of a single CSV ----
describe_csv <- function(path) {
  stopifnot(is.character(path), length(path) == 1L, file.exists(path))
  data_df <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(
    file        = basename(path),
    column      = names(data_df),
    type        = purrr::map_chr(data_df, \(x) class(x)[1]),
    n_missing   = purrr::map_int(data_df, \(x) sum(is.na(x))),
    range       = purrr::map_chr(data_df, describe_range),
    # completed by the user during Stage 2:
    description = NA_character_,
    unit        = NA_character_
  )
}

# describe every CSV in a project, skipping renv and git folders ----
describe_project_csvs <- function(project_dir) {
  stopifnot(dir.exists(project_dir))
  csv_paths <- list.files(
    project_dir,
    pattern = "\\.csv$",
    recursive = TRUE,
    full.names = TRUE,
    ignore.case = TRUE
  )
  csv_paths <- csv_paths[!grepl("(^|/)(renv|\\.git)/", csv_paths)]
  if (length(csv_paths) == 0L) {
    message("No CSV files found under ", project_dir)
    return(tibble::tibble())
  }
  csv_paths |>
    purrr::map(describe_csv) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
}










Notescripts/scan_packages.R






# scan_packages.R ----
# Purpose: read renv.lock and report the R version and pinned package
# versions. A missing lockfile is reported as a finding, not an error.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 4.

read_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  if (!file.exists(lock_path)) {
    return(list(found = FALSE, r_version = NA_character_, packages = tibble::tibble()))
  }
  lock <- jsonlite::read_json(lock_path)
  packages <- purrr::pluck(lock, "Packages", .default = list())

  packages_df <- tibble::tibble(
    package = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Package", .default = NA_character_))),
    version = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Version", .default = NA_character_)))
  ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(package)

  list(
    found = TRUE,
    r_version = purrr::pluck(lock, "R", "Version", .default = NA_character_),
    packages = packages_df
  )
}

print_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  info <- read_lockfile(lock_path)
  if (!info$found) {
    cat(
      "No lockfile found at ", lock_path, ".\n",
      "FINDING: package versions were not recorded.\n",
      "README text: **TODO: supply R version and key package versions: ",
      "not recorded; resolve before submission**\n",
      sep = ""
    )
    return(invisible(info))
  }
  cat("R version: ", info$r_version, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(info$packages, n = Inf)
  invisible(info)
}










NoteSKILL.md







---
name: research-readme
description: >-
  Writes a README.md for a research repository whose code and data accompany
  a paper. Use when asked to write a README for an analysis project, document
  a repository for a paper, or prepare code for journal submission or
  archiving (Zenodo, Figshare, OSF). Not for general software READMEs and not
  for auditing code.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Research README generator

Produces one README.md for a repository of R code and data that accompanies a
manuscript, including the metadata that journals and archives expect:
persistent identifiers, ORCIDs, funding, per-variable descriptions with units,
an explicit script run order, and a dependency record.

## Operating constraints
These hold for the whole conversation unless the user explicitly withdraws
them.
1. The only file you create or overwrite is README.md. Do not edit, rename or
   delete any other file. If you notice an apparent error in code or data,
   record it under "Open questions" in the README or report it in chat, and
   leave the file untouched.
2. Do not fabricate metadata. DOIs, ORCIDs, grant numbers, collection dates,
   units and affiliations come from the user or from a file the user points to.
   If a value is unknown, insert a placeholder (see Placeholders).
3. Automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. Report column type,
   missing count and range. Do not state what a variable means, its unit, or
   whether a value is plausible.
4. Work conversationally and write the file directly; do not build an app.

## Before executing
Present a short numbered plan: the folder to be scanned, that only README.md
will be written, and the five stages below. Wait for the user to confirm.

## Stage 1: Project information
Collect title, abstract, DOIs (paper; archived code and data), licences,
authors with ORCIDs and affiliations, and funders with grant numbers. Read
these from CITATION.cff, codemeta.json or DESCRIPTION if present, and ask only
for what is missing. Pair each author with their own ORCID and affiliation. If
no code licence is supplied, flag it prominently and use a placeholder; do not
choose a licence for the user.

## Stage 2: Files and variable summaries
List the data and code files. For CSV files, run
describe_project_csvs() from scripts/describe_csv.R and use its output as a
scaffold. Ask the user for each column's description and unit, and for
collection dates and locations per data file. List other tabular formats
(.xlsx, .tsv) and ask the user to describe their columns by hand. Never infer
units from column names.

## Stage 3: Script order
List executable files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd). Propose a run order using numeric
prefixes (01_, 02_) as the first signal, and ask the user to confirm or
reorder; the user's order is authoritative. Collect a one-line description of
each script. Do not run any script to determine the order.

## Stage 4: R packages and versions
Run print_lockfile() from scripts/scan_packages.R.
- If a lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states the R version, says
  that versions are pinned in renv.lock, gives the restore command
  renv::restore(), and includes the package table.
- If no lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states that package versions
  were not recorded, and contains the placeholder from print_lockfile(). Do not
  guess versions or scan the installed library.

## Stage 5: Assemble, preview and reader-test
Fill references/readme_template.md. Show the rendered Markdown in chat. Then
read it as a newcomer who has only the repository and the paper: could they
find the data, restore the environment, run the scripts in order and
understand every variable? List any section still holding a placeholder. On
confirmation, write README.md to the project root.

## Stage 6: Check the README against its sources
If the project has tests/test_readme.R, run it in a fresh R session
(Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_readme.R')") and report the
output verbatim. Otherwise compare the README yourself: the R and package
versions against read_lockfile(), every numbered script against the scripts
folder, and every unit against the user's answers. Report the number of
placeholders left.

## AI declaration
State that an AI assisted in generating this README, naming the model if the
user wishes, with the date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere in the
project unless the user states them, and then record exactly what they state.

## Placeholders
Write every unknown value as a visible placeholder, in exactly this form:
**TODO: supply [field]: not provided**
Flag a missing code licence and a missing code or data DOI as blocking for
submission, but still write the file so the user has a working draft.

## Scope
This skill does not audit code quality or reproducibility, and does not
produce figures. If asked to do either mid-run, say so and stop that part of
the request.

## References
- Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2023) Implementing code review in the scientific
  workflow. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36(10), 1347–1356.
- Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2025) TADA! Simple guidelines to improve
  analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility. EcoEvoRxiv.











Notereferences/readme_template.md





The Dependencies section is a single token, filled with one of the two versions defined in Stage 4 of SKILL.md, so the README is accurate whether or not a lockfile exists.

title: Block 9: AI-assisted code review
text:
Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI declaration
A statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded.


claimed execution
A statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.


false positive
In a code review, a problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or describes wrongly.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


rung
One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 3, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.


skill
A reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.

title: Block 8: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Step 0: check the protections
You let an agent turn working code into a function and prove that nothing changed. The proof is a characterisation testA test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct., as in the tidy-evaluation chapter: the new code must reproduce the original output exactly. That output is frozen as a referenceIn a characterisation test, the saved output of the original, trusted code (stored in tests/fixtures/). A trusted script captures it once, from the unchanged code, before any refactoring, and you commit it. After that, nothing regenerates it except your own recorded decision.. Then you decide whether the unchanged output is right. Changing it on purpose, and recording why, is an exercise for after the day.
⏱ ~25 minutes · Start on main (or checkpoint-cleaning), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.

text:
The code you will refactor
scripts/05_analysis.R loads the trial data and summarises post-treatment metabolic rate (mean, SD and count) by treatment arm and sex.






TipReference: the code you will refactor






# scripts/05_analysis.R: the original, trusted version ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "04_load_data.R"))

metabolic_summary <- voles |>
  group_by(treatment_arm, sex) |>
  summarise(
    mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
    sd_rate   = sd(metabolic_rate_post),
    n         = n(),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )










NoteThe data loading it relies on






# scripts/04_load_data.R ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))

voles <- load_voles()


# scripts/functions/load_voles.R ----
load_voles <- function() {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
    col_types = readr::cols(
      subject_id          = readr::col_character(),
      sex                 = readr::col_character(),
      treatment_arm       = readr::col_character(),
      mass_pre_g          = readr::col_double(),
      mass_post_g         = readr::col_double(),
      metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double()
    )
  )
}




One thing to notice and leave alone: the data have one missing metabolic_rate_post, and there is no na.rm, so one cell of the result is NA. Step 2 is about exactly this.
The whole block in one picture: the reference comes from the original code, you commit it before anything changes, and from then on only a decision of yours replaces it.



Step 1: refactor without changing the output


Skill: run make_reference.R on the original code





Commit the reference





Skill: refactor only





Read the diff





Skill: a test that reads your reference





Protect the new test (/permissions)





The test suite passes in a fresh R session




Step 2: when the behaviour should change


Decide the output is wrong





Change the function





Characterisation test fails, correctly





Known-answer test passes





Re-capture, with a commit message saying why



A reference made after the code changed is produced by the code under test, and can only confirm that the code agrees with itself. Committing it first is what makes it a reference.

title: Block 8: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Recipe check (3 minutes)


Goal: confirm the reference and its capture script are protected, and that no reference exists yet, so that the reference you capture in Step 1 can only come from the original code.
Start state: as at the top of the page.
1. Check the protections. In Claude Code, type /permissions. The deny rulesA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. Edit(/tests/fixtures/**) and Edit(/tests/make_reference.R) keep the agent’s edit tools off the reference and its capture script. The Git pane shows a change made by any other route.
2. Check there is no reference yet. In the Files pane, open tests/fixtures/. It should hold only raw_checksum.txt (Block 7).
You are done when you have seen the two rules, and tests/fixtures/ has no .rds file.
If it goes wrong: far behind? Switch to checkpoint-refactor in the Git pane’s branch menu and read on.








NoteThe shipped capture script, tests/make_reference.R





It runs the original 05_analysis.R and saves the result. The course team wrote it; a deny rule stops the agent editing it.

# tests/make_reference.R ----
# Run ONCE, by you, BEFORE any refactoring.
source(here::here("scripts", "05_analysis.R"))
dir.create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
saveRDS(
  metabolic_summary,
  here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds")
)
