title: Setting up Claude Code
section: Step 7: An API key for Block 6
text:
Step 7: An API key for Block 6
In Block 6 you build your own agent in R with the ellmer package. It calls Claude through the Anthropic API, which is billed per request and is separate from a Claude Pro or Max subscription.

Get a key. Create an account at https://console.anthropic.com. Add a little prepaid credit (check the current prices on Anthropic’s pricing page; the block needs only a few dozen requests). Then create an API key.

Save it outside every project. In the R console, run usethis::edit_r_environ(). It opens your user-level .Renviron. Add one line:
AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY=your-key-here
Save the file and restart R. The name is deliberate: Claude Code looks for ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and would offer to bill that key instead of your subscription. Never paste a key into a script. Claude Code asks before it reads a file outside your project; if it asks to read .Renviron, answer No.


Test it. In the R console:

ellmer::chat_anthropic(
  model = "claude-sonnet-5-5",
  credentials = \() Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY")
)$chat("Reply with the word OK.")



You are done when the model replies. If it reports a missing or invalid key, check the line in .Renviron and restart R.






TipOptional: GitHub Copilot, for the self-study page on inline completions





The self-study page on inline completions uses GitHub Copilot; Copilot Free is enough. It is not needed on the day.


RStudio: Tools → Global Options → Copilot, tick Enable GitHub Copilot, and sign in with your GitHub account.

Positron: choose GitHub Copilot as the completions provider, and sign in with your GitHub account when Positron prompts you, or from its AI assistant settings.

To check it, type # Calculate the mean of 1 to 100 in a new, unsaved R script: grey suggested text should appear.

title: Block 2: Debugging with AI
text:
A logic error (12 minutes)


Goal: find a bug that raises no error by inspecting the data first, so that you can check the agent’s diagnosis against evidence you have seen yourself.
Start state: your workshop repository on main; Claude Code in Manual mode, with a new conversation (/clear).






TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant: type /ask first. Ask mode is read-only: it cannot edit files or run R code, so the answer-only line is not needed. It does see the names and types of the objects in your session (not their values). It can also read your console history, so it may already have your distinct() output. That is a disclosure route too (Block 3). For step 4, type /normal so it can run the diagnostics in your live R session, and approve each call. /normal is also how you leave Ask mode.
A chat window: paste the same prompts, without the answer-only line, and skip step 4.



1. Set up. In the R console, run usethis::edit_file("scratch/debugging.R"). It creates this block’s practice script and opens it. Paste this in and run it. The last two commands are code you wrote to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles:

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
voles <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))

high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

It runs without error but returns NaN. The bug is in what you asked for. Put the evidence in front of you first, then in front of the assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files..
2. Inspect the data before asking for help. In the R console:

voles |> distinct(treatment_arm)
voles |> count(treatment_arm)
nrow(high_dose)

The values are Control, Low_dose and High_dose, and nrow() is zero: you have found the bug yourself in seconds.
3. Ask with the evidence in hand. Paste the code and the diagnostic output together, so that the answer rests on the real values, not a guess.
Prompt (Claude Code):
I am trying to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles.
My code:

  high_dose <- voles |>
    filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

  high_dose |>
    summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

returns NaN. But voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) returns
"Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose". I think the filter fails because of
the capitalisation. Is that the only problem?
Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
If it asks to run a command or edit a file despite the last line, choose No. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Ignore a first line # agents-md: active v1 in its code: Block 4 explains it.






NoteHow it works: asking an agent only to answer





Claude Code is an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.: given a question, it may search your project, read files and offer to run code. The answer-only line is only a request. Claude Code has no ask mode. Plan mode is not used here, because it still reads your files while it plans. Manual mode is the control: Claude Code must ask before it runs a command or edits a file, and your answer decides.
Claude Code cannot see the objects in your R console, such as voles. It sees your data only by reading files or running code. Each Rscript command it runs starts a fresh R process. Check its work in the R console (checking work).



4. Now let the agent gather the evidence. This is the one step in the block where it acts. Type /clear so that it starts without the evidence you pasted, then send this prompt:
Prompt (Claude Code):
Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and run R code with Rscript to find why
filtering treatment_arm for "high_dose" returns no rows. Don't edit any files.
Show each command and its output.
It reads the file without asking (reading needs no approval), but asks before it runs R. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. Here you can, so choose Yes if the Rscript command only reads the data and prints results. Then compare its diagnosis with yours from step 2.
5. Fix it. Correct the filter in scratch/debugging.R and run it again.
Keep this conversation open: in Block 3 you read its transcript to see what reached the model provider.


Solution


high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "High_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g, na.rm = TRUE))

The filter now matches the data. na.rm = TRUE is a precaution for real data, which usually have missing values.

You are done when nrow(high_dose) is 24, the mean is a number, not NaN, and the agent’s diagnosis in step 4 matches yours from step 2.
If it goes wrong: if nrow() is still zero, run voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) again and copy the value exactly as printed.

title: Block 2: Debugging with AI
section: Exercise 2: A correct-looking but wrong result
text:
Exercise 2: A correct-looking but wrong result


A correct-looking but wrong result (8 minutes)


Goal: catch a result that runs cleanly but is wrong by stating the expected answer before you ask, so that a plausible but wrong number does not reach your results.
Start state: scratch/debugging.R is open with voles loaded. Ask in Exercise 1’s conversation, without /clear, so that its transcript is still there for Block 3.
You wrote this to get the mean change in body mass by treatment arm. Paste it into scratch/debugging.R and run it:

voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

It runs, and the numbers look plausible. But the treatment was designed to increase mass, and they say mass falls. Only your knowledge of the study reveals the error: an AI catches it only if you tell it what the answer should be.
1. Write down what a correct result should look like, then compare. Here: positive values, rising from Control to High_dose. The mismatch is the diagnosis.
2. Ask for a second opinion, stating the expected direction.
Prompt (Claude Code):
This should show mass gain increasing with dose, but the values are negative
and decreasing. What is wrong?

  voles |>
    mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
    summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
3. Fix it. Correct the subtraction in scratch/debugging.R and run it again.


Solution


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

mass_change_g is post minus pre: gain, not loss. The original ran without complaint because subtraction works in either direction.

You are done when your corrected means are positive and increase from Control to High_dose, as you predicted in step 1.
If it goes wrong: if the values are still negative, check which mass you subtract from which: post minus pre is gain.


When AI helps most. AI helps most when you give it the evidence (the error, the data values) and say what the result should be. It cannot know your study design unless you tell it: that is why Exercise 2’s prompt states the expected direction.






NoteThe debugging checklist





Inspect the data first, ask the AI second.


Read the error in full: the function name and the phrase usually locate the bug.

Inspect the data: glimpse(), distinct(), summary(), and nrow() after a filter.

Check names exactly, including capitals and underscores.

Then ask, giving the code, the error and the diagnostic output together. Ask for an answer, not an action, until you have the evidence.

Explain the fix in one sentence before you accept it.

Before trusting a clean run, state what the result should look like (sign, size, order) and compare.










NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: use an assistant to diagnose and fix errors in your own code, trusted because you inspect the data first and explain each fix in a sentence.

Check: before trusting a clean run, state the sign and size the result should have, and compare.

Reproduce: rerun the fixed code in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., so it does not depend on a leftover object.

Record: nothing to log yet; the AI-use log starts in Block 3.

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Name the routes (3 minutes)


Goal: see exactly what reached the model provider when the agent investigated in Block 2, so that you can name every route your data take.
Start state: Claude Code running in the Terminal tab, as you left it in Block 2.






TipUsing another tool





The exercises use Claude Code. With Posit Assistant:


Exercise 1: scroll back to your Block 2 conversation in the same way, and use the Posit Assistant column of What each tool can see, below the diagram.

Exercise 2: use /plan for step 1 and Normal mode (/normal) for step 2. The checks are the same: the Git pane and the R console.

For GitHub Copilot, see GitHub Copilot and the remote rung in Going further.



1. Find the transcript. Scroll back in Claude Code to Block 2’s Exercise 1, where the agent read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and ran Rscript. Above each reply, Claude Code lists the actions it took. If you cleared the conversation, re-run that prompt from Block 2.
2. Name each route in the diagram below; the table under it gives the detail for each tool. A file it read is route 2. The output of a command it ran is route 4. What you pasted yourself, in Block 2’s Exercise 2 prompt, is route 1. Then add two routes that no action shows. One is AGENTS.md, which Claude Code reads at the start of every conversation (route 2). The other is the context it adds itself, including your recent commit messages (route 3).
You are done when you can name every file or command output that reached the model provider.
If it goes wrong: if the transcript shows files you did not expect, or a search of the project, name those too: an agent reads what it judges useful, which is why the habits below matter for confidential data.





Route 1. What you paste: errors, output, results


Route 2. Project files it reads, including AGENTS.md


Route 3. Context the tool adds by itself


Route 4. Output of the code and commands it runs



sent with each request


Model provider


Anything that reaches one of these four routes leaves your machine. The table below shows what each route carries in each tool.












Claude Code
Posit Assistant
Browser chat




Route 1: what you paste
Yes
Yes
Yes



Route 2: project files
Any file in the project, read without asking, unless a deny rule names it (habit 4, below)
Files in the project; it asks before reading outside it. .Renviron and .env are blocked
Only files you upload



Route 3: added by itself

AGENTS.md, the project folder, platform, date, git branch, uncommitted changes and recent commit messages

AGENTS.md, the R version, and the names and types of the objects in your session, not their values (this session context can be switched off)
Its memory or project files, if you have switched them on



Route 4: code it runs

Rscript, in a new R process that cannot see the objects in your console; it reads whatever the code prints
R code in your own live session, so the code can reach your objects; it reads whatever the code prints
None


Your console and plots
No
Yes: it can read your console history and view plots
Only what you paste









TipContext you hold in your head (instructor demonstration)





An assistant’s answer about your data is only as good as its context. It is reliable only when it has real information: something you pasted, a file it read, or output from a command it ran. A data file supplies column names, but not your question or your design.
Where to run it: a new browser chat (claude.ai or similar) with no project, files or memory attached, such as a temporary chat. Not Claude Code: inside the workshop repository it would read AGENTS.md and the data file (route 2), so even the first prompt would get a specific answer.
Your instructor asks a new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
and then, in another new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
The first gets a tour of options. The second can get a recommendation, because the design now exists outside your head. Treat it as a proposal to check: the primary analysis is your decision.
Try it yourself after the session: give each prompt to its own new browser chat and compare the answers. For a third run, give the first prompt to Claude Code in your workshop repository. It reads the data without being asked and names the columns, but it still cannot know your question.









ImportantWorking with confidential data: five habits, strongest first



An agent reads what it judges useful. If one route is closed, it often tries another: refused a file, it may offer R code that opens the same file. So the habits are listed from the one that always holds to the ones that only slow it down.


Keep it out of the project. Put a synthetic or anonymised copy in the project, and run the final analysis on the real data yourself, outside the agent’s folder. A file that is not there cannot be read by any route.

Know your account. Commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise, API) are not used for model training. On Pro or Max, set /privacy-settings. Check your institution’s approval, ethics approval and data agreements first.

Read every R command before you approve it. In Manual mode, Claude Code asks before it runs Rscript. Look for file paths in the code, and say No to any that would open a file you want kept out. You will see an agent offer this route in Block 7.

Add a deny rule as well, in /permissions, for example Read(/data/confidential/**). It stops Claude Code’s own file reads and simple commands such as cat and head. It does not stop R code that opens the file, or a search of the whole project such as grep -r, which runs without asking. Treat it as a speed bump, not a wall (Block 5).

Describe, don’t show. names() and dim() describe the data without showing values. summary() prints real minima and maxima. print(), glimpse() and str() print actual rows.







TipHow it works: tool notes







Claude Code:

There is no .claudeignore file.
Read-only commands such as cat, head, grep and ls never ask, even in Manual mode.
On macOS, Linux and WSL2, the /sandbox command adds an operating-system block on reading paths you list (sandbox.filesystem.denyRead). That block applies to R code too. The sandbox is not available on native Windows.



Posit Assistant:

It blocks .Renviron and .env by default.
Its session context, the names and types of your objects, can be switched off.
Code it runs in your live session can still print values.
Its documentation does not say whether a deny rule can name a folder, so test one before you rely on it.

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Exercise 2: What can it do?
The model is the same at every rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 3, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. of the autonomy ladder. What changes is what it may do without asking you, which in Claude Code is set by its permission modeThe setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).. Rung 3, act with approval, is where routine work stays checkable:

you start from a commit, so you can revert any change;
you see every edit and command first;
a test checks the result, whatever the agent reports.







NoteThe autonomy ladder



An assistant that advises leaves you to filter every change. An agent that acts removes that filter, unless you put it back. The rungs differ in how much of that filtering is left to you.
Each rung answers two questions: can the assistant change your files or run code, and what do you approve?









Rung
Changes files or runs code?
What you approve
Claude Code
Posit Assistant



0. Suggest
No: it completes the line you are typing
Each suggestion, by accepting it
—
Next Edit Suggestions


1. Ask
No: it answers in the chat
Nothing; it may still read files
— (no ask mode; Block 2’s answer-only line is a request)
Ask mode (/ask)


2. Plan
No edits: it proposes steps
The plan, before anything changes
/plan
/plan


3. Act, with approval
Yes
Every edit and every command, except read-only ones
Manual (default): the workshop’s starting mode
Normal mode


4. Act, partly unsupervised
Yes
Only actions outside a set it may take alone

acceptEdits (edits and file commands); auto (a classifier approves actions)
Auto mode (/auto)


5. Act, unsupervised
Yes
Nothing
bypassPermissions
YOLO mode (/yolo)



In Claude Code, reading a project file never needs approval, at any rung. From rung 3 up, what changes is which tool callsA single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls. run without your approval. Block 6, after lunch, builds that approval step in code. Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in Manual, although recent versions of Claude Code start in auto. Keep Manual for confidential data. /plan may run commands to explore, and on recent versions some run without asking you. Use only rungs 0 to 3 today. The quick reference lists the commands for the other modes.
Each rung up removes a moment when you would have seen the action. In acceptEdits, for example, file commands such as cp and mv run without asking, so a cp over a raw data file needs no approval. The higher the rung, the more an agent acts on its guesses about your conventions. That is why Block 4 writes them down.




Ask, plan, act (15 minutes)


Goal: have the agent add a column and a plot script at rung 3, then check its work with the diff and the tests, so that you trust the change because you checked it, not because the agent reported it.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code in Manual mode. Check its work from the R console and the Git pane (checking work).
1. Plan (rung 2). In Claude Code, type /clear, then:
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a mass_change_g column (mass_post_g
minus mass_pre_g) to the voles data frame itself. Create a new script
scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R that plots mass_change_g by
treatment_arm and saves the figure to outputs/ with ggsave(). Don't run
anything; I'll check the scripts myself.
Before you approve, check that the plan names both files, adds the column to voles itself, leaves data/raw/ alone and saves the figure to outputs/. If anything is missing, choose No, keep planning and say what to change.
2. Act, with approval (rung 3). Choose Yes, manually approve edits. It is not the first option: the first, Yes, and use auto mode (or Yes, auto-accept edits), switches the approvals off. Then read each edit before you approve it. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on.
If it asks to run git status before it edits (AGENTS.md asks it to check), answer Yes: that command only reads. It may also ask to run the new scripts and the test suite with Rscript. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. For these, choose No: you check the result yourself next.
3. Read the diff. Click Diff in the Git pane for each changed file. Read it as you would a colleague’s work: the diff shows every change, including any you did not ask for.
4. Record. Start your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.. The agent knows the date, its model and what it did, so let it draft the line. Only you know what you kept or changed, so that part stays yours.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Create docs/ai-log.md and add one line for the work you just did, in the
form: date (YYYY-MM-DD); Claude Code (your model name); task; TODO.
Leave the last field as TODO.
Approve the new file after reading it. Then open it (usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")) and replace TODO with what you kept or changed. Check that the date and the model match what is shown above the Claude Code prompt. The finished line looks like this:
2026-10-19; Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5); added mass_change_g and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff
Writing it before you test means the tests check it too.
5. Test, then commit. Restart R (Session → Restart R) so that nothing left in your session can make a test pass. Then run:
In the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

test_dir() runs every test*.R file in tests/. The template ships them; in this block, these are the ones that matter:


File
Checks
Before this block



test_explore.R

mass_change_g in voles really is post minus pre; the plot script runs in a fresh R session and saves a figure in outputs/

Skipped: no plot script yet


test_ai_log.R
Every log line has four parts and a real date
Skipped: no log yet


test_controls.R
Manual mode, the deny rules and AGENTS.md are still in place (Block 4)
Already passing



The other test files are for later blocks, and skip. Commit the log and both scripts together (git ignores outputs/).
Where tests like these come from in your own work. None of these checks needed the answer in advance. Each comes from what you asked for: the definition of the column, a script that runs from a fresh session and saves a file, a log line in the agreed form. So you can write them, or have the agent draft them for you to read, before the agent does the work. They cannot tell you whether the plot is a good one: you check that by looking. Block 8 writes a test from scratch.






NoteThe test you just ran: tests/test_explore.R






# tests/test_explore.R ----
# Block 3: the derived column and the plot script the agent wrote.
library(testthat)
testthat::local_edition(3)

test_that("mass_change_g is post-treatment mass minus pre-treatment mass", {
  script <- here::here("scripts", "explore_voles.R")
  # the plot script is Block 3's other output: once it exists, the column must too
  skip_if_not(
    file.exists(here::here("scripts", "explore_mass_change_plot.R")),
    "Block 3 not done yet: no plot script"
  )

  # run the script in a fresh R session, so its library() calls cannot change
  # this one, and bring back only the voles data it made
  voles <- callr::r(
    function(script) {
      env <- new.env()
      utils::capture.output(sys.source(script, envir = env))
      if (exists("voles", envir = env)) env$voles else NULL
    },
    args = list(script),
    wd = here::here()
  )
  expect_true(
    !is.null(voles) && "mass_change_g" %in% names(voles),
    label = "explore_voles.R adds mass_change_g to voles"
  )
  expect_equal(voles$mass_change_g, voles$mass_post_g - voles$mass_pre_g)
})

test_that("the plot script runs in a fresh R session and saves to outputs/", {
  script <- here::here("scripts", "explore_mass_change_plot.R")
  skip_if_not(file.exists(script), "Block 3 not done yet: no plot script")

  # an Rplots.pdf made earlier by something else is not this script's fault
  rplots <- here::here("Rplots.pdf")
  rplots_before <- file.exists(rplots)
  expect_no_error(
    callr::rscript(script, wd = here::here(), show = FALSE)
  )
  after <- list.files(here::here("outputs"), recursive = TRUE)

  expect_true(
    length(after) > 0 && any(grepl("\\.(png|pdf)$", after)),
    label = "a .png or .pdf in outputs/"
  )
  expect_false(
    !rplots_before && file.exists(rplots),
    label = "no stray Rplots.pdf (save the figure with ggsave())"
  )
})




You are done when you have read every line of the diff, the tests show no failures, the explore and ai_log lines of the test output show their tests under OK, not S (skipped), and your first log line is committed with both scripts.
If it goes wrong: select the unwanted change in the Git pane and click Revert, then ask again more clearly. If test_explore.R says voles has no mass_change_g, the agent made the column somewhere else: ask it to add the column to voles itself. An S on explore or ai_log means its file is missing or misnamed. Out of time? Carry on: at the end of Block 4, checkpoint-skills holds this block’s files (commit or discard your changes in the Git pane first, so the switch is not blocked).






TipStretch: reflect on the rungs





At which rung did you decide the most? Where would you have missed an unwanted change without the diff?
Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?









NoteAt the command line





The same checks from a terminal (after /exit, or in a second Terminal tab): git status, git diff, and Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')".











NoteThe safe vibe-coding recipe





Commit, so you start from a clean Git pane.

Protect the inputs: /permissions shows the deny rules, or you add one.

Have the checks ready: tests in tests/ before the agent starts.

Ask in one prompt or skill, in Manual mode, reading each approval.

Run the checks: the test suite in a fresh R session.

Read the diff in the Git pane, then commit or revert.

You will use these six steps in Blocks 7 and 8. The template ships the protections and the tests, so most of the work is checking that they are there.








NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand an agent a routine multi-file change at rung 3, trusted because you read every diff and a test you did not write checks the result.

Check: the Git pane’s diff after every agent action; the agent’s report that something “still runs” is a claim until a test confirms it.

Reproduce: work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert.

Record: your AI-use log starts here, in docs/ai-log.md.

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
text:
Edit, check, verify (12 minutes)


Goal: make AGENTS.md describe your own practice and prove Claude Code loads it, so that every later conversation starts from your conventions.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab (checking work).






TipUsing another tool





The activities use Claude Code. Posit Assistant reads the same AGENTS.md: open it from the gear menu (Open project memory), or describe your conventions and run /savememory. If the canary is missing, check that you trusted the workspace. It reads skills from .agents/skills/ directly, so it needs no copy in .claude/skills/. Invoke a skill by name in the same way. For other tools, see Instruction and skill files in other tools in Going further.



1. Baseline. See the starter file at work before you change it.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot
of mass_post_g by treatment arm. Show the R code in your reply; do not
create any files.
Look for the canaryA fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed., # agents-md: active v1, as the first line of the code: it shows AGENTS.md was loaded.
Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Here, answer No if it asks to create or run anything: you asked only to see the code.






NoteThe starter AGENTS.md





The canary is a fixed first line that the file asks the assistant to put in any R code it writes. When you see it, you know the file was loaded. Asking for the code in the reply gives the canary somewhere to appear. The “Tests” rules ask the agent to prove its own work after every edit; later blocks rely on this.


# Project conventions: voles analysis

## Canary
When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block:
# agents-md: active v1

## Structure
- Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified.
- Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/.
- Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/.

## R style
- Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment.
- Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F.
- Build every path with here::here() (or here() after library(here)). Never
  use setwd() or rm(list = ls()).
- Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types.

## Reproducibility
- Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before
  adding a package.
- Do not edit renv.lock.
- Set a seed immediately before any random step.
- Every script must run in a fresh R session.
- Before you report a task done, run each new script once with Rscript from
  the project root and report the exit status.
- Save figures with ggsave() to outputs/.

## Tests
- Before you report a task done, run Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')"
  once and paste the final summary line verbatim.
- Never edit anything in tests/fixtures/, an existing expectation or a
  tolerance to make a test pass.
- Every new function in scripts/functions/ gets a test with at least one
  known-answer case on a small tibble, including an NA; expected values are
  worked out by hand, never by running the code under test.

## Data integrity
- Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment.
- Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic.

## Statistics
- Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory.
- Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code.

## Version control
- Before you edit any file, run git status.
- If this folder is not a git repository, stop and ask me to set one up.
- If there are uncommitted changes, list them and ask whether I want to
  commit first.
- Never commit, push or change git settings unless I ask.

## Working with me
- Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval.
- Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/. The one
  exception: a skill may run tests/make_reference.R once, to capture a
  reference that does not exist yet.





2. Make it yours. Open AGENTS.md from the Files pane (or run usethis::edit_file("AGENTS.md")), and:

delete one rule you do not actually follow, from Structure, R style, Reproducibility or Data integrity;
add one convention you always follow, on one line and specific enough to check (“use the native pipe |>”, not “write clean code”).

Keep the canary and the Tests, Statistics, Version control and Working with me sections: later blocks and tests/test_controls.R rely on them. Save the file.






NoteWhat makes an instruction work





Use AGENTS.md for what is always true: structure, style, reproducibility rules. Instructions that work are:


One per line, and specific enough to check (“use the native pipe |>”, not “write clean code”).

True of your own code, or the model gets mixed signals.

Short, because the file loads into every request.

Added when a mistake repeats: a correction in chat is forgotten in the next conversation.

Not a guarantee: “never edit raw data” belongs here and in the enforced controls of Block 5.










NoteWhere an instruction file comes from in your own projects





Here you start from a file we wrote. In your own projects there are three routes:







Route
Strengths
Weaknesses



Write it yourself
Holds conventions the code cannot show; short; true of your practice
Slow; a blank page


/init
Fast; finds the layout, commands and packages
Writes a CLAUDE.md, which hides any AGENTS.md; describes what the code does, including habits you would not choose; cannot see unwritten conventions; tends to run long


Ask Claude to assess the project and draft an AGENTS.md
As fast as /init; you choose the file name and see the draft before any file exists
The same risks: rules inferred from your code that are not really yours, and length



The third route usually works best: let the agent draft, then delete every line that is not true of your practice, and add what it could not discover (your statistics rules, what must never be touched). Keep the file short: the Claude Code documentation suggests well under 200 lines. Draft an instruction file for a project of your own, in Going further, walks through it. Do not run /init in the workshop repository.



3. Verify. Type /memory and check that AGENTS.md is listed. Press Esc rather than choosing it: choosing it opens the file in an external editor. (When Claude Code starts, it may also print a line such as AGENTS.md loaded: ….) Type /clear, then repeat the step 1 prompt. The canary shows the file was loaded. To see whether it was followed, check the plot code against your new rule.
4. Check it with a test. Restart R (Session → Restart R), so the tests run in a clean session. Then run this in the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

Then commit AGENTS.md from the Git pane.
Why a test, when the canary already appeared? The canary shows the file was loaded today. tests/test_controls.R guards later: it fails if an edit, yours or one made by R code the agent runs, removes the canary or the git status rule, or loosens the settings (Manual mode, the deny rules, no command approved in advance). Blocks 5 and 8 rely on all of these. The test checks what the files say, not whether the model obeys them; that gap is the subject of Block 5. Your AGENTS.md also asks the agent to run this same suite before it reports a task done, so it is the agent’s check as well as yours.
You are done when the canary appears, the test suite has no failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your edited AGENTS.md is committed.
If it goes wrong: if /memory does not list AGENTS.md, look for a CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the project or in any folder above it, such as your Documents or OneDrive folder. Any of them hides AGENTS.md (How it works, below): rename or delete it. Also check that claude --version is 2.1.281 or later (setup). If test_controls.R fails, restore the canary or the git status line. A failure in test_explore.R or test_ai_log.R is left over from Block 3. Still stuck? Compare with the checkpoint-skills branch.








NoteHow it works: which files Claude Code reads








Instruction file: loaded into every conversation


AGENTS.md: your conventions


read by


Claude Code




Skills: loaded when invoked or judged relevant


.agents/skills/<your-skill>/ (the master copy)


you copy


.claude/skills/<your-skill>/


read by


Claude Code



The course’s own skills already ship in both folders; Activity 2 shows how to copy one you write.


Claude Code reads AGENTS.md, at the repository root, at the start of every conversation. /memory lists the instruction files that Claude Code loaded. Choosing one opens it in an external editor, which may be vi on macOS, so edit AGENTS.md from the Files pane instead.
Why AGENTS.md and not CLAUDE.md? CLAUDE.md is Claude Code’s own name for the file, and for Claude Code alone it works in exactly the same way. AGENTS.md is a name that several tools share, including Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot, so one file serves them all. This course uses AGENTS.md, and tests/test_controls.R looks for it, so keep that name here.
The two names do not combine by default. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md only when there is no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the project or any folder above it. Creating one, for example with /init, hides your conventions without any warning. (Your personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md does not count.) If a project needs both, put this line in its CLAUDE.md, and add any Claude-only instructions below it:
@AGENTS.md
The @ imports the file, so Claude Code reads both. On Windows, use this import rather than a symbolic link.

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
section: Activity 2: Write a skill and test it
text:
Activity 2: Write a skill and test it
A skill is a folder holding a SKILL.md file. Its front matterThe block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill’s name and description, or a Quarto document’s options., between two lines of three dashes, gives a name and a description, and the description is the trigger: “Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report, poster or paper” loads when it should; “for plots” loads erratically. The body is the procedure.


A house figure style (15 minutes)


Goal: write a skill and grade a figure made with it against your instructor’s baseline made without it, so that you judge the skill by what it changes, not by its own report.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean (your AGENTS.md committed), Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab.
1. The baseline, made without the skill. Your instructor runs this prompt on screen, before the skill exists; you don’t run it. Instructor: post the figure in the Zoom chat, because learners grade against it in step 4.
Prompt (Claude Code, run by your instructor):
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_baseline.R.
2. Create the skill. In the R console, usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md") creates and opens the file. Open the box below, copy the skill into the file, and save. Read its description and six rules as you do: step 4 grades three of them.






NoteThe house-figures skill: copy this into SKILL.md





---
name: house-figures
description: >-
  Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear
  in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a
  figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots.
---

# House figure style

## Rules
1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation
   (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar
   with error bars ("dynamite plot").
2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette
   (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same
   variable to point shape so the figure works without colour.
3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)".
4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12).
5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure.
6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a
   fitted model and asks for them.

## Before returning code
List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why.



Copy it into .claude/skills/, where Claude Code reads it:

fs::dir_copy(
  here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"),
  here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)

Type /skills: house-figures should be listed.






NoteHow it works: two skill folders





.agents/skills/ is the master copy, which other tools such as Posit Assistant read directly; Claude Code reads .claude/skills/, so copy the folder again whenever you change the skill. The deny rules keep the agent’s edit tools out of .claude/, so you make the copy yourself, but they do not cover .agents/skills/, so check the master copy in the Git pane too. On macOS or Linux you can link the folders instead of copying them: see Going further.
A skill suits a procedure, such as producing a publication figure or cleaning data against a codebook, and can hold scripts or templates beside SKILL.md. Its body is a procedure (when to use it, the steps, hard rules and a final check) and loads only when the skill is used, so it can be longer than AGENTS.md. Invoking it by name (/skill-name) always works. Claude Code picks up a new skill in .claude/skills/ without a restart; if /skills does not list it, type /reload-skills. For a skill that writes files, disable-model-invocation: true in the front matter makes it run only when you invoke it by name.



3. With the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_house.R.
If it asks to run git status before it edits (AGENTS.md asks it to check), that only reads, so Yes is fine. Read the edit before you approve it. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. So if it asks to run the new script, choose No: you run it yourself next.
4. Grade it. Restart R (Session → Restart R), run source(here::here("scripts", "fig_house.R")) and open the figure it saved in outputs/. Compare it with your instructor’s baseline on three rules you can see at a glance:


Rule
Baseline (no skill)
Your figure (with skill)



1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot




2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape




5. n per group shown





5. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md, as in Block 3, naming the skill and what you kept or changed in its output. Commit it with the skill (both folders) and scripts/fig_house.R.
You are done when the table is filled in from the figures you looked at, not from the agent’s list of rules it applied, and your log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if /skills does not list it, check that .claude/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md exists and its front matter starts and ends with three dashes. If no figure appears in outputs/, ask the agent to save it there with ggsave(), as AGENTS.md asks. Out of time? Commit or discard your changes in the Git pane first, so the switch is not blocked, then switch to checkpoint-skills.






TipStretch: test the trigger





In a new conversation (/clear), test the trigger: “Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm” should not load the skill; “Make a figure of metabolic_rate_post by treatment_arm for a poster” should. Or test rule 6: ask it to “add significance stars between the groups in scripts/fig_house.R” and see whether it declines. Either way, what makes the output trustworthy is the grading in step 4, which you can repeat on every figure.
Payoff. What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and would you use it for the next figure?











NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: state your conventions once, and package a procedure as a skill, trusted because the canary and tests/test_controls.R show the files are connected, and you grade the output rule by rule.

Check: a canary shows a file was loaded, not followed.

Reproduce: your AGENTS.md states the reproducibility rules; Blocks 7 and 8 check the agent kept to them.

Record: your log line from step 5.

title: Block 6: Build your own agent in R
text:
Talk to a model, then give it a tool (8 minutes)


Goal: see what one request to a model is, what a model cannot do on its own, and what a tool request is, so that nothing your agent does in Task 2 is a surprise.
1. Have a conversation. Run this in the R console:

library(ellmer)

key <- function() Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY")
chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", credentials = key)
chat$chat("Tell me a joke about R.")
chat$chat("Explain why it is funny, in one sentence.")
chat$chat("How many days is it until 25 December?")
chat

Printing chat shows the conversation as turnsOne message in a conversation with a model: either yours (the user turn) or the model’s reply (the assistant turn). Tool results go back to the model inside a user turn.. The second question works only because ellmer sends the whole conversation so far with each request: the model keeps nothing between requests (“the LLM API is stateless”, in Wickham’s words). That is the context window from Block 1. It is also why a long conversation costs more per question.
The memory is the chat object in your R session. It lasts as long as that object does, and nothing is saved to disk. Restart R, or create a new chat (as step 2 does), and the conversation starts again from nothing.
Now read the third answer. A model on its own only produces text. It has no clock, and it cannot run code, open your files or change them. Today’s date is “a question that cannot be part of its training data” (Wickham), so the model can only say it does not know, ask you, or guess, and a guess reads as confidently as a fact. The same holds for anything it tells you about data or code it has not been shown: it predicts; it does not check.
2. Give it a tool. A toolR functions (or other programs) that an agent may ask to have run, each described to the model by a name, a description and its arguments. The model only asks; the harness runs the tool on your computer and sends back the result. “is just a different name for a function, but importantly it’s a function that’s run on your computer” (Wickham). Tools let a model get data about the world as it is today, and take actions:

today <- tool(
  function() format(Sys.Date()),
  name = "today",
  description = "Get today's date."
)

chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", credentials = key)
chat$register_tool(today)
chat$chat("How many days is it until 25 December?")
chat

The model sees only the tool’s name, description and arguments (here, none), so the description is all it has to decide when the tool is useful. Its first reply is a request: “call today”. ellmer runs today() on your computer and sends the result back. Then the model answers, now from a fact rather than a guess. That is two requestsOne call to the model, with the whole conversation so far, and its reply. A single question can take several requests when the model asks for tools before it answers. for one question. This new chat knows nothing of the joke: it is a new conversation.
You are done when you can point, in the printed chat, to the tool request and to the tool result, say which of them ran on your computer, and say why the same question in step 1 could not get a reliable answer.
If it goes wrong: if the first chat$chat() reports a missing or invalid key, check Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY") != "". Restart R after you edit .Renviron.

title: Block 6: Build your own agent in R
text:
Your agent: agent/mini_agent.R

Your repository ships a complete agent of about 80 lines, built from the same parts. It has one job: translate a short base R function into tidyverse code, run a test that compares the two, and fix its code until they match. Your instructor walks through it. Each part matches something from this morning.
Three tools. Each is an R function, described to the model by a name, a description and its arguments:









Tool
The model sends
What runs on your computer
What goes back to the model
Asks you first?



read_file()
a path

readLines() on that file, if allowed() agrees
the file’s text
No


write_file()
a path under scripts/, and the whole new file

writeLines(), if allowed() agrees
“Wrote …”
Yes


run_test()
nothing
the shipped test tests/test_translation.R, in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.

the last 40 lines of the test’s report
Yes



run_test() is how the agent finds out whether its code works. It takes no arguments, so the model cannot choose another test or hand it code. The test does three things:

runs the original base R function, legacy_rate_summary(), which is defined inside the test file;
in a second fresh R session, sources scripts/functions/load_voles.R and the agent’s scripts/functions/summaries.R, then runs summarise_rate_tidy(load_voles());
compares the two results once types and row order are normalised: an equivalence checkA comparison showing that two versions of code, such as an original and an AI translation, give the same output once only presentation (types, row order) is normalised..

If they match, the report says the test passed. If not, it lists the values that differ, and the agent reads that list to choose its next fix.
allowed() is its deny rule. Each path is first made absolute and tidied (scripts/../tests becomes tests), then checked. The agent may read anything inside the project except files named .Renviron or .env. It may write only under scripts/, so it cannot edit its checks in tests/ or its own rules in agent/.
ask_first() is Manual mode. Reads go straight through. Every write and every test run is shown to you first, and is refused unless you choose Yes.
The system promptStanding instructions sent with every request, before the conversation itself. It does the job an instruction file such as AGENTS.md does for Claude Code. is its instruction file. The agent is not given your AGENTS.md, though it could still open the file, like any other. Like AGENTS.md, its prompt is only a request.
Predict: which of these does allowed() refuse? Decide before your instructor runs them.


read_file("data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv") 
refused
allowed


read_file("../.Renviron") 
refused
allowed


write_file("scripts/../tests/test_translation.R", …) 
refused
allowed


write_file("scripts/functions/load_voles.R", …) 
refused
allowed


read_file(".renviron"), on Windows or a Mac 
refused
allowed




Why?


The raw data are inside the project, so the agent may read them, and what it reads goes to the provider: Block 3’s disclosure route.

../ leaves the project. Your key is in your user-level .Renviron, outside every project, so it is refused on both counts.
The path is tidied before it is checked, so the .. trick ends in tests/.

load_voles.R is under scripts/, so the agent may rewrite it, yet the test relies on it: a changed loader could let a wrong translation pass. That is one reason to check, at the end, that the Git pane shows only summaries.R.
The check compares names exactly, but Windows and macOS ignore case in file names, so .renviron opens a project’s .Renviron, if it has one. A list of names covers the names you thought of, like a deny rule in Block 5: it prevents, on the routes it names.


The gap is still there. run_test() cannot be handed code, but the test it runs sources summaries.R, and the agent writes that file. Whatever the agent puts there runs when you choose Yes to run_test(): a line that overwrites data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv, or one that reads your key with Sys.getenv() and puts it in an error message, which goes back to the model in the test’s report. The model has no reason to do either, but nothing in the code stops it. allowed() decides where the agent’s code is saved, not what that code does when it runs. That is the gap Block 5 found: R code can write anywhere, whatever the deny rules say. What stands in the way is you, reading the code at the write_file approval before you let the test run it.






TipReference: the full agent/mini_agent.R






# agent/mini_agent.R ----
# A small coding agent: Claude, three tools, and the loop ellmer runs for you.
# Load it from your workshop repository with
#   source(here::here("agent", "mini_agent.R"))
# then talk to `chat`.
library(ellmer)

# the model: "claude-opus-5-5" is a larger model, at a higher price per token
model <- "claude-sonnet-5-5"

# your API key, from the AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY line in your user-level .Renviron;
# it has its own name so that Claude Code never offers to use it
agent_key <- function() Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY")
if (agent_key() == "") {
  stop("No AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY found: add it with usethis::edit_r_environ(), ",
       "then restart R.")
}

# the agent's deny rule: a path must sit inside `folder`, and never be a
# credentials file ----
root <- here::here()
allowed <- function(path, folder = root) {
  full <- fs::path_norm(fs::path_abs(path, start = root))
  if (!fs::path_has_parent(full, folder) || fs::path_file(full) %in% c(".Renviron", ".env")) {
    stop("Refused: ", path)
  }
  full
}

# the tools ----
read_file <- tool(
  function(path) paste(readLines(allowed(path), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"),
  name = "read_file",
  description = "Read a text file in the project.",
  arguments = list(path = type_string("A file, relative to the project root."))
)
write_file <- tool(
  function(path, content) {
    writeLines(content, allowed(path, folder = fs::path(root, "scripts")))
    paste("Wrote", path)
  },
  name = "write_file",
  description = "Replace the whole contents of a text file under scripts/.",
  arguments = list(
    path = type_string("A file under scripts/, relative to the project root."),
    content = type_string("The complete new contents of the file.")
  )
)
run_test <- tool(
  function() {
    # the one thing it can run: the translation test, in a fresh R session
    out <- callr::r(function() utils::capture.output(
      testthat::test_file("tests/test_translation.R", reporter = "summary")
    ))
    paste(utils::tail(out, 40), collapse = "\n")
  },
  name = "run_test",
  description = "Run tests/test_translation.R in a fresh R session and return its output."
)

# Manual mode: show every write or test run, and ask before it happens ----
ask_first <- function(request) {
  if (request@name %in% c("write_file", "run_test")) {
    cat("\nThe agent wants to call", request@name, "with:\n")
    for (arg in names(request@arguments)) {
      cat("--", arg, "--\n", request@arguments[[arg]], "\n")
    }
    if (utils::menu(c("Yes", "No"), title = "Allow it?") != 1) tool_reject()
  }
}

chat <- chat_anthropic(
  model = model,
  credentials = agent_key,
  system_prompt = paste(
    "You are a careful R assistant working in this project.",
    "Read files before you change them. Write files only under scripts/;",
    "never edit tests/. Code you write must work in a fresh R session, so load",
    "packages with library() or call them with pkg::. Say what you changed,",
    "and stop when the task is done."
  )
)
chat$register_tools(list(read_file, write_file, run_test))
chat$on_tool_request(ask_first)

An error in a tool does not stop the agent. ellmer sends the error message back to the model, which can try something else. So a refused write comes back as “Refused: …”. run_test() starts a fresh R session with callr::r(), and the test starts a second one for the agent’s code. Fresh sessions keep objects and loaded packages apart in both directions: nothing the test or the agent’s code loads reaches your session, and nothing loaded in yours can make the test pass. They do not protect files: code in a fresh session can still write anywhere. Only the last 40 lines of the test’s report go back to the model.

title: Block 6: Build your own agent in R
text:
Task 2: run your agent


Run your agent (15 minutes)


Goal: watch your own agent write, test and fix a translation while you approve every write and test run, so that you see exactly where Manual mode and a deny rule act, and what a passing test does and does not tell you.
Start state: main, Git pane clean, R’s working directory at the repository’s root (as it is when you open the project).
1. Load the agent. Nothing is sent to the model yet:

source(here::here("agent", "mini_agent.R"))

2. Give it the task. You ask for a tidyverse version of legacy_rate_summary(), the original base R code. It is in tests/test_translation.R, next to the check that compares the two:

chat$chat(paste(
  "Write a function summarise_rate_tidy(data) in scripts/functions/summaries.R",
  "whose output matches legacy_rate_summary() in tests/test_translation.R.",
  "Use dplyr and the native pipe; it must work in a fresh R session.",
  "Write only that file, and no tests. Then run the test with run_test,",
  "and fix the function until it passes."
))







TipThe original code, and what you are asking for






legacy_rate_summary <- function() {
  voles <- read.csv(
    here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
    stringsAsFactors = TRUE
  )
  rate_mean <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex,
                         data = voles, FUN = mean)
  rate_n <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex,
                      data = voles, FUN = length)
  names(rate_n)[3] <- "n"
  merge(rate_mean, rate_n, by = c("treatment_arm", "sex"))
}

It gives one row for each treatment arm and sex, with the mean metabolic rate (in a column still called metabolic_rate_post) and n, the number of animals. It makes two summaries and then joins them, which is typical of older base R; group_by() and summarise() do it in one step.
The test sets one difference: it calls summarise_rate_tidy(load_voles()), so the new function is handed the data instead of reading the file itself. Everything else must come out the same.
Predict before you run it: one animal has no metabolic_rate_post. What does the original do with that animal, and what would a straight group_by() and summarise() do? Step 6 checks your answer.



3. Decide each request. Reads run without asking. For a write_file request, read the code it prints: it is the code that run_test() will run. Choose Yes only for a write to scripts/functions/summaries.R. Refuse the first run_test on purpose, to see a refusal from the model’s side. ellmer sends back “Tool call rejected. The user has chosen to disallow the tool call.”, and the model decides what to do next. It usually stops and explains. If it asks again at once, answer No again. Then let it continue:

chat$chat("Go ahead and run the test.")

4. Look inside. Do this before step 5, because restarting R clears chat:

chat               # every turn: your prompt, its tool requests, the results
chat$get_tokens()  # the tokens it sent and received, one row per request

Find your refusal, any test report that failed, and the write that followed it. Note how many requests the task took (count the assistant turns) and how many tokens.
5. Check its work yourself. When the agent says “the test passes”, that is a claimA statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.. Read the diff of scripts/functions/summaries.R in the Git pane. Then restart R (Session → Restart R) and run:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

test_translation.R is the test that matters here: it now passes rather than skips. The other files pass or skip, as before.
6. Check what happened to the missing value. Find, in the diff, how the translation handles the animal with no metabolic_rate_post, and whether the agent’s last reply mentioned it. Then compare with your prediction.


What should happen to the missing value, and why

What the original does. aggregate() with a formula drops every row with a missing value in the formula’s variables (its default is na.action = na.omit), and it says nothing. So the original’s mean and n for that animal’s group leave the animal out.
What we expect from the agent. A straight translation, group_by(treatment_arm, sex) and then summarise(metabolic_rate_post = mean(metabolic_rate_post), n = n()), keeps the animal: that group gets an NA mean and an n one too high. The test fails, and its report shows exactly those two differences. A passing translation must leave the animal out too, for example with filter(!is.na(metabolic_rate_post)) before summarising. So the agent may notice the missing value only because the test failed, not because it read the original closely.
Why it matters. The test checks “the same as the original”, not “correct”. Whether to leave out an animal with a missing measurement is a scientific decision. The original made it silently, and a passing translation copies it, silently unless the agent tells you. If it did not, a passing test has hidden a decision from you; say so in your log line in step 7. Block 8 returns to the difference between “unchanged” and “right”.

7. Record and commit. Your agent can write only under scripts/, so it cannot draft this line as Claude Code did in Block 3: that is its write rule at work. Add the line to docs/ai-log.md yourself, with today’s date, for example 2026-10-22; mini agent (ellmer, claude-sonnet-5-5); translated the rate summary to tidyverse; kept after reading the diff and running the tests, noting that it drops the animal with a missing rate, as the original does. Then commit summaries.R and the log.
You are done when test_translation.R passes in your own run, the Git pane showed only summaries.R and your log changed (not load_voles.R, which the test also relies on), you can say how many requests and tokens the task took and what happened to the animal with the missing value, and both files are committed.
If it goes wrong:


The agent loops or goes off course: answer No at its next request, or press Esc to interrupt it. ellmer keeps the conversation, so you can then steer it with chat$chat("…"), or source() the file again to start a new conversation.

A refused write: the agent can write only under scripts/; read the path it asked for.

run_test cannot find tests/test_translation.R: check that getwd() is the repository’s root.

An unwanted change: Revert it in the Git pane.







TipWhat did it cost?





chat$get_cost() turns the tokens into money when ellmer knows the model’s price. If it shows NA, run ellmer::models_update_prices() once to refresh ellmer’s price list. Or multiply the tokens from chat$get_tokens() by the prices on Anthropic’s pricing page. claude-opus-5-5, named in the comment at the top of mini_agent.R, is a larger model at a higher price per token; to use it, change the model line.

title: Block 8: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Wrap-up for the day


Wrap-up (10 minutes)


Goal: finish with evidence: the whole suite passing in a fresh R session and a complete AI-use log, so that anyone can check the repository you leave with.
1. Run the whole suite after restarting R, as in Step 1. Expect FAIL 0; tests for any block you skipped may skip.
2. Complete your log. Every block in which an agent worked needs its line in docs/ai-log.md; add any that is missing, and commit.
3. What you leave with. AGENTS.md and a skill, tested deny rules, your own agent, a codebook with its logs, a characterisation test, and the AI-use log.
4. Where next. Self-study: Inline completions, Self-study: AI-assisted code review and Self-study: Reporting from your repository all work in this repository or beside it.
You are done when the suite shows FAIL 0 and your last log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: a failure names its test. In test_ai_log.R, a log line lacks one of its four parts; in test_controls.R, a protection has gone or a command was approved in advance. Fix what it names, then run the suite again.

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
The context demonstration (10 minutes)


Goal: see how the code above the cursor changes Copilot’s suggestion for the same comment, so that you know what to put in a script to get useful suggestions.
Start state: your workshop repository open, signed in to GitHub Copilot.
The data are voles_metabolism.csv: a synthetic trial in 72 voles, with columns subject_id, sex, treatment_arm, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g and metabolic_rate_post. The data are synthetic, so no model has seen this dataset before.
0. Check that Copilot works. This command creates the scratch/ folder and this page’s practice script, and opens it:
In the R console:

usethis::edit_file("scratch/completions.R")

In scratch/completions.R, type # Calculate the mean of 1 to 100. Within a few seconds you should see ghost text such as mean(1:100). If not, press Enter and wait.
1. No context. Delete everything in scratch/completions.R. Type only this comment, then wait.
In scratch/completions.R:

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment

Note the suggestion. With no data and no column names in view, the model has to guess.
2. Context in the file. Empty scratch/completions.R again. Type the lines below down to glimpse(voles), then run them so that voles is loaded. Then type the same comment on a new line and wait.
In scratch/completions.R:

# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
# 72 voles, three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose), two sexes
# Native pipe |>, tidyverse

library(tidyverse)

voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
glimpse(voles)

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment



A typical good result


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(
    mean_change = mean(mass_change_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = treatment_arm
  )

The exact form varies between people and sessions.

Compare the two suggestions. Did the second use real column names? Did it compute post minus pre?
You are done when you can say what the second suggestion had that the first did not.
If it goes wrong: if no ghost text appears, check that you are signed in to GitHub and the set-up route for your IDE (in Set-up routes, plans and data, just after this task), then type the comment again on a new line; if scratch/completions.R stops running, Session → Restart R and run it from the top.








NoteSet-up routes, plans and data







RStudio: enable GitHub Copilot in RStudio’s options and sign in to GitHub.

Positron: choose GitHub Copilot as the completions provider (see Positron’s completions documentation).

Copilot Free allows a limited number of completions per month (2,000 at the time of writing); paid plans do not meter them. Completions send the code around your cursor to the provider, so the disclosure points in Block 3 apply here too.









TipUsing another tool





Use one completion provider at a time, so you know which tool made each suggestion.
Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions (RStudio and Positron): in RStudio, turn it on from the Posit Assistant toolbar button; it needs a Posit AI account. In Positron, choose it as the completions provider. Posit AI does not meter completions. Unlike Copilot, it also sees your live R session: the columns of loaded data frames, the functions you have defined and the packages you have loaded. So, in the context demonstration:

restart R (Session → Restart R) before step 1, so that “no context” means none;
after step 2, keep voles loaded. Empty scratch/completions.R, then type only the comment from step 1. If the suggestion now uses the real column names, they came from your session, not from the file.

VS Code: select Use AI Features from the Copilot icon in the Status Bar and sign in with GitHub. As in Positron, Copilot may also use other open tabs.
