text:
Going further
This material goes beyond the two activities. Work through it if it is useful to you.






TipThe full four-step analysis





The second activity leaves out two steps of the full analysis below: the filter (step 1) and the model (step 3). Here is the full sequence. As before, write the comment for each step before you accept, reject or modify the suggestion:

Filter to subjects with non-missing metabolic_rate_post and create a derived variable mass_change_g.
Produce a summary table of the mean and standard deviation of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with the number of observations per cell.
Fit a linear model of metabolic_rate_post on treatment_arm and sex. Inspect the coefficients.
Produce one plot relating mass_change_g to metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm.

When you have finished steps 2 and 4, compare the code you kept for step 4 with the plot in An example in the second activity. Note whether you accepted, changed or rejected Copilot’s suggestion. Where the two differ, decide which is right and why: suggestions differ between people and between attempts, and so, often, do their bugs. If a colleague has worked through the same steps, compare your code with theirs too.

title: Block 9: AI-assisted code review
text:
Task 2: grade the machine


Grade the machine (12 minutes)


Goal: measure the reviewer against the twelve problems you found on Day 2, so that you learn which of its findings you can trust before you rely on one.
1. Score the review. Open the answer key beside the review in your terminal. The key is the P1–P12 table under The problems revealed in the manual code-review chapter (click Solution). Then mark:


Hits: which of P1–P12 did it identify correctly?

Misses: which did it miss? Look especially at P4 (precedence) and P8 (the 9999 code): they are silent, and their consequences are serious.

False positives: what did it flag that is not a real problem, or describe wrongly? Each one is a false positiveIn a code review, a problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or describes wrongly..

Execution claims: did it claim the script runs or reproduces? On what evidence?

2. Post in the chat: your group (with or without), your hit count, whether it caught P8, and its most confident false positive.
3. Record it. In your workshop repository, add a line to docs/ai-log.md (date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed). In the last part, give the reviewer’s hit count and its most confident false positive. Commit the file.
You are done when every P1–P12 problem is marked hit or miss, you have posted your result, and your AI-log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if your review never arrived, run it through the chat route in Using another tool. The grading works the same way.








TipBackground: what AI is, and is not, good for in code review





An AI reviewer reads every line and never tires, but it sounds equally sure whether it is right or wrong. Here is where to expect help, on the four Rs of code review (Ivimey-Cook et al., 2023):



AI capability mapped onto the four Rs

R
AI is likely to be...
Why



Reported
Useful for drafting
It can summarise what the script appears to do and flag missing documentation or undocumented exclusions. It cannot know the intended analysis unless you state it.


Run
Strong, if it can execute
An agent that runs the script in a fresh R session can show whether it runs. A chat window can only predict, and its prediction can read as though it ran the code.


Reliable
Weak
Silent semantic errors (P4 precedence, P8 sentinel, P9 incomparable models, P10 wrong family) depend on context. Expect some caught, some missed and some invented, all in the same confident tone.


Reproducible
Mixed
It can flag a missing lockfile or session record. It can confirm that results reproduce only by running the code and comparing outputs.





The rule: treat every AI finding as a claim to check, and the absence of a finding as no evidence that the problem is absent.
In software engineering, developers resolved about three-quarters of an AI reviewer’s comments, but mostly reported only minor gains in quality (Cihan et al., 2025). In a separate experiment, the models did worse when they were not told what the code was meant to do (Cihan, 2025). We know of no study that has measured this on analysis scripts like this one. That is what you have just done.









TipInstructor: debrief (5 minutes)







P8 by group. Compare the with and without results in the chat. Only the data and your knowledge reveal that 9999 is a code: what does that say about reviewing code without the data?

The most confident false positive. What would acting on it have cost?

Execution claims. Did any reviewer claim the script runs without having run it?

Trust. If an AI reviewer told you your analysis was clean, would you submit? Only for Run, not for Reliable?










TipAfter the day: keep your own review prompt





The prompt above is a starting point for your own scripts. Adapt it (your standard, your intended analysis, the codes your data use). Then keep it in your workshop repository. Run usethis::edit_file("docs/review-prompt.md") in the R console, paste the prompt, save, and commit the file. Run the prompt on a script before you share it, and spend your own attention on the Reliable questions.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: use AI as a code reviewer with a prompt that makes its output checkable, trusted because you graded it against the problems you found yourself on Day 2, and treat every finding as a claim.

Check: grade every AI finding against the P1–P12 answer key; the absence of a finding is no evidence that the problem is absent.

Reproduce: a claim that the script runs counts only with the command and the output from a fresh R session. To run one yourself, see checking work.

Record: a line in docs/ai-log.md, committed in your workshop repository: the tool, its hit count and its most confident false positive. An AI-assisted README for ~/ai-review is in Going further.

title: Block 9: AI-assisted code review
text:
Going further
This material goes beyond the review itself. Work through it if it is useful to you.






TipCopilot code review on a pull request





Copilot can also review a pull request and comment on the changed lines. The self-study page Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent shows how, and how to give it this block’s review standard.









TipGenerating the README with AI





Self-study: about 20 minutes.
A README is the documentation that lets you answer the Reported and Run questions. This block provides the research-readme skillA reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.: a SKILL.md, two helper scripts and a template.
Add the data first. A README describes the data as well as the code, so ~/ai-review now needs them. Run this in the R console of the ai-review window:

download.file("https://osf.io/download/xke5g/",
              here::here("celegans_repro_raw.csv"), mode = "wb")
download.file("https://osf.io/download/6ev3g/",
              here::here("celegans_repro_final.csv"), mode = "wb")

Install the skill before you start. Download the bundle with the button below. Then unzip it into ~/ai-review at .agents/skills/. In the R console of the ai-review window, run unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills")) and choose the downloaded file. The folder .agents/skills/research-readme/ should then contain SKILL.md, scripts/ and references/.


 Download research-readme.zip




Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot read .agents/skills/ directly.

Claude Code reads .claude/skills/. Link or copy the folder there, as described in Block 4.

Chat window: you do not need to install anything. You run the two scripts yourself and paste the template into the chat.

Check that the skill is visible before going on. In Claude Code, type /skills and look for research-readme. The .claude/skills/ folder did not exist when this session started, so type /reload-skills first (Block 4). In any tool, the real test is what it does. When you invoke /research-readme in Pass 2, its first reply should be the numbered plan that the skill’s “Before executing” section requires. If it is not, the skill did not load.
Put the folder under version control first. ~/ai-review is not a git repository, so there would be nothing to compare the README against. Open ~/ai-review in RStudio or Positron. Run usethis::use_git() in the R console and let it make the first commit.
You run this in two passes. The first shows the failure; the second shows the fix.
Pass 1: README from the AI alone (self-study: about 4 minutes)
Give the AI only ANALYSIS.R and the data, and ask for a README with no constraints:
Prompt (Claude Code):
Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository from ANALYSIS.R and
the two CSV files. Show it in your reply; do not write any file.
In a chat window, paste ANALYSIS.R and the data after the same request.
The result looks complete. It will give plausible units, describe variables it cannot have checked, and may state package versions it has no way to know. Note what it claims about the variables and dependencies. Pass 2 replaces each guess with a fact you generate.
Pass 2: README from verifiable inputs
The skill’s rules are that the AI must not fabricate metadata, and that automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. So you generate the facts with R, and the AI only assembles and words them.
Step 1: Generate the inputs yourself (R, not AI)
In the R console of the ai-review window (so that here::here() points at ~/ai-review, not at your workshop repository):

skill_dir <- here::here(".agents", "skills", "research-readme", "scripts")

source(file.path(skill_dir, "describe_csv.R"))
# type, missing count and range per column, printed in full for pasting
describe_project_csvs(here::here()) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

source(file.path(skill_dir, "scan_packages.R"))
print_lockfile(here::here("renv.lock"))  # R and package versions, or a finding

This project has no renv.lock. scan_packages.R reports that as an explicit finding rather than an error, and the README must say so. You cannot pin versions you never recorded.
Look at the TO (total offspring) column in the summary: its range reads -46 to 9999. Neither end is a plausible number of offspring. The 9999 code (P8) is a real number in the file, and the summary reports it without judgement. Judging plausibility is your job. That honest, uninterpreted range is where the sentinel value shows.
Step 2: Hand the AI the specification and the inputs
Agent path: in Manual mode, as in Run the review, invoke /research-readme and let its six stages run. The skill shows its plan as a message and waits. Read it, then reply in Claude Code: Yes, go ahead, or say what to change. It asks you for anything it cannot find.
Chat path: paste the structure from references/readme_template.md and the output you just generated, with this prompt:
Prompt (chat window):
Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository, using exactly the
sections in the template I paste below, in order.

Use ONLY the facts I provide. Do not invent DOIs, ORCIDs, units or package
versions. Where a value is missing, insert a visible placeholder:
  **TODO: supply [field]: not provided**

Per-column summaries: [paste describe_project_csvs() output]
Dependencies: [paste print_lockfile() output]
Run order: ANALYSIS.R (the only analysis script in the folder).

Add an AI declaration stating that an AI assisted in drafting this README,
naming the model and today's date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere.


Audit the README (10 minutes)


Goal: check the Pass 2 README against three of the skill’s rules, so that you know which of its statements you could put your name to.
Audit the draft against three of the skill’s rules:


No fabrication. Pick three facts. Can you trace each to an input you gave? If not, it is invented.

Describe, do not interpret. Did the AI assign units or meanings you did not supply? Did the -46 to 9999 range survive, or was it “tidied” into something plausible and wrong?

README only. The Git pane should show that nothing except README.md changed since the commit you made before Pass 1.

Note the worst fabrication or interpretation you caught. Note also whether the README’s offspring range alone would have led you back to P8. The AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. should say no more than you told it.
You are done when each of the three rules is marked kept or broken, you have noted the worst fabrication or interpretation, and the Git pane shows only README.md changed.


The skill bundle
The bundle you downloaded above is shown here for reference. You do not need to edit it. Read it before you use it, as you would any skill you did not write.
research-readme/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   ├── describe_csv.R
│   └── scan_packages.R
└── references/
    └── readme_template.md






Notescripts/describe_csv.R






# describe_csv.R ----
# Purpose: one row per column of a CSV file: name, the type readr assigns,
# missing-value count, and a brief range (numeric) or distinct-value count
# (other). Describes; does not interpret.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 2.

describe_range <- function(x) {
  if (all(is.na(x))) {
    return("all values missing")
  }
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    return(paste(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), "to", max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
  }
  paste(dplyr::n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE), "distinct values")
}

# one-row-per-column summary of a single CSV ----
describe_csv <- function(path) {
  stopifnot(is.character(path), length(path) == 1L, file.exists(path))
  data_df <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(
    file        = basename(path),
    column      = names(data_df),
    type        = purrr::map_chr(data_df, \(x) class(x)[1]),
    n_missing   = purrr::map_int(data_df, \(x) sum(is.na(x))),
    range       = purrr::map_chr(data_df, describe_range),
    # completed by the user during Stage 2:
    description = NA_character_,
    unit        = NA_character_
  )
}

# describe every CSV in a project, skipping renv and git folders ----
describe_project_csvs <- function(project_dir) {
  stopifnot(dir.exists(project_dir))
  csv_paths <- list.files(
    project_dir,
    pattern = "\\.csv$",
    recursive = TRUE,
    full.names = TRUE,
    ignore.case = TRUE
  )
  csv_paths <- csv_paths[!grepl("(^|/)(renv|\\.git)/", csv_paths)]
  if (length(csv_paths) == 0L) {
    message("No CSV files found under ", project_dir)
    return(tibble::tibble())
  }
  csv_paths |>
    purrr::map(describe_csv) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
}










Notescripts/scan_packages.R






# scan_packages.R ----
# Purpose: read renv.lock and report the R version and pinned package
# versions. A missing lockfile is reported as a finding, not an error.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 4.

read_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  if (!file.exists(lock_path)) {
    return(list(found = FALSE, r_version = NA_character_, packages = tibble::tibble()))
  }
  lock <- jsonlite::read_json(lock_path)
  packages <- purrr::pluck(lock, "Packages", .default = list())

  packages_df <- tibble::tibble(
    package = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Package", .default = NA_character_))),
    version = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Version", .default = NA_character_)))
  ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(package)

  list(
    found = TRUE,
    r_version = purrr::pluck(lock, "R", "Version", .default = NA_character_),
    packages = packages_df
  )
}

print_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  info <- read_lockfile(lock_path)
  if (!info$found) {
    cat(
      "No lockfile found at ", lock_path, ".\n",
      "FINDING: package versions were not recorded.\n",
      "README text: **TODO: supply R version and key package versions: ",
      "not recorded; resolve before submission**\n",
      sep = ""
    )
    return(invisible(info))
  }
  cat("R version: ", info$r_version, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(info$packages, n = Inf)
  invisible(info)
}










NoteSKILL.md







---
name: research-readme
description: >-
  Writes a README.md for a research repository whose code and data accompany
  a paper. Use when asked to write a README for an analysis project, document
  a repository for a paper, or prepare code for journal submission or
  archiving (Zenodo, Figshare, OSF). Not for general software READMEs and not
  for auditing code.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Research README generator

Produces one README.md for a repository of R code and data that accompanies a
manuscript, including the metadata that journals and archives expect:
persistent identifiers, ORCIDs, funding, per-variable descriptions with units,
an explicit script run order, and a dependency record.

## Operating constraints
These hold for the whole conversation unless the user explicitly withdraws
them.
1. The only file you create or overwrite is README.md. Do not edit, rename or
   delete any other file. If you notice an apparent error in code or data,
   record it under "Open questions" in the README or report it in chat, and
   leave the file untouched.
2. Do not fabricate metadata. DOIs, ORCIDs, grant numbers, collection dates,
   units and affiliations come from the user or from a file the user points to.
   If a value is unknown, insert a placeholder (see Placeholders).
3. Automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. Report column type,
   missing count and range. Do not state what a variable means, its unit, or
   whether a value is plausible.
4. Work conversationally and write the file directly; do not build an app.

## Before executing
Present a short numbered plan: the folder to be scanned, that only README.md
will be written, and the six stages below. Wait for the user to confirm.

## Stage 1: Project information
Collect title, abstract, DOIs (paper; archived code and data), licences,
authors with ORCIDs and affiliations, and funders with grant numbers. Read
these from CITATION.cff, codemeta.json or DESCRIPTION if present, and ask only
for what is missing. Pair each author with their own ORCID and affiliation. If
no code licence is supplied, flag it prominently and use a placeholder; do not
choose a licence for the user.

## Stage 2: Files and variable summaries
List the data and code files. For CSV files, run
describe_project_csvs() from scripts/describe_csv.R and use its output as a
scaffold. Ask the user for each column's description and unit, and for
collection dates and locations per data file. List other tabular formats
(.xlsx, .tsv) and ask the user to describe their columns by hand. Never infer
units from column names.

## Stage 3: Script order
List executable files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd). Propose a run order using numeric
prefixes (01_, 02_) as the first signal, and ask the user to confirm or
reorder; the user's order is authoritative. Collect a one-line description of
each script. Do not run any script to determine the order.

## Stage 4: R packages and versions
Run print_lockfile() from scripts/scan_packages.R.
- If a lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states the R version, says
  that versions are pinned in renv.lock, gives the restore command
  renv::restore(), and includes the package table.
- If no lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states that package versions
  were not recorded, and contains the placeholder from print_lockfile(). Do not
  guess versions or scan the installed library.

## Stage 5: Assemble, preview and reader-test
Fill references/readme_template.md. Show the rendered Markdown in chat. Then
read it as a newcomer who has only the repository and the paper: could they
find the data, restore the environment, run the scripts in order and
understand every variable? List any section still holding a placeholder. On
confirmation, write README.md to the project root.

## Stage 6: Check the README against its sources
Compare the README with its sources: the R and package
versions against read_lockfile(), every numbered script against the scripts
folder, and every unit against the user's answers. Report the number of
placeholders left.

## AI declaration
State that an AI assisted in generating this README, naming the model if the
user wishes, with the date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere in the
project unless the user states them, and then record exactly what they state.

## Placeholders
Write every unknown value as a visible placeholder, in exactly this form:
**TODO: supply [field]: not provided**
Flag a missing code licence and a missing code or data DOI as blocking for
submission, but still write the file so the user has a working draft.

## Scope
This skill does not audit code quality or reproducibility, and does not
produce figures. If asked to do either mid-run, say so and stop that part of
the request.

## References
- Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2023) Implementing code review in the scientific
  workflow. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36(10), 1347–1356.
- Ivimey-Cook, E.R. et al. (2025) TADA! Simple guidelines to improve
  analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility. EcoEvoRxiv.











Notereferences/readme_template.md





The Dependencies section is a single token. It is filled with one of the two versions defined in Stage 4 of SKILL.md, so the README is accurate whether or not a lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment. exists.

title: Self-study: Reporting from your repository
text:
Scan a report


Goal: find the results in a report that were typed rather than computed, so that each can become inline code that updates when the data change.
Start state: the template’s reports/example_report.qmd, an interim summary of the voles trial with some numbers typed in.
1. Scan it. In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "typed_numbers.R"))
find_typed_numbers(here::here("reports", "example_report.qmd")) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

2. Sort the hits. The scan flags five lines. Decide for each one whether it is a typed result that should be inline code, or a number that is fine as text.


Which are which

Lines 37 and 38 are typed results (the 1.53 g difference with its interval, and the mean of 29.4 g): both should be inline code. The other three can stay: the date in the YAML header (line 3), the design size of 12 per arm-by-sex combination (line 28), and “95%” in “95% CI” (line 34).

You are done when you can say which two lines are typed results and why the other three can stay.
If it goes wrong: if find_typed_numbers() is not found, check that the source() line ran without an error.









NoteHow it works: inline code, and what the scan checks





A typed number can be mistyped, or go stale when the data change, and an assistant drafting text may restate numbers it saw earlier. So every number in the prose comes from inline code: a code chunk computes the result, and the text calls it with `r round(primary$estimate, 2)`. reports/example_report.qmd, the report you scanned, does this in the first paragraph of its Results.
Your AGENTS.md asks for this; the shipped find_typed_numbers() checks it, by listing prose lines that still contain numbers outside inline code.









Notescripts/functions/typed_numbers.R






# scripts/functions/typed_numbers.R ----
# List the prose lines of a .qmd file that still contain numbers outside
# inline code, for you to review by eye. Years, design sizes and YAML values
# are flagged too, so treat each hit as a question, not an error.
find_typed_numbers <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  is_fence <- grepl("^```", lines)
  in_chunk <- cumsum(is_fence) %% 2 == 1

  tibble::tibble(line = seq_along(lines), text = lines) |>
    dplyr::filter(!in_chunk, !is_fence) |>
    dplyr::mutate(prose = gsub("`\\{?r\\}? [^`]*`", "", text)) |>
    dplyr::filter(grepl("[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+|\\b[0-9]{2,}\\b", prose, perl = TRUE)) |>
    dplyr::select(line, text)
}

title: Self-study: Reporting from your repository
section: Part B: A README from the record
text:
Part B: A README from the record
Your repository now holds most of what a reader needs: a codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI., cleaning logs, numbered scripts, a lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., tests and an AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.. A README pulls them together. The rule: the AI may only phrase facts you can trace to a file; anything else becomes a visible placeholder for you to fill.


Draft from the record, then test it


Goal: a README drafted only from your repository’s files and checked against them by a test, so that a reader can trace every statement in it to a source.
Start state: your workshop repository on main (or checkpoint-cleaning), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab.
1. Draft.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Draft README.md from these files only, naming the source of each section:
- Data dictionary, as a Markdown table whose first column is the column
  name: docs/codebook.csv
- Scripts and run order: the numbered scripts in scripts/
- Dependencies: the R version in renv.lock, and renv::restore()
- How to verify, from a terminal: Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')",
  and what the tests in tests/ check
- AI declaration: docs/ai-log.md, claiming nothing beyond it
Anything these files do not give (authors, licence, DOI, a unit the codebook
leaves blank or as <unit>) becomes a placeholder in exactly this form:
**TODO: supply [field]: not provided**
Edit README.md only.
Approve the edit when asked, after reading it. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on.
2. Let the tests audit it. Restart R (Session → Restart R), then in the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

The shipped tests/test_readme.R checks the README against the files it was drafted from, and reports how many placeholders are left; How it works, after this task, lists what it checks.
3. Check the scope, log it and commit. The Git pane should show only README.md as changed. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md, for example:
2026-10-20; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); drafted README.md from the repository's files; kept the draft after test_readme.R passed, placeholders still to fill
Then commit README.md and the log from the Git pane.
You are done when test_readme.R passes, the agent changed only README.md, and the README and your log line are committed.
If it goes wrong: if the agent changed any file other than README.md, select it in the Git pane and choose Revert. If the README test fails, ask Claude Code to fix only the statements the test names, and run the suite again.


Ask yourself: what did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?






NoteHow it works: the README’s sources, and what the test checks








docs/codebook.csv


numbered scripts in scripts/


tests in tests/


renv.lock


docs/ai-log.md



the only sources


Drafts README.md, with placeholders for anything missing





You trace every statement to a file


The shipped tests/test_readme.R checks the R version in renv.lock and the renv::restore() command, every numbered script, no leftover {{ tokens, and no invented unit in the data-dictionary table row for a column the codebook leaves without a unit: that row must hold a TODO instead. It also reports how many placeholders are left.









TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant can do Part B with the same prompt. Use it in Normal mode, so it asks before each change. The checks do not change: the test suite in a fresh R session, and the Git pane.









TipStretch: audit the README by hand





The test checks the R version, the scripts, leftover tokens and blank units. Trace the statements it cannot check yourself: confirm that the AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. says no more than your log, and that each section names a source you gave it.
Before you share it, the placeholders are your to-do list. Work through licence, ORCIDs, DOI and archiving with the SORTEE checklist from Day 2, then commit.
A fuller version, with a README skill, is in Going further in Block 9.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: find the results in a report that were typed rather than computed, and have an agent draft a README, trusted because a scan lists every number outside inline code, a shipped test checks the README against its sources, and the whole suite passes in a fresh R session.

Check: a scan for typed numbers; every README statement traced to a file.

Reproduce: numbers come from code, so the report updates when the data do; the README’s dependencies come from renv.lock, not from memory.

Record: the README and the AI-use log complete the record. Together with the codebook, logs, tests and lockfile, they are what a reviewer, a co-author or you in a year’s time will need. Check your institution’s and target journal’s policy on declaring AI use.

title: Self-study: Reporting from your repository
text:
Going further
This material is optional. Work through it if it is useful to you.






TipRobustness, not choice





AI should not choose your primary analysis. The BLADE benchmark compared language-model agents with expert analysts on open-ended research questions. It found that the models were often limited to basic analyses, and that agents able to explore the data made more varied but still sub-optimal analytical decisions (Gu et al., 2024). Its useful role is narrower: listing defensible alternatives to an analysis you have already fixed, so you can check whether your conclusion depends on the choice.
Run the steps yourself, and judge each answer before running it.


Enumerate, judge, run


Goal: run defensible alternatives beside your fixed primary analysis, so that you know whether your conclusion depends on the analysis choice, without letting the AI make that choice.
1. Ask for alternatives, not a recommendation:
My pre-registered primary analysis is an ANCOVA:
mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, estimating the High_dose
versus Control difference. List alternative specifications a reasonable
analyst might use for the same question, and for each, say whether it
estimates the same quantity. Do not recommend one.
2. Judge each one yourself. Mark each alternative defensible or not, with a reason. Check especially whether it estimates the same quantity.
3. Run the defensible ones and report them beside the primary analysis.

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))

voles_df <- load_voles() |>
  mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")))

specs_df <- tribble(
  ~spec,                       ~formula,
  "Primary: ANCOVA",           "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex",
  "Change score",              "I(mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) ~ treatment_arm + sex",
  "ANCOVA with arm-by-sex",    "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm * sex"
)

spec_results_df <- specs_df |>
  mutate(result = map(formula, \(f) {
    fit <- lm(as.formula(f), data = voles_df)
    ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
    tibble(
      estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
      lower = unname(ci[1]),
      upper = unname(ci[2])
    )
  })) |>
  unnest(result)

spec_results_df



A trap in the table

In the third specification, the coefficient treatment_armHigh_dose is the High_dose effect in females only (the reference level of sex), because the model includes an interaction. It sits in the same column as the other estimates but answers a different question. It belongs in a separate analysis of whether the effect differs by sex, not in a table of estimates of the same quantity. An AI that lists it as an “alternative” without saying so has made exactly the error step 2 asks you to catch.

4. Log it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md in the same form as in Part B: the tool and model, the alternatives it listed, and which you kept as defensible.
You are done when every alternative is marked defensible or not, with a reason, and the table beside your primary estimate holds only specifications that estimate the same quantity.








Warning



Running many specifications and reporting the one you like best is selective reporting. The primary analysis is fixed in advance; the others are reported as sensitivity analyses whatever they show.


Check your understanding: robustness
Why should the arm-by-sex interaction model not appear in the same robustness table as the primary ANCOVA?

Interaction models cannot be fitted with lm()Its High_dose coefficient estimates the effect in the reference sex only, a different quantity from the primary estimandIt always gives a larger estimateRobustness tables may contain only two models











TipSimulation and parameter recovery





If you simulate data from a mechanism whose parameters you chose, a correct analysis should recover those parameters on average, and its 95% confidence intervals should contain the true values about 95% of the time. This tests the analysis code against a known answer, which real data never provide.
Morris, White and Crowther (2019) give a structure for planning simulation studies: the aims, the data-generating mechanism, the estimand, the methods and the performance measures (ADEMP). Here:


Aim: check that the analysis code estimates the high-dose effect correctly.

Data-generating mechanism: 12 voles per arm-by-sex cell. Pre-treatment mass is normal with mean 28 g and SD 2 g. Post-treatment mass equals 2.8 g plus 0.9 times pre-treatment mass, plus 0.8 g for Low_dose, plus 1.5 g for High_dose, plus 1.0 g for males, plus normal error with SD 0.8 g.

Estimand: the difference in post-treatment mass between High_dose and Control, adjusted for pre-treatment mass and sex. True value: 1.5 g.

Method: linear model (ANCOVA), mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex.

Performance measures: bias and confidence-interval coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error.

The written mechanism is yours. It is the equivalent of the codebook in Block 7: the AI turns it into code, and you check the code against it.


Write, check, recover


Goal: run your analysis code on data simulated from a mechanism you wrote, so that you test it against a known answer, which real data never give.
1. Simulation code. Give the AI the data-generating mechanism above, word for word, and ask for a function simulate_voles() returning a tibble with columns treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g and mass_post_g.
2. Check the simulated data against the specification. Before using the function, run it once and check that it matches what you wrote:

set.seed(1)
sim_df <- simulate_voles()
sim_df |> count(treatment_arm, sex)            # 12 per cell?
sim_df |> summarise(mean(mass_pre_g), sd(mass_pre_g))
sim_df |>
  summarise(mean_post = mean(mass_post_g), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex))

High_dose should be about 1.5 g above Control within each sex, and males about 1 g above females. If not, the simulation is wrong, and nothing built on it can be trusted.
3. Analysis code, in a separate session. Without showing it the simulation code, ask the AI for a function estimate_high_vs_control(data) that fits the model above and returns the High_dose estimate and its 95% confidence interval.
4. Run the recovery.


Reference code


simulate_voles <- function(n_per_cell = 12, effect_low = 0.8,
                           effect_high = 1.5, sex_effect = 1.0,
                           slope_pre = 0.9, sd_pre = 2, sd_resid = 0.8) {
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    treatment_arm = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"),
    sex = c("F", "M"),
    animal = seq_len(n_per_cell)
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      mass_pre_g = stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), mean = 28, sd = sd_pre),
      arm_effect = dplyr::case_when(
        treatment_arm == "Low_dose" ~ effect_low,
        treatment_arm == "High_dose" ~ effect_high,
        .default = 0
      ),
      mass_post_g = 28 * (1 - slope_pre) + slope_pre * mass_pre_g +
        arm_effect + sex_effect * (sex == "M") +
        stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), sd = sd_resid)
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g)
}

estimate_high_vs_control <- function(data) {
  data <- dplyr::mutate(
    data,
    treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"))
  )
  fit <- stats::lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = data)
  ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
    lower = unname(ci[1]),
    upper = unname(ci[2])
  )
}



set.seed(2026)
n_sim <- 1000
true_effect <- 1.5

results_df <- seq_len(n_sim) |>
  map(\(i) estimate_high_vs_control(simulate_voles(effect_high = true_effect))) |>
  list_rbind()

results_df |>
  summarise(
    bias          = mean(estimate) - true_effect,
    bias_mcse     = sd(estimate) / sqrt(n_sim),
    coverage      = mean(lower <= true_effect & upper >= true_effect),
    coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim),
    empirical_se  = sd(estimate)
  )

Bias should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero. Coverage should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.95, roughly 0.936 to 0.964 with 1,000 runs.
5. Prove the check can fail. Replace the analysis with a version that models the change the wrong way round, as in Block 2:

estimate_buggy <- function(data) {
  data <- dplyr::mutate(
    data,
    treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")),
    mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g
  )
  fit <- stats::lm(mass_change_g ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = data)
  ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
    lower = unname(ci[1]),
    upper = unname(ci[2])
  )
}

Rerun the recovery with estimate_buggy(). Bias should be about −3 g and coverage near zero. A check you have never seen fail is a check you are assuming works.
6. Log it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md in the same form as in Part B: the tool and model, the two functions it wrote, and what the recovery check showed.
You are done when estimate_high_vs_control() gives bias and coverage within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of their targets, and estimate_buggy() fails the same check.








Warning



What recovery does not prove. It shows that the code estimates the right quantity under the mechanism you simulated. It says nothing about whether real voles behave like that. A change-score model fitted to these simulated data would also be nearly unbiased (randomisation makes both estimators valid), but less precise; compare empirical_se to see the cost. Recovery tests code, not scientific assumptions.


Check your understanding: simulation
A simulation recovers the true effect with negligible bias and 95% coverage. What has it shown?

That the real data follow the simulated mechanismThat the analysis code estimates the intended quantity correctly when the data follow the simulated mechanismThat the study has adequate powerThat the model's assumptions hold for the real data











TipTranslating from SPSS, Stata or SAS





Translation with an equivalence check was the task your own agent did in Block 6: tests/test_translation.R compared its tidyverse translation with the original base R code, run side by side in R. Block 8 explains why “the same as the original” is not the same as “correct”.
From other software, export the original’s results to a file and compare the translation against those. Expect differences in defaults (missing values, quantiles, rounding); each needs a decision, not a looser tolerance.

title: Block 9: AI-assisted code review
text:
Wrap-up for the day


Wrap-up (10 minutes)


Goal: finish with evidence: the whole suite passing in a fresh R session and a complete AI-use log, so that anyone can check the repository you leave with.
1. Run the whole suite in your workshop repository: restart R (Session → Restart R), then run testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests")). Expect FAIL 0; tests for any block you skipped may skip.
2. Complete your log. Every block in which an agent worked needs its line in docs/ai-log.md. Add any line that is missing, then commit.
3. What you leave with. AGENTS.md and a skill, tested deny rules, your own agent, a codebook with its logs, a characterisation test, a graded AI review, and the AI-use log. For your own projects, Set up guardrails in your own project in Block 5 lists the steps in order.
4. Where next. Self-study: Inline completions and Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent both work in your workshop repository.
You are done when the suite shows FAIL 0 and your last log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: a failure names its test. A failure in test_ai_log.R means a log line lacks one of its four parts, its date is not YYYY-MM-DD, or a semicolon is not followed by a space. A failure in test_controls.R means a protection has gone or a command was approved in advance. Fix what it names, then run the suite again.

title: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent
text:
Task 1: put the review gate in place
All day you worked with an agent on your own machine, which you could watch and interrupt. Here you hand a task to an agent that works on GitHub’s servers while you do something else. It returns a pull request. You check it the way the day taught you: a reference you captured, a test it did not write, and your own review.
Self-study: about 45 minutes, after the workshop day. Start state: your workshop repository, committed, pushed to your fork on GitHub, with scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R from Block 3 on main. If you did not finish it, copy it from checkpoint-skills in the Terminal (git checkout checkpoint-skills -- scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R). Then commit and push: the cloud agent works from main on GitHub. You need a Copilot plan that includes the cloud agent (see below).
crumbs: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent

title: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent
text:
The review gate (10 minutes)


Goal: make every change to your tests, references and settings wait for your review and a passing check, so that an agent you cannot watch still cannot merge anything you have not seen.
1. Name yourself code owner of the protected paths. Create .github/CODEOWNERS on your default branch with these lines, using your own username:
/data/raw/            @your-github-username
/tests/               @your-github-username
/.github/             @your-github-username
/agent/               @your-github-username
/.claude/             @your-github-username
2. Add an independent check. Create .github/workflows/r-checks.yml. It runs the whole test suite from a clean checkout on every pull request:
name: r-checks
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  r-checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: renv   # the R version recorded in renv.lock
          use-public-rspm: true
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
      - name: Run tests
        run: Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests", stop_on_failure = TRUE)'
3. Push, then protect main. Commit and push steps 1–2. A fork starts with its workflows turned off. Open the Actions tab and enable them. Wait for the r-checks run to finish: GitHub offers a status check only after it has run. Then open your fork’s Settings → Branches and add a branch protection rule for main. Set it to require a pull request before merging, and to require the r-checks status check to pass. Leave Do not allow bypassing the above settings unticked: as the owner, you push the set-up commits in Tasks 2 and 3 straight to main.
You are done when the r-checks run on main is green in the Actions tab, and the branch rule lists both requirements.








NoteHow it works: what each piece protects







CODEOWNERS asks you to review any pull request that changes a path you own. It works in public repositories on free plans; for private repositories it needs a paid plan.

r-checks runs on GitHub, independent of your machine and of the agent’s environment. It is not tamper-proof: a pull request could change the workflow or the reference it checks against. CODEOWNERS and branch protection make a green run meaningful. Every change to those paths is flagged for your review, and reaches main only when you merge it.

Approving the agent’s pull request. GitHub does not count an approval from the person who asked Copilot for the pull request. Where approvals are required, someone else must approve. In your own fork there is no one else, so this rule does not require approvals. Instead, CODEOWNERS requests your review, r-checks must pass, and nothing reaches main until you merge it. In a shared repository, also require a code owner’s approval, so that a colleague reviews what the agent wrote for you.
crumbs: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent

title: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent
section: Task 2: give the agent its environment
text:
Task 2: give the agent its environment


The agent’s environment (5 minutes)


Goal: have the cloud agent run R with your locked package versions, so that its test runs mean the same as yours and as r-checks.
1. Add the setup workflow. Create .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml on your default branch, following GitHub’s documented pattern:
name: "Copilot Setup Steps"

# Runs when this file changes, so you can see whether setup succeeds,
# and can be run by hand from the Actions tab.
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

jobs:
  # The job must be called copilot-setup-steps or Copilot will not use it.
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up R
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: renv   # the R version recorded in renv.lock
          use-public-rspm: true
      - name: Restore packages from renv.lock
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
2. Run it once. Commit and push it, then run it by hand from the Actions tab (Copilot Setup Steps → Run workflow).
You are done when the Copilot Setup Steps run is green.








NoteHow it works: four requirements, four failure modes





Checked against GitHub’s documentation on the agent’s environment on 23 October 2026.


The job must be called exactly copilot-setup-steps, or Copilot ignores the file and works without your packages. That failure is usually loud: the tests error on the first missing function.

The file must be on the default branch, or it is not used.

The runner must be Ubuntu x64 Linux or Windows 64-bit. The cloud agent does not support macOS runners. Ubuntu is the usual choice for R. A timeout-minutes setting may be at most 59.

The lockfile must be restored. If the wrong versions are installed, the failure is quiet. Tests pass against different package behaviour, and your reference confirms sameness against the wrong baseline.

When the agent’s test run and r-checks disagree, suspect the environment before the code.

title: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent
text:
Task 3: capture the reference yourself


Capture the reference (5 minutes)


Goal: freeze what the plot looks like now, from the original code, so that the agent’s refactor can be checked against something it did not produce.
1. Write the capture script. In the R console, run usethis::edit_file("tests/make_plot_reference.R"). Then copy this into the file and save it:

# tests/make_plot_reference.R ----
# Run ONCE, by you, BEFORE any refactoring.
source(here::here("scripts", "explore_mass_change_plot.R"))
dir.create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"), showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(
  ggplot2::layer_data(ggplot2::last_plot()),
  here::here("tests", "fixtures", "mass_change_plot.rds")
)

layer_data() is the data ggplot2 draws for the plot’s first layer: every position, group and colour it plots. It is what “the plot is unchanged” means in a test.
2. Run it in a fresh session, then commit and push. Restart R (Session → Restart R). Run source(here::here("tests", "make_plot_reference.R")). Commit the script and tests/fixtures/mass_change_plot.rds with the message “Capture plot reference before refactoring”. Then push.
You are done when the reference is on main on GitHub.
If it goes wrong: if the plot jitters its points, layer_data() changes every time the plot is drawn, and set.seed() before the plot does not stop it. Fix the jitter inside the plot instead, for example with geom_jitter(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, seed = 2026)). Commit that first, then capture the reference.

title: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent
text:
Task 4: hand over the refactor


Issue 1: refactor only (15 minutes)


Goal: have the cloud agent move the plot into a function and review its pull request, so that you check its work before anything reaches main.
1. Open an issue and assign it to Copilot. On your fork, choose Issues → New issue. Use the text below, then set the assignee to Copilot:
Title: Move the mass-change plot into a function

Move the plot in scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R into a documented
function plot_mass_change(data) in scripts/functions/plot_functions.R. It
takes the tibble returned by load_voles(), which has no mass_change_g
column, so the function computes mass_post_g - mass_pre_g itself. It returns
the ggplot object.
Make explore_mass_change_plot.R call it and still save the figure.

Acceptance criteria:
- Do not add or change anything under tests/, data/ or .github/.
- The plot must be unchanged: same layers, same data, same order.
The agent works on its own branch. You can follow its session log from the pull request it opens, and stop or steer it there.
2. Review the pull request when it arrives.


Files changed: only scripts/functions/plot_functions.R and scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R. Anything else, especially under tests/ or .github/, should not merge.

Checks: workflows do not run on the agent’s pull requests until someone approves them. If the pull request shows Approve and run workflows, click it. Then r-checks must pass.

Your own run: in the Git pane, click Pull. Choose the agent’s copilot/… branch from the branch menu. Restart R, then run the script and the test suite. When the agent says “it works”, that is a claim; your run is the check.

3. Merge, or ask for a revision by commenting on the pull request.
4. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md (date; GitHub Copilot cloud agent and model; task; what you kept or changed), then commit.
You are done when the refactor is merged, with r-checks green and only the two expected files changed.
crumbs: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent

title: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent
text:
Task 5: hand over the test


Issue 2: the test, after issue 1 is merged (10 minutes)


Goal: have the agent write a test that compares its function with your reference, in a separate pull request, so that one misunderstanding cannot shape both the code and its check.
1. Open and assign the second issue only after the first is merged:
Title: Add a characterisation test for plot_mass_change()

Add tests/test_plot_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source
scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/plot_functions.R, and
compare ggplot2::layer_data(plot_mass_change(load_voles())) with
readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "mass_change_plot.rds")) using
expect_equal(). Build every path with here::here(): the tests run with tests/
as the working directory.

Acceptance criteria:
- Do not create, modify or regenerate anything under tests/fixtures/, and do
  not run tests/make_plot_reference.R.
- Run the tests and report the result in the pull request description.
2. Review it. CODEOWNERS asks for your review because the pull request touches tests/. As in Block 8, check that:

the test reads your .rds, calls the function, and does not type numbers in;
nothing under tests/fixtures/ changed;

r-checks passed.

Then run the test suite yourself.
3. Merge, and record it in docs/ai-log.md.
You are done when the test is merged, r-checks is green, and tests/fixtures/ is unchanged since your commit in Task 3.








NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand an asynchronous agent a task as an issue and accept its work only through a pull request, trusted because a review gate, an independent CI check and your own run stand between it and main.

Check: Files changed, r-checks, and the test against a reference you captured.

Reproduce: the agent and r-checks run with the versions in renv.lock, so a green run means the same everywhere.

Record: an AI-log line per pull request; the issues and pull requests are the record of what you asked for and what you accepted.

Check your understanding
Where do the cloud agent’s changes land?

In your local working directory, as it worksOn its own branch on GitHub, proposed as a pull request that you review before anything reaches mainDirectly on main, with an email to you afterwardsNowhere until you run it in your IDE

text:
Going further






TipCopilot code review on a pull request





You can also request Copilot as a reviewer on any pull request. Its comments appear on the changed lines, like a colleague’s. It reads the repository’s instruction files (.github/copilot-instructions.md, or AGENTS.md as in Block 4). Block 9’s review prompt sets a standard: the four Rs, the intended analysis, no praise, NEEDS HUMAN CHECK. To have Copilot apply it, first add those rules to .github/copilot-instructions.md. title: Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent
text:
Glossary




term
definition



branch protection
GitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.


CODEOWNERS
A GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review.


continuous integration
Automated checks, such as tests, that run on a server each time changes are pushed or a pull request is opened. In this course, GitHub Actions.


rung
One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 3, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
section: Activity 2: Install a skill and test it
text:
Activity 2: Install a skill and test it
If AGENTS.md is the list of rules on the lab wall, a skill is a standard operating procedure in the drawer. It is the written-down way to do one kind of task, such as making a publication figure, and the agent takes it out only when that task comes up. Only the skill’s name and one-line description sit in every conversation. The full procedure, and any scripts or templates beside it, load when you invoke the skill by name (/house-figures) or when the agent judges from the description that your request fits. So a skill can be long without costing anything in conversations that do not use it.
On disk, a skill is a folder that holds a SKILL.md file. The file starts with front matterThe block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill’s name and description, or a Quarto document’s options. between two lines of three dashes. The front matter gives a name and a description, and the description is the trigger. A skill described as “Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report, poster or paper” loads when it should; one described as “for plots” loads unpredictably. The body is the procedure.


A house figure style (15 minutes)


Goal: install a skill and grade a figure made with it against your instructor’s baseline made without it, so that you judge the skill by what it changes, not by its own report.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean (your AGENTS.md committed), Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab.
1. The baseline, made without the skill. Your instructor runs this prompt on screen, before the skill exists. You do not run it. Instructor: post the figure in the Zoom chat; learners grade against it in step 4.
Prompt (Claude Code, run by your instructor):
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_baseline.R.
2. Create the skill. In the R console, run usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md"). It creates and opens the file. Open the box below and copy the skill into the file, then save it. As you copy, read its description and six rules: step 4 grades three of them.






NoteThe house-figures skill: copy this into SKILL.md





---
name: house-figures
description: >-
  Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear
  in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a
  figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots.
---

# House figure style

## Rules
1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation
   (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar
   with error bars ("dynamite plot").
2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette
   (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same
   variable to point shape so the figure works without colour.
3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)".
4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12).
5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure.
6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a
   fitted model and asks for them.

## Before returning code
List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why.



Rules 2 and 4 differ on purpose from the defaults you used in the ggplot chapter, colorspace Dark2 and theme_project(). Okabe-Ito is also safe for colour-vision deficiency, and because it is distinctive, you can see at a glance in step 4 whether the skill was applied.
Copy it into .claude/skills/, where Claude Code reads it:

fs::dir_copy(
  here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"),
  here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)

Type /skills: house-figures should be listed.






NoteHow it works: two skill folders





.agents/skills/ holds the master copy. Other tools, such as Posit Assistant, read it directly. Claude Code reads .claude/skills/, so copy the folder again whenever you change the skill. The deny rules keep the agent’s edit tools out of .claude/, so you make the copy yourself. They do not cover .agents/skills/, so check the master copy in the Git pane too. On macOS or Linux you can link the folders instead of copying them: see Going further.
A skill suits a procedure, such as producing a publication figure or cleaning data against a codebook. It can hold scripts or templates beside SKILL.md. Its body sets out the procedure: when to use it, the steps, hard rules and a final check. The body loads only when the skill is used, so it can be longer than AGENTS.md. Invoking a skill by name (/skill-name) always works. Claude Code picks up a new skill in .claude/skills/ without a restart. If /skills does not list it, type /reload-skills. For a skill that writes files, disable-model-invocation: true in the front matter makes it run only when you invoke it by name.



3. With the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_house.R.
It may ask to run git status before it edits, because AGENTS.md asks it to check. That command only reads, so Yes is fine. Read the edit before you approve it. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. So if it asks to run the new script, choose No: you run it yourself next.
4. Grade it. Restart R (Session → Restart R). Run source(here::here("scripts", "fig_house.R")), then open the figure it saved in outputs/. Compare it with your instructor’s baseline on three rules you can see at a glance:


Rule
Baseline (no skill)
Your figure (with skill)



1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot




2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape




5. n per group shown





5. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md, as in Block 3. Name the skill and say what you kept or changed in its output. Commit the log with the skill (both folders) and scripts/fig_house.R.
You are done when the table is filled in from the figures you looked at, not from the agent’s list of rules it applied, and your log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if /skills does not list it, check that .claude/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md exists, and that its front matter starts and ends with three dashes. If no figure appears in outputs/, ask the agent to save it there with ggsave(), as AGENTS.md asks. Out of time? First commit or discard your changes in the Git pane, so that nothing blocks the switch. Then switch to checkpoint-skills.






TipStretch: test the trigger





Start a new conversation (/clear) and test the trigger. “Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm” should not load the skill. “Make a figure of metabolic_rate_post by treatment_arm for a poster” should. Or test rule 6: ask it to “add significance stars between the groups in scripts/fig_house.R” and see whether it declines. Either way, the grading in step 4 is what makes the output trustworthy, and you can repeat it on every figure.
Payoff. What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and would you use it for the next figure?











TipSkills in your own work





You wrote house-figures from a finished list of rules. In practice you rarely start from one. The usual route: work with the agent until an output is right, correcting it over several rounds. Then ask it to “turn what we just did into a skill in .agents/skills/<name>/”. Read the draft before you install it:

Remove details that applied to that one task only.
Check that the description says when to use the skill and when not to.
Check that nothing contradicts AGENTS.md or your other skills.

Then copy it to .claude/skills/, start a new conversation and grade the output, as in step 4. Next time, one request gets you to where those rounds of correction ended. Turn a conversation into a skill, in Going further, walks through it.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: state your conventions once, and package a procedure as a skill, trusted because the canary and tests/test_controls.R show the files are connected, and you grade the output rule by rule.

Check: a canary shows a file was loaded, not followed.

Reproduce: your AGENTS.md states the reproducibility rules; Blocks 7 and 8 check the agent kept to them.

Record: your log line from step 5.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Framing: tools, models and context
This block introduces the two words you will use all day, the three tools and how they differ, what a large language model is, and why its context window matters.
⏱ ~20 minutes: presentation, a short discussion and a quiz, while any set-up problems are sorted out.
Assistants and agents
Two words recur all day. An assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. is any AI tool that helps you write or understand code. An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. is an assistant that acts: it reads your project and, if you let it, edits files and runs commands. Claude Code and Posit Assistant are agents; a chat window that only answers is not. To see how one works inside, you build a small one yourself in Block 6: Build your own agent in R.
Three tools, and the models behind them
The course uses three tools. They differ in where you type, what they can read and what they may do. GitHub Copilot appears twice: in the editor, and as a cloud agent on GitHub.



Claude Code: the main tool all day


Type in the Terminal tab


it reads


Your project folder and the output of its own commands, but not your R console


and may


Edit files and run commands, asking first in Manual mode




Posit Assistant: the alternative in most blocks


Type in its chat pane in RStudio or Positron


it reads


Project files and your live R session, including the names and types of your objects


and may


Edit files and run R code in your session, as its mode allows




GitHub Copilot in the editor: self-study


Type code in a script


it reads


Your open files


and offers


Grey suggestions you accept with Tab or ignore




The Copilot cloud agent: self-study


Write a task on github.com


it reads


Your repository, on GitHub’s servers


and returns


A pull request for you to review



For each tool, read in order: where you type, what the tool reads, and what it may do. The more a tool reads and does, the more there is to check.


A tool is not a model. The tool decides where you type, what it can read and what it may do. It then sends your request, with the context it has gathered, to a large language modelA model trained on a large body of text, code included, that predicts the next fragment of text from what came before. Claude, GPT and Gemini are families of large language models; tools such as Claude Code, Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot send your requests to one., which writes the answer.


You type a request


into


The tool (Claude Code, Posit Assistant or Copilot), which adds the context it has read


and sends everything, over the internet, to


The model (for example Claude, GPT or Gemini), which writes the reply


The reply comes back through the tool, which shows it to you or asks you to approve an action. Claude is a family of models: Claude Code is one tool that uses them, and Posit Assistant and Copilot can use Claude models too.










Tool
Where you use it
Models it can use
In this course



Claude Code
The Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron
Anthropic’s Claude models
The main tool, in every block from Block 2


Posit Assistant
A chat pane inside RStudio or Positron
Models through Posit AI Pass, or your own provider key (for example, Claude models with an Anthropic API key)
The alternative in most blocks: see each block’s Using another tool callout


GitHub Copilot
Inline suggestions in the editor; the cloud agent on github.com
A choice of models, including Claude, GPT and Gemini
The two self-study pages only



You do not need strong opinions about which model is best. You only need to know that the choice exists and changes the output.
What is a large language model?
A large language model (LLM) predicts the next fragment of text from what came before. It has learnt from a large share of the public internet, code included. Every tool today is built on one. Models differ in code quality and in how often they invent functions that do not exist. If a model gives you consistently poor suggestions and your plan lets you switch, try another: switching is a cheap experiment.
Model and effort level. Two settings change what you get. The model is which LLM answers: larger models, such as Opus, are more capable and cost more per token; smaller ones, such as Sonnet and Haiku, are faster and cheaper. The effort levelHow much a model reasons before it answers. In Claude Code it runs from low to max; a higher level can help with hard problems, but it is slower and uses more tokens. sets how much the model thinks before it answers: higher effort can help with hard problems, but it is slower and uses more tokens. The quick reference shows how to change both. Whatever you use, record the model in your AI-use log.
Why the context window matters
An LLM has no memory between calls: each one starts with only what you supply, up to the limit of its context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.. That one fact explains the day. Instruction files and skills give the model context it would not otherwise have. They are only requests, so Block 5 adds controls that hold whether or not the model follows them, and tests check the result.
Remember: the model sees only what reaches its context window, and everything that reaches it has left your machine.
Discussion
Take three minutes, then post a short answer to each question in the Zoom chat:

What is one task you would like to hand to an agent by the end of the day, and how would you check it? Is there anything you would not delegate at all?
How do you use AI tools now: browser chat, IDE chat, a terminal agent?
Check your understanding
Your instruction file asks the agent never to edit data/raw/. Why does the course still add permission rules and tests?

Claude Code ignores AGENTS.md, so the instruction never reaches the modelAn instruction file only adds context the model may or may not follow; rules and tests hold whether or not the model follows itPermission rules make the model more accurate, so it follows the instruction more closelyTests stop the agent reading the raw data, so it never sees the files it might edit

True or false: a large language model has no memory between calls, so each interaction starts with only the context you supply. 
TRUE
FALSE
True or false: Claude models can be used only through Claude Code. 
TRUE
FALSE

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Permissions decide what the agent may do without asking, and what it may never do. In Claude Code they live in .claude/settings.json: a starting mode (Manual asks before every edit and command) and deny rules. A deny rule prevents, but only on the routes it names.

Hooks are your own code, which Claude Code runs at set moments: before a tool call, after an edit, before it stops. They suit “every time X happens, do Y”. A hook that blocks by matching text is a tripwire, not a wall. The workshop ships none, on purpose: see Do you need a hook?, below.

Version tracking lets you detect and undo. Git, through the Git pane, shows every change since your last commit, whatever made it, and reverts it. Claude Code’s own undo, /rewind, is quicker but covers only changes made with its edit tools. Tests and checksums detect what should not have changed.








NoteHow your workshop repository is guarded





Every guardrail below came with the template. You have been relying on them since Block 2.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Exercise 1: What protects what?


Match each asset to its guardrails (3 minutes)


Goal: for each thing worth protecting, find what in your repository prevents the damage and how you would notice it, so that you know which guardrail you are relying on before an agent works near it.
Your instructor posts the table. Use How your workshop repository is guarded, above, and answer in the Zoom chat, row by row: what prevents this here, and if it went wrong anyway, how would you notice?








Asset
What could go wrong
What prevents it here
How you would notice



data/raw/
Overwritten or “tidied” in place




tests/fixtures/
The reference regenerated by the code under test

A failing test edited until it passes





.claude/, .posit/

The agent’s own guardrails switched off





.Renviron, .env

Credentials read and sent to the model provider





The last two are easy to miss: the files that hold your controls are assets too.
You are done when the group has an answer for both columns in every row. Most “prevents” answers will be a deny rule; most “notice” answers will be “the Git pane would show it” or “a test would fail”.


Git detects only the changes since your last commit, so commit before an agent starts. Some controls prevent and some only detect; Exercise 2 shows which.






NoteThe layers of control, and how each fails













Layer
Example
What it does
How it fails



Instruction

AGENTS.md, a skill

Prevents

Sandbox

/sandbox (macOS, Linux, WSL2)

Not available on native Windows


Version control
The Git pane
Detects and undoes

Claude Code’s undo
/rewind

Tests and checksums
testthat, tools::md5sum()

Detects

Your repository’s AGENTS.md asks the agent to run git status before it edits anything, and to stop if there is no repository. That request helps, but your commit is the control.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
section: Set up guardrails in your own project
text:
Set up guardrails in your own project
Your workshop repository came with its guardrails. A new project of your own starts with none, so set them up before the agent’s first task. This is not covered live; it takes about 15 minutes.


Version tracking first. In the R console, run usethis::use_git(), then make a first commit. From then on, commit before every agent task. To undo, use /rewind for changes Claude made with its edit tools, and the Git pane for everything else.

Permissions. Download the starter settings.json below and save it as .claude/settings.json. Edit the paths to match your project. It starts in Manual mode and protects raw data, test references, the lockfile, credentials and itself. Add project-specific rules with /permissions.

Instructions. Copy the Version control section of your workshop AGENTS.md into your project’s instruction file.

Hooks, only if you need one. Work through Do you need a hook?, above. If you will let /init set hooks up, run it before step 2, because Edit(/.claude/**) refuses its writes to the settings.

Test it. Ask the agent to edit a protected file, and watch the rule refuse. Copy tests/test_controls.R and change its list of rules to yours. Delete the tests for the AGENTS.md canary and test_summary_functions.R, unless your project has them. Then commit.



 Download the starter settings.json








TipReference: the starter settings.json







{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}





Let Claude draft rules, never decide them. You can ask it to propose deny rules for a project, but read each one. A rule with a wrong path, such as a missing leading /, protects nothing and fails silently. Claude Code asks before every write to .claude/. The starter file’s Edit(/.claude/**) refuses such writes outright, so you install the rules yourself.
Protecting something new takes 30 seconds in /permissions. For confidential data, add the five habits in Block 3. Settings and hooks are code, so trust only repositories whose configuration you have read.

title: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation
text:
Two meanings of “variable”
dplyr’s own guide to programming (vignette("programming", package = "dplyr")) explains this by splitting the word “variable” in two:

An env-variable is a programming object that lives in your R session or in a function. You make one with <-, or it arrives as a function argument.
A data-variable is a column that lives inside a data frame.


df <- tibble::tibble(x = 1:3)   # df is an env-variable
df$x                            # x is a data-variable inside it

Inside filter(), mutate(), summarise() and friends, dplyr lets you type a data-variable as if it were an env-variable: summarise(mean = mean(body_mass_g)) finds the column. This is data masking: the data frame “masks” your session, so its columns are found first. It is what makes interactive dplyr so pleasant.
The trouble starts with indirection: the column name is no longer typed in the verb, but held in an env-variable, here the argument var. dplyr sees the name var, finds no column called var, and never discovers that var holds the column name you meant.
Think of the argument as an envelope with a column name written inside. dplyr reads the label on the envelope (var), not what is inside it. You need to tell it to open the envelope.






NoteWhy exactly does the error say body_mass_g?





dplyr looks for a column called var, does not find one, and so falls back to the function’s own objects, where it finds the argument var. R evaluates arguments lazily: only now does it work out what var holds, by evaluating the expression the user typed, body_mass_g. It evaluates that in the calling environment, your workspace, not inside the data frame. Your workspace has no object called body_mass_g, hence “object ‘body_mass_g’ not found”. The data mask was applied to the name var, never to the column name the user meant.
crumbs: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation

title: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation
