title: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation
text:
Two kinds of column argument
Column names are used in two different ways in the tidyverse:








Data masking
Tidy selection



What the column name does
Stands for the column’s values, which you compute with
Labels a column you want to pick



Typical code

filter(body_mass_g > 4000), mutate(kg = body_mass_g / 1000), summarise(m = mean(body_mass_g)), arrange(desc(body_mass_g)), aes(x = body_mass_g)


select(species, body_mass_g), select(starts_with("bill")), pivot_longer(cols = ends_with("_mm")), across(.cols = where(is.numeric)), .by = species



Helpers such as starts_with(), where()
No
Yes



To filter penguins by mass you compute body_mass_g > 4000 for every row: the values matter, so it is data masking. To select the mass column you compute nothing; only the name matters, so it is tidy selection.
How to tell, without memorising. Two quick tests:


Read the help page. In ?filter or ?select, each argument is labelled <data-masking> or <tidy-select>.

Ask what you could write there. If you could write body_mass_g + 1, it is data masking. If you could write bill_length_mm:body_mass_g or starts_with("bill"), it is tidy selection. (This test comes from R for Data Science, chapter 25.)

Either way, a bare column name passed through your function is embraced with { }. The two kinds differ only when the name arrives as a string, which is the next section.
Activity 2: identify the kind


Activity 2: identify the kind


For each call, choose whether the column reference is data masking, tidy selection, or both (in different arguments).


filter(penguins_clean, body_mass_g > 4000) 
data masking
tidy selection
both


select(penguins_clean, species, body_mass_g) 
data masking
tidy selection
both


mutate(penguins_clean, mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) 
data masking
tidy selection
both


pivot_longer(penguins_clean, cols = ends_with("_mm")) 
data masking
tidy selection
both


summarise(penguins_clean, mean(body_mass_g), .by = species) 
data masking
tidy selection
both


select(penguins_clean, starts_with("bill")) 
data masking
tidy selection
both


arrange(penguins_clean, desc(body_mass_g)) 
data masking
tidy selection
both


filter_out(penguins_clean, body_mass_g > 4000) 
data masking
tidy selection
both


summarise(penguins_clean, across(where(is.numeric), mean)) 
data masking
tidy selection
both






Explanations



Data masking. A comparison is computed for every row.

Tidy selection. Columns picked by name.

Data masking. A new value computed from existing values.

Tidy selection (the cols argument).

Both. mean(body_mass_g) is data masking; .by is tidy selection (it picks the grouping column by name).

Tidy selection. A helper picks by name pattern.

Data masking. Sorting by computed values.

Data masking. A comparison is computed for every row, as in filter().

Both. summarise() is data masking, and across() is used inside it, but across()’s .cols argument is tidy selection, so where() works there. across() is the bridge between the two kinds; Activity 4 uses it.
crumbs: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation

title: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation
section: When the name arrives as a string
text:
When the name arrives as a string
So far the column name arrived bare, as the user typed it. Often it arrives as a string instead: from a vector of names you loop over, a configuration file, or a Shiny input. { } is for bare names only. A string needs a different pattern, and here the two kinds of argument part ways:


Data masking: look the string up with the .data pronoun, .data[[var_name]].

Tidy selection: wrap the string, or a character vector of strings, in all_of().

The commonest reason for strings is a loop over column names, as in Block 4:

for (var in c("bill_length_mm", "flipper_length_mm")) {
  penguins_clean |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(.data[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), .by = species) |>
    print()
}
# # A tibble: 3 x 2
#   species    mean
#   <chr>     <dbl>
# 1 Adelie     38.8
# 2 Gentoo     47.5
# 3 Chinstrap  48.8
# # A tibble: 3 x 2
#   species    mean
#   <chr>     <dbl>
# 1 Adelie     190.
# 2 Gentoo     217.
# 3 Chinstrap  196.

In the envelope picture, .data[[var]] says: “this envelope holds a string; find the column with that name”. .data is not a data frame you can use elsewhere: it works only inside data-masking verbs.
The same idea, wrapped in a function:

summarise_by_string <- function(data, var_name) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(.data[[var_name]], na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}

summarise_by_string(penguins_clean, "body_mass_g")

Activity 3: fix the warning


Activity 3: fix the warning


This one runs, but not cleanly. Identify and fix the problem.

keep_columns <- function(data, cols) {
  data |> dplyr::select(cols)
}
keep_columns(penguins_clean, c("species", "body_mass_g"))
# Warning message:
# Using an external vector in selections was deprecated in tidyselect 1.1.0.
# ℹ Please use `all_of()` or `any_of()` instead.
#   # Was:
#   data %>% select(cols)
#
#   # Now:
#   data %>% select(all_of(cols))





Solution

It returns the right two columns, but only because tidyselect guesses that cols is an external character vector of names rather than a column called cols. That guess is ambiguous (if the data ever gained a column named cols, it would be selected instead) and is deprecated, so it warns today and may error in future. Say what you mean by wrapping the vector in all_of():

keep_columns <- function(data, cols) {
  data |> dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(cols))
}

If instead the function takes a bare name, embracing works: select({{ cols }}). The right tool depends on how the input arrives: bare ({ }) or as strings (all_of()).

Activity 4: predict the result


Activity 4: predict the result


Before running anything, predict what each call does: does it succeed, return the wrong answer, or error? Then explain why, using the envelope picture.

# (i) embracing a string
summarise_mean <- function(data, var) {
  data |> dplyr::summarise(mean = mean({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}
summarise_mean(penguins_clean, "body_mass_g")

# (ii) a string into a data-masking verb without .data
summarise_mean_str <- function(data, var_name) {
  data |> dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(var_name, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
}
summarise_mean_str(penguins_clean, "body_mass_g")





Solution

Both return the wrong answer, with only a warning: a column of NA.

{ } opens the envelope and finds the string "body_mass_g", not a column name. mean() then receives a single piece of text, and the mean of a piece of text is NA, with the warning “argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA”. Embracing is for bare names; a string needs .data[[ ]].
var_name is not embraced, so dplyr looks for a column called var_name, fails, and finds the argument, which holds the string "body_mass_g". It computes the mean of that string: NA again. Nothing told dplyr to treat the string as a column name; that is the job of .data[[var_name]].

The general lesson: passing the wrong kind of name to a data-masking verb rarely errors loudly. It often produces NA with at most a warning, which is more dangerous than an error. Match the pattern to how the name arrives.
crumbs: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation

title: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation
text:
The bridge: across()

Sometimes you need both kinds in one call: pick several columns, then compute with each. across() does exactly that. It is used inside a data-masking verb such as summarise() or mutate(), and its .cols argument is tidy selection, so all_of(), starts_with() and where() all work there.
Activity 5: the bridge


Activity 5: the bridge


Write mean_of_columns(data, cols) that takes a character vector of column names and returns the mean of each, grouped by species.




Solution


mean_of_columns <- function(data, cols) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(cols), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      .by = species
    )
}

mean_of_columns(penguins_clean, c("body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm"))
# # A tibble: 3 x 3
#   species   body_mass_g flipper_length_mm
#   <chr>           <dbl>             <dbl>
# 1 Adelie          3701.              190.
# 2 Gentoo          5076.              217.
# 3 Chinstrap       3733.              196.

The strings arrive in .cols, a tidy-selection argument, so they are wrapped in all_of(). The function \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) is then applied to each selected column. If the user should pass bare names or helpers instead, embrace the argument: across({{ cols }}, ...) accepts c(body_mass_g, bill_length_mm) or ends_with("_mm").
crumbs: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation

title: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation
text:
Naming the output columns
For output column names built from an argument, = is not enough: with = the name is used literally, so "{{ var }}_mean" = … makes a column called { var }_mean. The walrus operator := lets rlang fill in { var }, using glue-style name injection:

summarise_dynamic <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      "{{ var }}_mean" := mean({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      "{{ var }}_sd"   := sd({{ var }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      .by = species
    )
}

summarise_dynamic(penguins_clean, body_mass_g)
# # A tibble: 3 x 3
#   species   body_mass_g_mean body_mass_g_sd
#   <chr>                <dbl>          <dbl>
# 1 Adelie               3701.           459.
# 2 Gentoo               5076.           504.
# 3 Chinstrap            3733.           384.

Two things happen on the left of :=. "{{ var }}_mean" is glue-style injection, replacing { var } with the argument’s name; := is the assignment that lets rlang do that injection (with = the name is used literally). Both are needed. If the name is held in a string instead, use single braces: "{var_name}_mean" :=.
The same trick works for text that is not a column name, such as a plot title or axis label: rlang::englue("Mean of {{ var }}") returns the string "Mean of body_mass_g". The payoff uses it.
crumbs: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation

title: Block 5: Generalising functions with tidy evaluation
text:
The payoff: generalising the pipeline
Until now this block has practised on small, stand-alone functions. Now go back to the analysis you have been improving all day. Blocks 3 and 4 left two functions that hardcode the same pair of columns: make_scatter_plot() in R/functions/plotting_functions.R, and fit_model() in R/functions/modelling_functions.R.

make_scatter_plot <- function(data, sp) {
  data |>
    dplyr::filter(species == sp) |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    ggplot2::labs(title = sp, x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal()
}

fit_model <- function(data) {
  lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = data)
}

You generalise both, so that each works for any pair of columns:


Activity 7, the plot. aes() uses data masking, so this is the main pattern of the block, { }, plus englue() from Naming the output columns for the axis labels.

Activity 8, the model. lm() is not a tidyverse function, so { } does not work there. This activity shows what to do instead, and when to take column names as strings.

In both, the new arguments default to the columns the functions use now. Existing calls, including the Block 4 pipeline, keep working unchanged, and the characterisation test at the end of this section checks that they do. Edit each function in its file, then source() the file again.
Activity 7: generalise the plot


Activity 7: generalise the plot


Give make_scatter_plot() two new arguments, x and y, that take bare column names. Default them to flipper_length_mm and body_mass_g, so existing calls still work. Label the axes with the column names. Then plot bill depth against bill length for Gentoo penguins.
Hint: aes() uses data masking.




Solution


make_scatter_plot <- function(data, sp,
                              x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g) {
  data |>
    dplyr::filter(species == sp) |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes({{ x }}, {{ y }})) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = sp,
      x = rlang::englue("{{ x }}"),
      y = rlang::englue("{{ y }}")
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal()
}

make_scatter_plot(penguins_clean, "Adelie")                                 # as before
make_scatter_plot(penguins_clean, "Gentoo", bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)  # new

aes() uses data masking, so x and y are embraced, exactly as in summarise(). englue() turns the same arguments into text for the axis labels. Note that sp is not embraced: it is an ordinary value ("Adelie") compared with the species column, not a column name.

Activity 8: generalise the model


Activity 8: generalise the model


Now let fit_model() fit any response on any predictor, defaulting to body mass on flipper length. First, predict: does this work?

fit_model <- function(data,
                      response  = body_mass_g,
                      predictor = flipper_length_mm) {
  lm({{ response }} ~ {{ predictor }}, data = data)
}

Then find a version that does work. Hint: lm() is base R, not the tidyverse. How does base R already let you pass column names to lm() without evaluating them?




Solution

It does not work:

fit_model(penguins_clean)
# Error in eval(mf, parent.frame()) : object 'body_mass_g' not found

{ } is understood only by functions that use tidy evaluation: dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2’s aes(). lm() is not one of them, so to it { response } is just response wrapped in two pairs of braces, and the column name is never found.
Base R already has its own way to pass column names without evaluating them: the formula. So the simplest generalisation takes a formula:

fit_model <- function(data, formula = body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm) {
  lm(formula, data = data)
}

fit_model(penguins_clean)                                 # as before
fit_model(penguins_clean, bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm) # new

No tidy evaluation at all. The lesson: before reaching for { }, check whether the function you are calling is a tidyverse function. If it is not, it usually has its own way of taking column names.
When the names come from a vector. To fit the same model to several responses, as you iterated in Block 4, take the names as strings and build the formula with base R’s reformulate():

fit_model <- function(data,
                      response  = "body_mass_g",
                      predictor = "flipper_length_mm") {
  lm(reformulate(predictor, response = response), data = data)
}

c("body_mass_g", "bill_length_mm") |>
  purrr::set_names() |>
  purrr::map(\(r) fit_model(penguins_clean, r)) |>
  purrr::map(broom::tidy) |>
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "response")
# # A tibble: 4 x 6
#   response       term               estimate std.error statistic   p.value
#   <chr>          <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
# 1 body_mass_g    (Intercept)       -5781.     306.        -18.9  5.59e- 55
# 2 body_mass_g    flipper_length_mm    49.7      1.52       32.7  4.37e-107
# 3 bill_length_mm (Intercept)          -7.26     3.20       -2.27 2.38e-  2
# 4 bill_length_mm flipper_length_mm     0.255    0.0159     16.0  1.74e- 43

predictor can also be a vector, such as c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"), for a model with two predictors. Strings are the right choice whenever the names come from a vector, a loop or a file: the same reason you met .data[[ ]] and all_of().







TipOptional: bare names for lm()





If you want fit_model(penguins_clean, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) with bare names, you must inject the names into the call yourself, with rlang:

fit_model <- function(data,
                      response  = body_mass_g,
                      predictor = flipper_length_mm) {
  rlang::inject(
    lm(!!rlang::ensym(response) ~ !!rlang::ensym(predictor), data = data)
  )
}

rlang::ensym() captures the bare name the user typed, and !! inside rlang::inject() places it into the formula before lm() sees it. This works, but it is the kind of rlang machinery that most code never needs; the formula and string versions above are simpler to read and to test.



When you change a function’s interface, pin the old behaviour down first with a characterisation test, then confirm the change preserves it. Both versions of fit_model() above pass this test with their defaults:

test_that("fit_model defaults reproduce previous behaviour", {
  m_old <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm,
              data = test_data |> dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie"))
  m_new <- fit_model(test_data |> dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie"))
  expect_equal(coef(m_old), coef(m_new))
})







NoteThe four patterns, on one card










How the column name arrives
Into data masking
Into tidy selection



Bare name
{ var }
{ var }


String
.data[[var]]
all_of(var)


Character vector
across(all_of(vars), f)
all_of(vars)


New output name

"{{ var }}_mean" := or "{var_name}_mean" :=

—





Which kind of argument? Check the help page for <data-masking> or <tidy-select>; or ask whether you could write x + 1 there (data masking) or starts_with("x") (tidy selection).

Not a tidyverse function? { } does nothing there. Look for its own way of taking column names, such as a formula for lm().

rlang has more machinery (enquo(), !!, enquos(), !!!), but most code never needs it.








Note



Where this leaves us. The analysis that began Block 3 as three copy-pasted blocks is now a set of small, tested functions, applied to every group by one pipeline, with no hardcoded columns: make_scatter_plot() and fit_model() take whichever columns you name. Day 2 asks whether someone else could rerun it: reproducibility and code review.

title: Advancing in R
text:
Which penguins?
Most chapters use the Palmer penguins data, but not always from the same place. Each chapter says which version it uses; this table puts them side by side.








In the code
Where it comes from
Column names look like
Used in



palmerpenguins::penguins
The palmerpenguins package: a ready-cleaned table

bill_length_mm, body_mass_g

Day 3 (as penguins_complete), Quarto, GitHub


palmerpenguins::penguins_raw
The same package: the data as first recorded

Culmen Length (mm), Body Mass (g)

Day 1: you save it as data/raw/penguins_raw.csv, standing in for a file you would receive


penguins_clean
You build it on Day 1, from data/raw/penguins_raw.csv


bill_length_mm, body_mass_g, species as "Adelie"

Day 1, Blocks 2 to 5



penguins, loaded from files/chapter5.RData or files/chapter5.RDS

A download: a cleaned copy made earlier

culmen_length_mm, body_mass_g

The appendices on tables (gt) and ggplot









WarningSince R 4.5, base R has its own penguins



It has different column names: bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len and body_mass. If you use penguins without first running library(palmerpenguins), R 4.5 and later quietly give you that version, and code that expects body_mass_g stops with “object ‘body_mass_g’ not found”. On R 4.3 or 4.4 you get “object ‘penguins’ not found” instead.
So always run library(palmerpenguins) first, or write palmerpenguins::penguins in full. Don’t use data(penguins): without the package loaded, it silently loads base R’s version.

title: Block 1: Project-based workflows
section: Save the raw data into your project
text:
Save the raw data into your project
The palmerpenguins package ships the data in two versions: penguins, a ready-cleaned table, and penguins_raw, the data as first recorded, with the original column names such as Culmen Length (mm). Save the raw version into data/raw/ now. It stands in for a file you would receive from the people who collected the data. From here on, Day 1 reads this file, never the package.

library(here)

readr::write_csv(
  palmerpenguins::penguins_raw,
  here("data", "raw", "penguins_raw.csv")
)

You write this file once. After that, data/raw/ is read-only: your code reads it and never changes it. The here() lines and the de-path solution above now run in your project. Other chapters use other versions of the same data; Which penguins? on the Overview page lists them.

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Exercise: spot it
We’ll go through the tabs one at a time. Each plot hides one odd point among 80. Count the seconds it takes you to find it, and note them down; don’t click ahead to the next tab. After the third tab, post your three times in Slack (for example 1, 3, 14).


Colour
Shape
Colour and shape, mixed up


































Compare the times in Slack: the colour target is found almost instantly, the shape target a moment later. In the third tab the odd point is the only grey triangle, and no single feature gives it away, so everyone has to check points one by one. This is the cost of making readers combine features (a conjunction search).

title: Block 1: Foundations and graph crimes
text:
Exercise: estimate the value
Each round shows five values, and A is always the same. For each round, estimate what percentage of A is B, write it down, then check it in the box. Do one round at a time, without looking at the next tab. When you’ve done all four, post your four estimates in Slack and say which round was hardest.


Round 1
Round 2
Round 3
Round 4











B is what % of A?  (within 5 points counts)










B is what % of A?  (from here on, within 10 points counts)










B is what % of A? 










B is what % of A?  (use the key: white is 0, black is 100)





What just happened?

The answers were 62%, 38%, 45% and 71%. Look back at Slack: Round 1 guesses are usually tight, and they spread out with each round after that. In Round 3 most guesses are too high, because we underestimate differences in area: the small circle looks closer in size to the big one than it really is. In Round 4, even with a key, the shades are hard to place.
You have just played a version of Cleveland and McGill’s (1984) experiment (they tested bars and pie slices; Rounds 3 and 4 go further). People read the same ratio most accurately as position on a common scale, then length, angle, area, and last shading and colour saturation. Mackinlay (1986) extended the ranking to categorical data: position is still best, but colour hue rises to second. Shape is weaker but useful as a redundant cue.

title: Block 4: Extensions in action
text:
Capstone exercise: recreate this figure
Time to put the whole block together on data you have not seen. CO2 is built into R: CO2 uptake by 12 grass plants from Quebec and Mississippi, half of them chilled overnight, each measured at seven CO2 concentrations. Here is your target:










Recreate the figure: how far can you get? (15 minutes)


Work through the three levels in order, and post in Slack each time you finish one (level 1, level 2, level 3) with a screenshot. Stuck? Post your error message in Slack, and help others with theirs if you can. Each level has a solution below; use it to check your figure, or to unblock yourself and move on.


Level 1: panel B. Raw points for each Treatment, dodged by Type, with a median bar, in the two Type colours. Hint: position_jitterdodge() and stat_summary(geom = "crossbar").

Level 2: panel A. One line per plant, colour by Type, linetype by Treatment, and direct labels instead of a colour legend. Hint: group = Plant, and ggrepel on a small data frame of line ends.

Level 3: the full figure. Both panels side by side (A twice as wide), tagged A and B, with the coloured rich-text title and proper sub/superscripts in the axis titles. Hint: patchwork, plot_annotation() and ggtext::element_markdown().





Solution: level 1


co2_pal <- c(Quebec = "#1B9E77", Mississippi = "#D95F02")

CO2 |>
  ggplot(aes(Treatment, uptake, colour = Type)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6),
             alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.25,
               position = position_dodge(0.6), linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)




Solution: levels 2 and 3

The full code for the target figure. Level 2 is target_a; level 3 adds the composition at the end.

co2_ends <- CO2 |>
  filter(conc == max(conc)) |>
  summarise(uptake = mean(uptake), .by = Type) |>
  mutate(conc = 1000)

target_a <- CO2 |>
  ggplot(aes(conc, uptake, colour = Type, group = Plant, linetype = Treatment)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = co2_ends, aes(conc, uptake, label = Type, colour = Type),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, nudge_x = 80, direction = "y", hjust = 0,
    fontface = "bold", segment.colour = NA) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1250), breaks = seq(0, 1000, 250)) +
  labs(x = "Ambient CO<sub>2</sub> (mL L<sup>-1</sup>)",
       y = "CO<sub>2</sub> uptake (µmol m<sup>-2</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>)",
       linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
        axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(),
        legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

target_b <- CO2 |>
  ggplot(aes(Treatment, uptake, colour = Type)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6),
             alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.25,
               position = position_dodge(0.6), linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

(target_a + target_b + plot_layout(widths = c(2, 1))) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = "A",
    title = "Chilling cuts CO<sub>2</sub> uptake in <span style='color:#D95F02'>**Mississippi**</span> grasses far more than in <span style='color:#1B9E77'>**Quebec**</span> ones",
    theme = theme(plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 13)))

title: Block 6: Writing figure legends
text:
Exercise: legend triage
We’ll put each fragment on screen in turn. Post your verdict in Slack, then choose it below to see if you agree.


“Body mass of three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing

Good. A neutral descriptive sentence: what is shown (body mass), for whom (three species) and where, without claiming a result.



“Gentoo penguins are heavier.”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing

A result, not a description. The first element describes what the figure shows; the conclusion belongs in the text.



“n = 342.”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing

Too vague. It gives only the total. The reader needs the sample size for each group, the data source and any exclusions.



“Shows a raincloud plot.”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing

Names the plot but defines nothing. It tells the reader what kind of plot it is, but not what the cloud, the box or the points mean.



“ANOVA showed differences (p < 0.05).”

Good
Bad: a result, not a description
Bad: too vague or missing details
Bad: names the plot but defines nothing

Too vague. It names a test, but gives no test statistic, no degrees of freedom and only a threshold rather than the p-value.

title: Block 6: Writing figure legends
text:
Exercise: legend repair









Figure 1. Gentoo penguins are heavier. Data from a survey (n = 342). Species differed significantly (p < 0.05). Shows a raincloud plot.



Exercise: legend repair (10 minutes)


The legend above breaks every rule. Rewrite it as a four-element legend for this figure.
What you need to know:

The data are body masses from the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020). Penguins with no recorded body mass were excluded.
A one-way ANOVA of body mass on species was fitted, with Tukey-adjusted pairwise contrasts.
Work out the sample sizes and the ANOVA result yourself:


legend_data <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>
  tidyr::drop_na(body_mass_g)

count(legend_data, species)

anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = legend_data))

Post your legend in Slack, then check it against the four elements: is each one present and correct, and does it define every visual layer (cloud, box, points)? Compare yours with the model answer below. We’ll read out a couple and talk through the differences.




Solution: a four-element legend


Figure 1. Body mass (g) of three penguin species (Pygoscelis adeliae, P. antarcticus and P. papua) in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. Data are from the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020); penguins with no recorded body mass were excluded, giving 151 Adelie, 68 Chinstrap and 123 Gentoo individuals. A one-way ANOVA showed that body mass differed between species (F(2, 339) = 343.6, p < 0.001); pairwise contrasts were Tukey-adjusted. The shaded region shows a kernel density estimate of each distribution; the box shows the interquartile range with the median as a horizontal line; points are individual penguins, jittered horizontally.

The four elements are, in order: the descriptive sentence; the source, exclusions and sample sizes; the test and its result; and the definitions of the cloud, box and points. Note that the legend still describes: the conclusion (“Gentoo are heavier”) belongs in the main text or, for a talk or poster, in an explanatory title (Block 2).







Note



In the Quarto session you will put a legend like this into a figure’s fig-cap option, so the caption travels with the figure and can be cross-referenced in your text.
